items.title: No Retreat, No Add Vance
items.content_text:
No Retreat, No Add Vance

By Michael Every of Rabobank

It’s Friday the 13th, traditionally a day when bad things happen - so far we have bad omens; not just a spike in JGB and Australian bond yields this morning, but that Microsoft Outlook and Teams are both down, so I don’t know who will be able to read this.

The US has decided it can’t reach a deal to end the Ukraine war without Europe, yet the Ukrainian press says, ‘Europe wants a seat at the table with Russia. It can't agree on who gets it.’

There seems little chance of any agreement being struck regardless of who gets that hot seat. Putin stated deploying foreign peacekeeping troops to Ukraine after a peace agreement is "absolutely unacceptable" and would be a continuation of war, implying risks of a military conflict with Moscow. Europe is preparing those peacekeepers now.

Worse, Russia’s demands re: security architecture are obviously unacceptable to Europe. Moscow wants limits on future NATO expansion, a rollback of NATO forces from post-1997 members, restrictions on military exercises near Russia's borders, and a ‘sphere of Influence’ granting it effective ‘Finlandising’ vetoes over the sovereignty, foreign policy, and defence choices of neighbouring EU, European, and NATO nations.

That only seems to leave escalation, the questions being how soon and to what level.

In the Middle East, things look little better. Yemen's Houthis attacked a pumping station on Saudi Arabia's East-West oil pipeline again, underlining that key energy infrastructure remains a target – yet oil doesn’t seem too excited about all the above yet with Brent at $95 at time of writing. Indeed, some see the market having adapted to the level of physical disruption in Hormuz. A former Iranian regime journalist claims the UAE is now buying Gulf oil at a $30 discount, then shuttling it via Oman for large enough profits to offset the security costs. As such, the implication is we would need to see far more aggressive Iranian military actions against shipping and the Saudis (via the Houthis) to choke crude flows again, which would then invite a US military response in turn. In short, things are perhaps stable if still uncomfortable…. but for how long?

Trump said no deal is needed with Iran now and shut-down Vice-President Vance negotiations with Tehran. This was a clear public put-down of Vance, widely seen to have started to use the unpopular Iran War as a 2028 election issue favouring himself, as well as to Iran. While Trump said Gulf allies had urged him to pause Iran strikes, which he has agreed to for now, he added he’d renew military strikes against Iran “without hesitation” if needed – and would consider it a defeat if the Iranian regime were still in power by end of his term. That kind of threat is where things can really escalate; so are reports Iran may quit the Nuclear Non-Proliferation Treaty, openly showing it aims to develop a nuclear weapon.

In Israel, caretaker PM Netanyahu and PM candidate Eisenkot held their first security briefing, the latter reportedly told that the IDF sees no urgent need to strike Iran; then again, another report from Israel’s Kan news says the US has informed the IDF to prepare for war ahead.

If there are no negotiations, regime-change aspirations, and military and nuclear preparations, it seems we are heading for escalation – the only questions being when and to what extent.

Nvidia’s CEO Huang resigned, as news of a third affair surfaced, seeing headlines such as: ‘I’m a Piece of Sh--: Jensen Huang’s Last Hours as Nvidia’s CEO’; ‘Jensen Huang’s Exit Will Test AI’s Stocks, and Great-Man Theory’; ‘Nvidia Shareholders Won’t Miss Jensen Huang for Long’; and ‘Hire Tim Cook to lead Nvidia, Trump says.’ Yet key point is that Huang’s departure may signal tighter US controls on AI chip exports to China – with unpredictable consequences.

That’s as US Treasury Secretary Bessent claimed that the recent cyber attack on 700 French industrial fridges, which Paris said was carried out by Iran, used Chinese AI to do so – though that may just be Bessent trying to increase the pressure on Commerce Secretary Lutnick, who is reportedly fighting for his job.

What kind of post-Huang escalation could we see between the US and China?

In more traditional geopolitics, Hong Kong’s South China Morning Post (SCMP) notes in parallel, ‘As Japan looks to strengthen defences and security strategy, analysts warn of escalation.’ There is certainly a lot of it about.

Meanwhile, like Friday the 13th, which has now had 12 iterations, the geopolitics/geoeconomics Great Game continues in its own regional takes.

In the Americas, the Wall Street Journal notes that ‘The US Cut Cuba Off From the World’s Oil. Now It Runs on American Fuel’, and that the ‘US Collected $12 Billion in Venezuelan Oil Sales, Returning Nearly All of It’, while the SCMP says, ‘US invests in Peru’s Callao as port battle with China’s Chancay megaport continues.’

In Europe, Mercedes-Benz is halting new investment in its German plants and considering closures in the face of Chinese competition; and UK PM Burnham said he will discuss “problem” Chinese imports in the final days of planned Brexit reset talks with the EU, showing he still may not have decided who side of which tariff, or rare earth, wall he wants to be on.

France also announced an €8.7bn 10-year drive to boost ‘food sovereignty’ by reviving its agricultural industries. This can’t neomercantilism because it wasn’t drawn up in the charming medieval market town of Neomercantile, so it’s just sparkling economic statecraft.

items.title: Most Americans, Including Republicans, Want Congress To Pass Legislation To End Iran War; New Poll Finds
items.content_text:
Most Americans, Including Republicans, Want Congress To Pass Legislation To End Iran War; New Poll Finds

Authored by Dave DeCamp via Antiwar.com,

A new poll from Reuters/Ipsos has found that a majority of US adults, including the majority of Republicans, want Congress to pass legislation to end the Iran war, a conflict that's been extremely unpopular among the American people.

The poll asked if respondents would support or oppose the incoming Democrat-led Congress passing legislation to end the Iran war, and 71%, including 51% of Republicans, said they would support the effort.

The poll was conducted in the days following the midterm elections, which saw a major Republican defeat, and the war and the increase in the cost of living as a result of it were identified as the major factors in the Democrats' victory.

Both Vice President JD Vance and President Trump have acknowledged that the war cost the GOP the midterms, though Trump continues to defend his decision to launch it and continues to escalate the ongoing blockade and sanctions campaign against the Islamic Republic.

The current Congress has already passed a War Powers Resolution directing President Trump to end the war, but it's been ignored by the administration.

Democratic leadership has threatened to use the "power of the purse" to end the war by potentially blocking funding for the federal government until the conflict ends. The issue could become a major battle before the new Congress is sworn in, as lawmakers must pass a continuing resolution by December 11 to keep the government funded.

Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent joined CNBC earlier this morning to describe why the Secret Service has relocated him from his Washington, DC, home following Iranian death threats. There was no word on whether these new threats were connected to a plot reported in 2024 to kill then-President-elect Donald Trump and some of his closest allies.

"They have initiated death threats against me," Bessent said during a CNBC Squawk Box interview this morning. "I'm not going to be cowed."

Bessent continued, "You know what I got to say, Joe, is F the Iranian leadership. I'm not going to be cowed. They have initiated death threats against me," adding, "Why am I going to be afraid when our, the brave military personnel in the Gulf, President Trump, constantly receive death threats?"

Bessent described his "Operation Economic Outcast" sanctions campaign against Tehran as working and suggested its effectiveness was likely why Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps would be targeting him on US soil.

Bessent bashed The Wall Street Journal for publishing a photograph of his Georgetown house that he said could be geolocated. He said his team asked the outlet's editor to withhold his home's location, but the newspaper published it anyway.

"Highly irresponsible and dangerous, and things like that have to stop," he said.

The IRGC's plotting to kill Trump and his closest allies dates back to his first administration, when the US military killed Qasem Soleimani, then commander of the IRGC's Quds Force.

items.title: Dem Lawmakers Launch New Probe Of RFK Jr.
items.content_text:
Dem Lawmakers Launch New Probe Of RFK Jr.

Authored by Zachary Stieber via The Epoch Times,

Democratic lawmakers have begun new probes into Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr., including whether he lied to Congress.

One investigation looks into Kennedy's testimony during confirmation hearings in 2025 when he told senators that a trip he took to Samoa had "nothing to do with vaccines."

Lawmakers cited recent media reports that showed Kennedy writing in 2019, the year of the trip, to the prime minister of Samoa, saying that deaths associated with the measles, mumps, rubella (MMR) vaccine may have stemmed from the shot and proposing that his team conduct a "detailed health informatics assessment in Samoa of what happened with your MMR vaccines."

While in Samoa, Kennedy met with activists who have spoken out against immunizations, according to the reports.

"Evidence thus suggests that Kennedy's 2019 trip to Samoa was focused, in whole or in part, on vaccines," Sen. Ron Wyden (D-Ore.), the top Democrat on the Senate Finance Committee, and Sen. Angela Alsobrooks (D-Md.), a member of the Senate Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions, wrote in a letter on Nov. 11.

They said they intend to hold Kennedy "accountable for any false statements made to Congress, a crime that undermines the Senate's ability to fulfill its constitutional duties."

The letter was sent to the general counsel of Children's Health Defense, a nonprofit Kennedy headed before he ran for president and became health secretary. It requested documents related to Kennedy traveling to Samoa, documents related to meetings between Samoan government officials and Children's Health Defense employees, and documents related to Kennedy's Senate confirmation process.

Children's Health Defense did not respond to a request for comment by publication time.

The other investigation concerns gifts given to Kennedy by Gavin de Becker, a former donor to Kennedy's presidential campaign, including flights and a stay at a property owned by de Becker.

"Federal ethics rules clearly state that Executive Branch officials may not accept gifts from any 'prohibited source,'" Wyden and Alsobrooks told Kennedy in a missive dated Nov. 10. "Prohibited sources include anyone who 'conducts activities regulated by the employee's agency' or who 'has interests that may be substantially affected by the performance or nonperformance of the employee's official duties.' It seems abundantly clear that Mr. de Becker is a prohibited source and that you are not permitted to accept gifts from him while you serve as Secretary."

De Becker has promoted ketamine, a therapy being reviewed by Kennedy's agency, and published a book in 2025 that promotes many of the same theories about vaccines that Kennedy has, the senators said.

They asked for details of Kennedy's relationship with de Becker, how long Kennedy stayed at de Becker's home, the purpose of trips he reportedly took with de Becker, and whether the men had ever discussed vaccines or ketamine.

De Becker declined to comment. The Department of Health and Human Services did not respond to a request for comment by the time of publication. A department spokesperson told The Associated Press, which first reported on the letter to the prime minister of Samoa, that Kennedy's visit to Samoa was unrelated to vaccines and that "any claim or insinuation based on these letters that Secretary Kennedy lied under oath or to Congress is not only false but outright defamatory."

Kennedy was not asked about the developments during a press conference in Washington on Thursday.

Alsobrooks and some other lawmakers have recently called on Kennedy to resign or be fired, pointing to growing outbreaks of measles and other health issues they say officials have failed to control under his watch. Democrats are set to gain control of Congress in early 2027, which comes with subpoena power, after winning a number of races in the midterms.

Kennedy has not appeared concerned, telling supporters on Nov. 9 that with the help of new White House chief of staff Stephen Miller, he expects major reforms that he has not yet been able to enact.

"The Senate no longer has any leverage over me, and that's a big deal," Kennedy said. "And then we have Steve Miller in, who's a friend of our movement, and I don't think anything is going to get in our way now."

items.title: Fresh Off Turning Down Trump, Dana White Finds Himself In A Fight With... 'Power Spank'
items.content_text:
Fresh Off Turning Down Trump, Dana White Finds Himself In A Fight With... 'Power Spank'

Power Slap, the slap-fighting league co-owned by UFC CEO Dana White, has sent a cease-and-desist letter demanding that Lingerie Fighting Championships stop using the name "Power Spank" - the lingerie promotion's parody in which women take turns slapping each other on the backside instead of the face.

The fight went public on Nov. 10, a day after White stood at the White House briefing room podium and turned down the press secretary job President Trump had offered him: "No, I do not want to be in politics."

LFC, a Las Vegas-based promotion, announced on X that it had received the letter from counsel for Schiaffo LLC, the company that does business as Power Slap. 

"We're not backing down," the promotion wrote.

"We respect Power Slap and its founders, but we will not be bullied into abandoning protected speech," LFC CEO Shaun Donnelly said in a statement.

LFC's case is that Power Spank is a deliberate parody, protected speech under the First Amendment, and that no reasonable viewer would think Power Slap made, sponsored or endorsed it. Donnelly also pitched his version as the safer one.

"Power Spank is our answer: same energy, same theatrics, none of the brain damage," Donnelly said.

 "And let's be honest, a spank is a lot more fun to watch than a slap."

In both formats, competitors take turns landing blows until one is knocked out or gives up, and neither league lets the one on the receiving end defend herself or soften the hit. Power Spank is women-only, and its competitors fight in lingerie.

With no lawsuit filed, LFC says Power Spank will keep opening its US events while it weighs its options with legal counsel, and it has no plans to change its programming.

White's week started with Trump's Truth Social post on Nov. 7, which, as we reported, announced that "the Great Dana White, a violent Fighter and Warrior" had been offered the press secretary job, with a plea attached: "Dana, please take the job!" Trump later said he had been kidding, and when White took the podium on Monday, the president warned reporters that "he's going to beat the hell out of you."

White has since told TMZ that the trip was mainly about getting Trump's signature on a one-of-one Topps trading card commemorating the UFC Freedom 250 event on the White House South Lawn in June.

Donnelly says LFC will take the fight as far as it needs to: "We will defend our right, and the right of every American, to free speech, and if that takes us to the Supreme Court, we are prepared to go."

items.title: 'Speechless At The Dysfunction': Ebola 'Out Of Control' In Congo As Deaths Top 5,400
items.content_text:
'Speechless At The Dysfunction': Ebola 'Out Of Control' In Congo As Deaths Top 5,400

Authored by Victoria Friedman via The Epoch Times,

Congo's Ebola outbreak remains out of control six months into the response, Médecins Sans Frontières (MSF) has said, with there being a disconnect between the resources available and what is actually reaching patients, communities, and medics.

MSF, also known as Doctors Without Borders, said on Thursday that urgent action is needed to ensure resources are directed to where they are needed most, and that critical shortcomings were undermining efforts to contain the outbreak and save lives.

The Ebola outbreak was declared in DRC six months ago.

Our teams see a troubling disconnect between the considerable resources mobilised for the response and the resources reaching communities. Without urgent action, we risk playing catch-up for years.https://t.co/jqA2Q0Ht2v

— MSF International (@MSF) November 12, 2026

"Despite the vast amounts of money provided for the response, many frontline responders are left trying to contain the outbreak with empty hands and empty pockets," said Dr. Javid Abdelmoneim, the president of MSF International.

"Our teams are often left speechless by the dysfunctions they witness in many areas. Six months into the response, this situation is simply unacceptable."

According to a Nov. 11 statement from Congo's National Institute of Public Health, there have been 11,114 confirmed cases and 5,433 deaths as a result of Ebola, representing a case fatality rate of 48.9 percent.

Some of the problems highlighted by MSF include that response staff are untrained and unpaid, ambulances do not have any fuel, and healthcare staff are left without the supplies or technical support they need to handle suspected cases.

"One of our greatest concerns is the persistent failure of the epidemiological surveillance system, a cornerstone of any Ebola response," the statement said. "Despite the resources officially allocated to this critical activity, surveillance remains deeply problematic, with entire areas poorly covered or even completely neglected."

The current outbreak is caused by the rare Bundibugyo ebolavirus and was detected in mid-May in Congo, which has dealt with more than a dozen Ebola outbreaks in the past.

It has become the deadliest outbreak in Congo's history, surpassing the 2018-2020 epidemic, in which 2,299 people died.

Across Africa, this epidemic is now second only to the 2014-2016 West African outbreak, which infected at least 28,600 people and killed more than 11,000 across Guinea, Liberia, and Sierra Leone.

MSF acknowledged that in the six months since the start of the outbreak, authorities in Congo and international partners have achieved some tangible results, including in the expansion of isolation and treatment units and diagnostic capability. However, the shortcomings "remain profound and largely unaddressed, despite being widely acknowledged," the statement said.

The Epoch Times contacted the government of Congo and the World Health Organization (WHO) for comment, but did not receive responses by the time of publication.

Lack of Security Is an Obstacle

WHO Director-General Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus acknowledged issues such as safety and frontline worker pay delays in his opening remarks to a member state briefing on the outbreak on Nov. 11 in Geneva.

"Insecurity is now one of the greatest obstacles to the response," Tedros said, listing a number of attacks against civilians, healthcare workers, and health facilities.

He said that during an attack in Cantine-Aloya last week, 66 civilians were killed, including three healthcare workers.

Other incidents included gunfire near an Ebola treatment center, an arson attempt on a treatment center, and threats against healthcare workers.

"These incidents restrict humanitarian access, disrupt operations, make it harder to reach communities quickly, and give the virus an advantage," the WHO chief said.

Dr. Andrew Peter Obat, the regional Ebola coordinator for the International Organization for Migration (IOM), an intergovernmental organization within the U.N. migration agency, said that since the outbreak, the IOM has conducted 55 million screenings in Congo and 11 other neighboring countries.

"IOM is expanding our screening into the informal areas based on the data that we are seeing," Obat said in a Nov. 11 post on X. "And we must also involve the community and make sure that the mobility corridors and other crossing points are included in the response, so that we mitigate the cross border infection."

items.title: First-Take On Almonty Earnings: "Sangdong Ramping, With First Cargo Loaded"
items.content_text:
First-Take On Almonty Earnings: "Sangdong Ramping, With First Cargo Loaded"

Almonty Industries, a leading supplier of conflict-free tungsten to Western markets, reported third-quarter earnings below Wall Street expectations, but Bank of America analysts describe initial shipments from its Sangdong mine in South Korea as "ramping up well" and the first cargo loaded. 

BofA metals and mining analyst Lawson Winder wrote in a note on Friday morning that while Almonty reported third-quarter earnings below forecasts, it delivered "substantial earnings improvement QoQ and YoY."

Almonty's flagship Sangdong Tungsten Mine in South Korea is seen as one of the world's largest and highest-grade tungsten deposits. Once fully operational, it is expected to account for over 80% of global tungsten production outside China, addressing the critical supply shortage in the West and supporting the upcoming rearmament supercycle. 

Winder said work on Sangdong's second phase is underway, equipment has been ordered, and construction is scheduled to be completed in 2027. He noted that more than 90% of first-phase production is already contracted, providing a solid revenue outlook as the mine ramps up into next year.

"This and a strong balance sheet further de-risks the Sangdong project and positions the company well to execute its growth plans," the analyst said, adding, "ALM has been active on its share buyback program through to this quarter. We maintain our Buy rating given ALM's strong volume growth, relatively low-cost structure, and a solid balance sheet."

He described Almonty as one of two publicly traded Western producers and the only US-listed company in that group, offering investors exposure to elevated tungsten prices and efforts to diversify the West's critical material supply chains away from China.

Winder added more color on the earnings:

Q3 EBITDA below BofAe, but first deliveries now loaded 

ALM reported Q3'26 adjusted EBITDA of C$14.6 million (m), below BofAe at C$49.4m and Bloomberg (BBG) / Visible Alpha (VA) consensus at $42.9m/C$33.7m. The miss vs BofAe was driven by lower Panasqueira sales (lower grade and timing), higher G&A expenses and the deferral of commercial sales from Sangdong to Q4. While Sangdong achieved concentrate production in September, the first shipment was loaded at the port subsequent to quarter end. Despite lower-than-expected sales and higher royalties, Panasqueira generated a 62% EBITDA margin in Q3 (benefitting of strong tungsten pricing). Per ALM, the Portuguese government intends to reduce the royalty rate to 4.0% (from 19.7%), retroactive from the start of 2026, implying a potential $15m in refunds for 9M'26. Reported Q3'26 EPS at C$0.17 vs. BofAe/BBG/VA at C$0.16/C$0.13/C$0.09, benefitted from $47.9m of non-cash gains on the revaluing derivatives and warrants.

Balance sheet strong; $68m shares repurchased in Q3'26 

On 24-Aug-26, ALM announced a share repurchase program for up to 14.4m shares, for an aggregate purchase price of up to $300m, over a 36-month period. During Q3'26, ALM repurchased 2.9m shares at $16.58/sh ($67.7m invested) and in Q4-to-date, bought back 0.7m more shares. At quarter-end, ALM's cash position remained solid at C$1.15 billion (bn) and net cash of $338 m vs. cash of C$1.23bn and net cash of $414m at 30-Jun-26. In addition to the share buyback, the build-out of Sangdong Phase 2 through 2027 will be a key capital allocation for ALM in the near-term. We forecast a meaningful inflection higher in free cash flow to over $700m in 2027E (vs. around $100m this year). We forecast Phase 2 contributing from early H2'27E with Phase 1 ramped-up by Q1'27E.

Winder maintained his Buy rating with a 12-month price target of $24 a share. 

D.A. Davidson analyst Matt Summerville's first take after earnings:

After the close, ALM reported 3Q26 sales of USD $30M, which was $7M below our estimate, though rose +382% Y/Y, with the entirety of variance attributable to lower head grade and shipment timing. Panasqueira's income from mining operations rose considerably Y/Y to $19M, driven by higher pricing, partially offset by a 13% Y/Y reduction in shipments with $4.3M in deferred revenue recorded during the first week of October (which would effectively all drop to mining income). Sangdong Phase I continues to ramp with its first cargo of tungsten loaded and shipped in October. Our LT thesis remains well intact amid deep primary supply deficits. BUY 

Stifel mining analyst Brock Cannon wrote:

Stifel View - waiting period: Quarterly results came in mostly as expected with Panasqueira continuing to be the consistent driver of earnings and no input from Sangdong, yet. Earnings continue to benefit from elevated APT prices even as the price has started to come off record highs – as expected and included in our model (see chart on page 2). Sangdong is now in what CEO Lewis Black described as the "long silence" that follows the commissioning of a new mine as all the kinks are worked out, and the mine ramps to full capacity. We continue to expect Phase I to hit full cadence in 2027 and see our ~C$30m estimate for revenue contribution in 4Q as reasonable but would not sound the alarms at any slippage into 2027. We have made limited changes to our model outside updating for the 3Q results and remain Buy rated but have updated our target price to $18 as we brought our multiple down to 11.5x 2027E EBITDA multiple (12.5x previously).

Almonty, like the broader mining stocks, has been battered in the second half of the year by higher rates and a strong-dollar environment. Weaker commodity prices have also been seen in recent weeks, such as gold tumbling below $4,000 and copper tumbling in London from the $14,500 level to around $13,588. 

More broadly, VanEck's REMX rare earth and strategic metals ETF has been halved since summer and retraced much of the run-up sparked early last year by China's restrictions on critical material supplies to the West.

We pointed out earlier on Friday that President Trump's $40 billion critical materials deal push will likely come under the Democratic Party's crosshairs, as miners that accepted government equity and other financing deals will likely face scrutiny.

As we noted in that report, Almonty accepted no government equity investment or other financing deals, which may help it avoid hearings on Capitol Hill next year.

"We've always believed government's place in our business is as a customer, not a shareholder, and look forward to continuing to provide the U.S. and its allies with tungsten to support critical defense and industrial needs," said Lewis Black, CEO of tungsten miner Almonty Industries.

We continue to favor the "owning the bottlenecks" theme as China restricts critical material supplies to the West. The focus remains on producing miners with conflict-free supply chains outside China that are also entirely independent of US government-backed financing.

As we've also pointed out: The Great Rare Earth Disconnect: Prices Up 23%, Miners Down 28%...

items.title: Quality Over Quantity: The Missing Signal In Jobs Data That Explains The Vibecession
items.content_text:
Quality Over Quantity: The Missing Signal In Jobs Data That Explains The Vibecession

Authored by Lance Roberts via RealInvestmentAdvice.com,

Recession Indicators Turned Green. Job Quality Hasn’t.

October’s jobs report pushed the headline recession indicators back to green, but “labor hoarding” explains why the earnings boom still isn’t reaching full-time workers.

Key Takeaways

  • S&P 500 earnings are on track to grow 31.4% in the third quarter, yet fewer Americans work full-time today than in September 2025.
  • October payrolls beat every forecast at 165,000, but full-time employment, at 49.0% of the working-age population, remains well below its 2019 level of 50.6%.
  • Companies are “hoarding” labor: output rose 3.7% last quarter while hours worked rose 0.1%, so productivity, not hiring, is carrying profits.
  • Involuntary part-time work jumped 339,000 to 4.8 million in October, and pay growth of 3.1% still trails 3.7% inflation.
  • The recession indicators flashing green – claims and layoffs – are the ones labor hoarding suppresses the longest.

Here is the puzzle investors face right now. S&P 500 companies are on track to report 31.4% earnings growth for the third quarter, the eighth straight quarter of double-digit gains. Last Friday, the October jobs report beat every forecast, with payrolls up 165,000 and unemployment back down to 4.1%. On the surface, the recession indicators have turned green. Beneath the surface, the quality of the jobs tells a different story. Such is the question worth answering: is the labor market healing, or are companies still “hoarding” labor while profits do the heavy lifting?

Why The Recession Indicators Disagree

Let’s start with the economic indicators that say all is well. In the most recent reports:

  • Initial jobless claims fell to 189,000 in the week ended October 31, the lowest reading since 1969.
  • The Job Openings and Labor Turnover Survey (JOLTS), which printed a layoff rate of 1.0% in September, near the floor of its 25-year history
  • The October payrolls rose 165,000 against a consensus near 65,000, and revisions added 84,000 jobs to August and September.

In other words, if your only recession indicators are layoffs, claims, and the headline payroll count, there is no recession anywhere in sight.

Now look at the other half of the labor data. The JOLTS hiring rate sits at 3.4%, in line with its 2013 average and well below the 3.9% pace of 2019. The number of people working part-time because they can’t find full-time work jumped by 339,000 in October to 4.8 million. Workers unemployed for six months or longer now make up 27.6% of the unemployed. Average hourly earnings grew 3.1% from a year earlier, still short of the 3.7% inflation rate.

Employers are not firing anyone, and they are hiring far more cautiously than the headline suggests. That is the “low hire, low fire” economy, and the chart below shows how unusual the combination is. In 2009, hiring collapsed as layoffs surged and companies shed workers as quickly as they could process paperwork. Today, hiring has slowed to 2013 levels with layoffs near record lows. The two lines usually move together. This time they are not.

Labor Hoarding: I’ve Seen This Movie Before

In early 2014, I wrote a piece arguing that the headline jobs data was missing the point. My view was that the only employment chart that mattered was full-time employment relative to the working-age population. The reason was simple. Full-time jobs pay the wages that support household formation, consumption and tax receipts. Part-time work and headline payroll counts don’t.

The argument centered on a behavior I called “labor hoarding.” Businesses had cut costs to the bone after the financial crisis and could cut no further. To wit:

“At this point businesses have to begin to ‘hoard’ what labor they have, maximize that labor force’s productivity (increase output with minimal increases in labor costs) and hire additional labor, primarily temporary, only when demand forces expansion.”Lance Roberts, ” – The Only Employment Chart That Matters, 2014

Swap the 2014 headwinds for today’s tariffs and energy costs, and that description fits almost word for word. So let’s update the chart. Full-time employment as a share of the civilian population age 16 and over peaked at 54.0% in April 2000. It stood at 47.6% when I wrote that piece and recovered to 50.6% by the end of 2019. As of October, it’s 49.0%, roughly where it was in 2016 and still below September 2025’s 49.3%.

Let’s dig into the BLS’s household survey for October. That report showed a jump of 714,000 full-time workers, a welcome sign. However, the household survey swings widely from month to month, and one month doesn’t make a trend.

What was important in that data was that there are still 67,000 fewer people working full-time than in September 2025. However, the working-age population has grown by nearly 1.5 million over the same period. Since November 2023, full-time employment has increased by just 271,000, even though there are 7.9 million more working-age Americans. Companies are protecting the workers they have and adding very few new full-time positions. Calling that a “healing” labor market is generous.

4.4 Million

Additional full-time workers the U.S. would have today if the full-time employment ratio were back at its 2019 level.

Where The Earnings Boom Actually Comes From

If companies aren’t adding full-time workers, how are earnings growing 31%? Part of the answer arrived last week. Nonfarm productivity rose at a 3.6% annualized rate in the third quarter as output grew 3.7% and hours worked rose just 0.1%. Unit labor costs fell 0.7%. In other words, companies produced more without paying for more hours, and the difference dropped straight to the bottom line.

Pay attention to this data. It is the textbook payoff from “labor hoarding.” The playbook is simple:

  • Hold headcount steady,
  • Squeeze more output from the existing workforce, and
  • Let margins expand.

This is completely rational behavior for any single company. However, when it spans the entire economy, it means the profit boom is not reaching paychecks.

The other piece is concentration. Energy and Information Technology have delivered the biggest upside earnings surprises this season, and as of mid-October, Micron and NVIDIA were the two largest contributors to S&P 500 earnings growth. Elevated oil prices fattened energy profits, while AI spending fattened chip profits.

Neither industry employs many people relative to what it earns. As I discussed in “Capex Spending On AI Is Masking Economic Weakness,” a narrow capex boom can mask economic weakness while the broader economy stalls. Some of those profits are also flattered by accounting timing, a point I made in “AI Capex Depreciation Risk Is The Catch To Record Earnings.”

Is A Recession Coming? The Case Against My View

The other side of this debate has merit, and October’s jobs report handed it more ammunition. Payrolls beat every forecast, and unemployment fell back to 4.1%. Job openings rose by 333,000 in September, lifting the openings rate to 4.5%. Quits hit an 18-month high the same month, which usually means workers feel confident enough to leave. Claims at a 57-year low are hard to argue with. Here’s how one strategist read Friday’s numbers:

“[The report] is a strong rebuttal to fears that the economy is heading into a meaningful slowdown.” – Seema Shah, Chief Global Strategist, Principal Asset Management

Productivity growth is also good news in its own right. If the AI buildout is lifting output per hour, the economy can grow faster without adding workers or adding inflation.

“You made this same argument in 2014, and the economy kept growing for six more years.” Yes, that is true. However, the process of “labor hoarding” doesn’t cause a recession on its own. It changes HOW the next one unfolds. In 2014, the Fed held rates at zero and ran QE, which bought companies years to grow their workforces. On October 28, the Fed held rates at 3.75%-4.00%, and two members dissented in favor of a rate hike. After Friday’s report, investors now lean toward a December hike. There is no zero-rate cushion this time to buy companies that kind of patience.

What These Recession Indicators Mean For Investors

For investors, let’s go back to the beginning. Pay attention to which recession indicators are flashing green. They’re the layoff numbers and the headline counts. Crucially, the payroll survey doesn’t distinguish between full-time and part-time jobs. That distinction matters in a month when involuntary part-time work jumped by 339,000. Furthermore, both claims and layoffs are precisely the signals labor hoarding suppresses, because a company that hoards workers doesn’t let anyone go until it has to. Then it lets a lot of people go at once. When hoarding ends, claims don’t drift higher. They jump.

So, what will eventually force corporate hands is falling profit margins. For now, productivity gains and falling unit labor costs are protecting profits. But wage growth of 3.1% still trails inflation at 3.7%. As I laid out in “Real Wages 2026: Why Consumer Stocks Feel It First,” households are covering the gap with longer hours, less saving, and more credit.

Therein lies the risk. When demand softens enough that output stops growing, and there’s no more productivity to squeeze, then headcount becomes the only lever left. As is always the case, a “low fire” economy turns into a “high fire” one almost overnight.

“Labor hoarding doesn’t prevent a recession. It delays the layoffs, and then it delivers them all at once.”

For investors, the practical point is that the earnings estimates underpinning today’s valuations assume this setup will persist. Analysts expect 28.4% growth in the fourth quarter and 33.3% for all of 2026. Those numbers depend on a narrow group of sectors and on margins built by not hiring. That makes this a good time to review how concentrated a portfolio is in the handful of companies producing those earnings. It’s also worth knowing in advance which signal would change your mind. For me, it’s a sustained break higher in weekly claims, particularly continuing claims, which recently ticked up to 1.718 million. Claims are the recession indicator that hoards the longest, which makes them the ones that matter most when they finally move.

Bottom Line

The labor data tells you how long the earnings boom can last, and the answer is only as long as companies can keep avoiding the need to hire.

October’s jobs report bought the bulls another month. Watch the claims data anyway. The quietest layoff market in 57 years is also the one with the least room for error.

items.title: Back To The Fax Machine: Microsoft's Meltdown Exposes The Agentic Economy's Weakest Link
items.content_text:
Back To The Fax Machine: Microsoft's Meltdown Exposes The Agentic Economy's Weakest Link

Traders reached for fax machines, Japan's finance ministry pinned paper notices to the wall, and the AI assistants meant to automate the office went dark right along with the inbox.

For more than 18 hours, the AI agents Silicon Valley says will soon do your job couldn't read your email, because nobody could. A Microsoft 365 failure that began Thursday knocked out Outlook for businesses and governments in more than 70 countries and took Microsoft's own Copilot down with it, along with the Microsoft connectors that Anthropic's Claude and OpenAI's ChatGPT use to reach users' mail and calendars.

Every one of those failures has one thing in common: Exchange Online, Microsoft's cloud email and calendar backend. In its status notice Friday morning, Microsoft said features across its 365 services "that interact with Exchange Online and email services are impacted," while "elements of those services that do not depend on interaction with Exchange Online remain functional." Teams calls and group chats mostly kept working. Anything that had to touch a mailbox did not.

What Went Down With Exchange Online

ServiceWhat broke
Outlook / Exchange OnlineMailbox access through Outlook on the web, desktop and mobile sync; delayed email delivery
Microsoft 365 CopilotCopilot Chat failed to load; Copilot cut off from email, calendar and files
TeamsCalendar, invites and meeting edits failed, along with Copilot answers about Outlook and files
Microsoft Graph APIRequests for mail, calendar and contacts timing out
Claude (Anthropic)Microsoft 365 connector's mail, calendar and search tools failing for most requests; Claude for Outlook add-in wouldn't open for some
ChatGPT (OpenAI)Errors in its Microsoft 365 connectors
Defender for Office 365 / PurviewDelays or failures in data-protection and policy enforcement
Planner, To Do, IntuneTask failures; device enrollment and compliance checks hit
Still standingTeams calls and chats; files stored directly in SharePoint

Source: Microsoft service status updates of November 13, Anthropic status, FinanceX

As we reported Thursday, Microsoft first blamed elevated load on part of its infrastructure and said it was reviewing "an unexpected increase in a specific type of service traffic" to see whether it was contributing. It then ruled that out, saying the load "isn't driven by an increase in traffic" but by a large number of servers dropping out after failing automated health checks, which dumped their traffic onto the machines still running. Overnight, Microsoft warned that servers it had brought back "can become unresponsive again once they receive traffic," and several did. It paused all deployments, patched an authentication and routing component and stretched its email timeout window to 48 hours so delayed messages wouldn't be lost.

By 9 a.m. ET Friday, Microsoft said email queues were "significantly reduced and approaching normal levels," though some users could still hit intermittent access problems or delayed mail. It says it has seen no evidence of malicious activity and has promised a full post-incident report with "root cause and defense-in-depth actions" once mitigation is complete. Microsoft executive Charles Lamanna said as much early Friday:

We regret that today's outages caused disruptions for our customers, and we are working to address the issue. We will continue to share more information as soon as we have it, and for now I can confirm that there is no indication this is the result of malicious or cyber activity.

— Charles Lamanna (@clamanna) November 13, 2026

The Agents Went Down With The Inbox

"Copilot experiences may be unable to access work data such as email, calendar, and files," Microsoft's status notice said Friday of its own AI assistant, and some users couldn't load Copilot Chat at all. Inside Teams, Copilot answers about Outlook, calendars and documents failed.

The same notice says requests to Microsoft Graph that touch Exchange Online data, "such as mail, calendar, and contacts, may time out." Graph is the API outside software uses to read and act on a company's Microsoft 365 data, the usual on-ramp for third-party AI assistants wired into a corporate inbox. Even some Google Workspace customers who read their mail through Outlook's desktop and mobile apps reported trouble.

Anthropic users were hosed too - opening an incident titled "Elevated errors affecting the Microsoft 365 connector" at 12:52 p.m. ET Thursday, around the time Microsoft posted its first public alert. By evening, its status page said the connector's mail, calendar and search tools were "still failing for most requests," that some users "may not be able to open" the Claude for Outlook add-in, and that the cause was "a Microsoft 365 service incident." OpenAI also reported errors affecting its Microsoft 365 connectors, FinanceX reported, and Calcalist said both companies had trouble reaching Microsoft services.

Microsoft opens its Ignite conference in San Francisco next week with a program built around Agent 365, its system for managing fleets of AI agents across a company's apps and data. As we reported in February, Microsoft AI chief Mustafa Suleyman told the Financial Times that "most of the tasks will be fully automated by an AI within the next 12 to 18 months." Nine months later, Japanese firms were trading by fax.

Phones, Fax Machines And Paper Notices

Desks fell back on phones, WhatsApp and fax machines, Bloomberg reported: Deutsche Bank's email access was patchy, traders in Singapore said some banks couldn't close financing deals, and Euronext and Nasdaq both reported email problems. The outage halted at least one bond repurchase in Europe, according to Reuters, while bankers at Goldman Sachs and Morgan Stanley in Hong Kong told CNN they couldn't reach email or Teams from the moment they signed on.

At Goldman itself, TMT specialist Sean Johnstone opened his Friday morning note with "Paraskevidekatriaphobia meets its modern upgrade," a nod to the fear of Friday the 13th, before describing the floor: "MSFT here is still down and most operating off backup email so reading email has never felt more mythological... or more dependent on tech that clearly didn't get the memo about not being the unlucky guest."

Cartier owner Richemont delayed its first-half results, due at 0600 GMT Friday, before publishing later in the morning. Electric truck maker Workhorse pushed its results to Nov. 16, British insurer Aviva set up backup arrangements for its earnings calls, and Maersk warned customers that email updates could be delayed.

In Tokyo, the finance ministry couldn't receive email for most of the day, and ministries pinned up paper notices to give journalists the day's schedule. Chief Cabinet Secretary Minoru Kihara confirmed that communications between ministries were disrupted. In Australia, the spy agency ASIO and the Australian Federal Police were among those hit, Service NSW centres in regional New South Wales closed and the state's online bail court was disrupted. Tony Burke, Australia's home affairs and cyber security minister, said Microsoft itself likened the disruption to the 2024 CrowdStrike outage.

Singapore's government email went down, the Philippines' Supreme Court said some operations were affected, and New York City Emergency Management warned that email to city agencies could be delayed. In Toronto, the Unity Health hospital network declared a code grey, its signal for an infrastructure failure, while saying patient care was not affected. Police forces, hospitals, GP surgeries and councils across southern England posted workarounds, and Air India rerouted its email while Alaska Airlines and IndiGo said their email-based customer service channels were hit.

Outage reports peaked at 19,650 a minute across five Microsoft services on Downdetector, against fewer than 15 on a typical Thursday. Meanwhile, Iran war hawk fossil Mark Levin is still using AOL.

My AOL email is back and working great. How's it going with Microsoft Outlook email users?

— Mark R. Levin (@marklevinshow) November 13, 2026

The Scam Window

The failure also took out part of the security layer around the inbox. Standard Chartered and ING Australia warned customers about scammers posing as tech support, noting that the email security filters that normally catch such messages were disrupted too. Microsoft's notice says some Defender for Office 365 features that rely on Purview data-protection signals face "delays or failures in policy evaluation and governance action enforcement."

Organizations that run Microsoft services on their own servers rather than in Microsoft's cloud came through better: Reuters reported they were "somewhat spared."

The outage follows a Microsoft 365 failure of nearly 10 hours on Jan. 22. "The bigger worry is that this is not the first Microsoft 365 outage this year," eToro analyst Josh Gilbert told Reuters. 

Sorry Clippy...

items.title: ICE Sets All-Time Records: 483,200 Deported, Arrests Nearly Double
items.content_text:
ICE Sets All-Time Records: 483,200 Deported, Arrests Nearly Double

Authored by AG News Staff via American Greatness,

U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement arrested and deported more people over the last year than at any point in its 23-year history, the agency announced Thursday, according to an Associated Press report published by ABC News.

ICE deported 483,200 people in the fiscal year that ended Sept. 30. That was 9% more than the previous record of 442,640 set a year earlier, and 78 percent more than the 271,480 deported in 2024, the final year of Joe Biden's presidency.

Arrests rose even faster. ICE made 474,850 arrests in the most recent 12-month period, roughly double the 239,890 from the year before and more than four times the 113,430 recorded in 2024.

"Thanks to President Trump's leadership, ICE has been unleashed to target and remove illegal aliens so that we can save American lives," said Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin.

The agency made more than 48,000 arrests in September, following two straight months of record highs that peaked at 50,925 in August.

It is the first time ICE has released such precise figures since Trump returned to the White House, including for 2025. The press release did not break down how many of those arrested or deported had criminal records, something previous administrations had reported.

The numbers mark a dramatic turnaround from the Biden years, when millions crossed the southern border and interior enforcement was sharply scaled back. Trump campaigned on carrying out the largest deportation operation in American history, and the latest figures show the administration is following through.

items.title: "Commerce Has The Pen": Bessent Throws Lutnick Under The Bus Amid Agreement To Testify In Nvidia Spy Scandal
items.content_text:
"Commerce Has The Pen": Bessent Throws Lutnick Under The Bus Amid Agreement To Testify In Nvidia Spy Scandal

Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent on Friday publicly pinned the failure to blacklist Megaspeed on Howard Lutnick's Commerce Department, as Lutnick agreed to testify before the Senate Banking Committee over the Nvidia spy scandal.

Asked on CNBC's "Squawk Box" about reported tension between the two over why the Singapore-based Nvidia customer still isn't on the Entity List, and whether only Commerce could have put it there, Bessent said: "I can tell you there was coordination. Treasury, War, USTR, and State were in favor of putting Megaspeed on the entity list for months."

"But Commerce has the pen. Commerce BIS has the pen. And you will have to ask them about their internal processes."

U.S. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent blames Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick over Nvidia chip mess: "Treasury, War, USTR and State were in favor of putting Megaspeed on the entity list for months." pic.twitter.com/0BTlHymwUY

— CNBC (@CNBC) November 13, 2026

BIS is Commerce's Bureau of Industry and Security, the export-control arm run by Under Secretary Jeffrey Kessler. Axios reported this week that Kessler was repeatedly warned about Megaspeed in deputy meetings, and Sen. Elizabeth Warren (D-Mass.), the top Democrat on the Banking Committee, said Thursday that Lutnick and Kessler "must explain why they have not closed export control loopholes and act today to ensure our advanced technology is not fueling China's military."

Bessent also turned on Nvidia itself. Asked whether higher-end chips had made it to China through Megaspeed, he said "there is a lot of leakage in the system and we are constantly working to close that down."

"The story has been thus far on Jensen Huang's personal foibles," he said. "The real story here should be, did Nvidia know their client? And was there a robust effort at Nvidia to make sure that there was no leakage and that they were selling to what were obviously pass-through shell companies?"

"And I think it's important that anyone at the company there be held accountable for that," he added.

U.S. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent weighs in on Nvidia and Megaspeed: "Was there a robust effort at Nvidia to make sure that there was no leakage and that they were selling to what were obviously pass-through shell companies?" pic.twitter.com/d55K9R3Bo7

— CNBC (@CNBC) November 13, 2026

Lutnick, meanwhile, has "proactively agreed to appear voluntarily" before Senate Banking, Commerce spokesperson Kristen Eichamer said in a statement. Chairman Tim Scott (R-S.C.) asked Lutnick and former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang on Thursday to appear before the committee in early December.

"Given the Department of Commerce's central role in issuing and enforcing export control regulations, your testimony before the Committee will be essential to our oversight of these efforts," Scott wrote.

It's the same wording House Oversight Chairman James Comer used in March, when Lutnick "proactively agreed to appear voluntarily" for questions about his ties to Jeffrey Epstein on the eve of a threatened subpoena. He sat for that closed-door interview in May.

As we reported Thursday, Bessent asked Lutnick in the White House Situation Room on Nov. 5 why Megaspeed wasn't on the Entity List, and Lutnick reportedly answered, "I don't know. I'll look into it." Commerce denied the conversation took place. Axios also reported that Trump approved action against suspected chip diversion three times this year, and that Lutnick held it up each time over fears of a trade war with China.

Commerce's own investigation of Megaspeed was halted after Nvidia's general counsel contacted the agents running it, and the case reportedly moved to the Justice Department. Commerce hasn't added a single company to the Entity List in more than a year.

items.title: Soaring Electricity Costs Force Britain To Rethink Its Green Agenda
items.content_text:
Soaring Electricity Costs Force Britain To Rethink Its Green Agenda

Via City A.M.,

  • Labour is making affordable energy a central priority as high electricity prices undermine British industrial competitiveness.
  • Decisions on North Sea drilling and electric vehicle targets are testing the government's commitment to net zero.
  • Ministers face pressure to reform electricity levies while balancing economic growth against long-term climate goals.

While it didn't make the headlines, Chancellor John Healey's Budget speech signaled a huge shift in positioning from previous governments over net zero.

"Today I'm setting a new course on energy: to get UK energy costs down in line with Europe," Healey said. "From this point, our government priority is first and foremost cheaper energy, with clean power key to achieving this."

The lines raised eyebrows in Westminster. The test of that new commitment came when the energy secretary, Miatta Fahnbulleh, approved the gas field project at Jackdaw - apparently against her instincts - and will once again come into focus this week as Andy Burnham takes a double trip on Thursday to the COP 31 climate summit in Turkey before looking to clinch an energy market deal with European leaders in Dublin.

While higher international energy prices caused by the Iran war have raised the stakes of diplomacy across government, policy researchers working under the new Prime Minister are tasked with finding effective ways of easing the cost of living for both households and businesses.

In particular, Healey and Fahnbulleh may struggle to align Labour manifesto commitments on net zero with a renewed push to get costs down - in what could divide the party between environmental zealots and centrists conscious of economic trade-offs.

The crunch energy decisions facing ministers

The energy giant Equinor is awaiting a decision on whether Rosebank's oil field will get the go-ahead for an opening, with ministers including Fahnbulleh and Healey reportedly sparring over the coherence of a policy to allow more drilling for fossil fuels with a manifesto promise not to offer new licenses for oil and gas fields. Labour backbenchers are lining up to publicly condemn Rosebank.

Meanwhile, Louise Haigh, who enforces Burnham's agenda in government, is expected to dial down electric vehicle sales targets to help carmakers despite the risk of derailing Labour's decarbonization agenda.

And most emphatically of all, Fahnbulleh has suggested that the party's ambition to eliminate almost all fossil fuels from the power supply by 2030 would be thrown out if the UK's "affordability challenge" was not solved first. That affordability crisis facing households, firms have argued, stems from sky-high energy costs facing manufacturers up and down the country.

Getting industry on electricity

The Labour government has talked up its policy to give about 10,000 energy-intensive businesses a discount of up to 25 percent from April on electricity bills, costing taxpayers billions by 2030. Additional funding will come from aligning UK and EU carbon markets and exempting businesses from existing levies, according to the government.

But the UK falls short, on some metrics, to fully "electrify" industry, which remains heavily reliant on fossil fuels.

Sky-high costs

Even for manufacturers using greener power, British industry has struggled to keep up with both European and significant international counterparts in keeping costs low.

Data taken from government analysis and international agencies suggests British firms pay four times as much on electricity as American companies, and about twice as much as European counterparts.

How to apply taxes

The consensus among energy market observers is for the government to strip levies from bills and use general taxation to fund subsidies. A cross-party group of MPs on the Energy Security and Net Zero Committee, led by Labour's Bill Esterson, said all net zero costs should be stripped off the price of electricity as a "critical means for substantially bringing down bills".

Research by the Institute for Fiscal Policy showed that taxes and policy costs, such as the climate change levy, made up over a third of industrial electricity costs for businesses that are not energy-intensive. The think tank suggested that the government could spread the cost of decarbonization across the entire economy or take all fixed costs off the unit price.

Climate change damage

But even as the Conservatives and Reform UK have pledged to scrap net zero legislation and take out levies in order to bring electricity costs down, opposition parties face questions over measuring the long-term costs of climate change for the UK economy.

Research by Transira Energy and Onward, backed by the Tories, suggested abandoning net zero regulations and taxes could save households as much as £540 a year between 2030 and 2050. But the report concedes that the UK economy could be left more exposed to international gas price shocks by slowing the race for electrification.

In its 2025 fiscal risks report, the Office for Budget Responsibility warned in one scenario for global temperatures rising by three degrees Celsius that climate change damage could contribute to around three-fifths of the addition to public sector debt by 2074.

It's in the context of the sky-high costs for British industry today that Burnham and Healey appear to be taking Labour down a "new course on energy". In negotiations with EU chiefs and international representatives in Turkey this week, the Prime Minister faces a tussle in balancing advocacy for long-term net zero policy with a reality that Britain is unattractive for manufacturers - complicating his effort for "re-industrialization".

Helsinki Warns Ukraine Against Expanding War Into Gulf Of Finland After Russian Warship Struck

In a rare moment of the Ukraine war spilling far outside its boundaries into the north, Finland's military on Thursday alerted the world that its military detected a rare strike on a Russian navy vessel in the Baltic Sea.

A spokesperson for the Finnish armed forces told Reuters they "detected… a strike on a Russian warship in the Gulf of Finland area and has monitored the development of the situation," but also noted somewhat ominously that Finland is not under "any immediate military threat."

No other information was given to the mysterious alert, such as precise strike location and from where it originated, or exactly when it happeneed. Also, there's no information on casualties or damage. 

Reuters has, however, noted that there's been an uptick in drone activity over the Baltic Sea region:

Estonia, ⁠Latvia and Lithuania early on Wednesday issued warnings to citizens to take shelter due to drones in their airspace, and NATO scrambled warplanes ⁠in ​response.

The Gulf of Finland is a narrow ​arm of the Baltic Sea between Finland and Estonia that extends eastwards to St ​Petersburg.

While there's been a ratcheting Black Sea war involving tit-for-tat attacks on both Russian and Ukrainian vessels, such a crisis has yet to come to Baltic Sea waters, which would mean northern Europe.

The Gulf of Finland remains a vital export outlet for Russian oil and grain - which could explain why it might be targeted in long-range Ukrainian drones strikes.

Al Jazeera fills in another detail as follows: "Estonian media reported that the vessel was a small Russian navy ship that later returned to St Petersburg," it writes Thursday.

Finland’s Defense Minister Antti Hakkanen has confirmed that Helsinki raised the issue of the provocative and dangerous new strike with the Zelensky government.

"We have told the Ukrainians this time, and a little earlier too, how sensitive this narrow stretch of the Gulf of Finland, right between us and Estonia, is in terms of environmental safety and the safety of civilian shipping," he said as cited in Finnish broadcaster Yle.

He said it is urgently important that things don't escalate in the narrow waterway, as for now "You can still cruise with peace of mind."

items.content_text:
Blanche Says DOJ Has Not Confirmed If Ex-Nvidia CEO's Affair Partner Was A Spy

Authored by Jacki Thrapp via The Epoch Times,

Attorney General Todd Blanche said neither the Department of Justice (DOJ) nor the FBI has confirmed whether a woman associated with ex-Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang was a Chinese spy.

Blanche made the remarks at a press conference on Nov. 12 after a reporter asked when the DOJ learned that Alice Huang - not a relative of the CEO - was a suspected asset of the Chinese Ministry of State Security.

"Well, your first question assumes something that I have never said and that I don't know to be true," Blanche said. "So you assume that DOJ learns that she is in fact a spy. I'm not - nobody said that. I certainly haven't said that."

National security concerns were raised after the tech billionaire allegedly had an affair with the alleged spy, who was a top executive at Megaspeed, a Singapore-based data center company that's one of Nvidia's biggest customers in Southeast Asia.

"Of course DOJ is investigating or looking at it," Blanche said. "So there's no conclusions reached by the Department of Justice, or by me, or by [FBI] Director [Kash] Patel, around who she is or is not."

Chinese intelligence had allegedly recruited her to potentially influence Nvidia to make more advanced AI chips available to Chinese customers. Certain chips are restricted from being exported from the United States.

"The DOJ has a role in investigating if there are chips that shouldn't be sold," Blanche said.

"It could potentially be a violation of our export laws, and that could be civil, regulatory, it could also be criminal, depending on the case, and that investigation is ongoing."

Huang apologized for being unfaithful to his wife and letting his co-workers down in a message to Nvidia employees obtained by The Epoch Times.

"I owe my family and all of you an apology," Huang wrote. "I was unfaithful to my wife. My actions hurt her and our children. There is no excuse for what I did. Throughout my life, my family has given me love and support. I am deeply sorry.

"To my wife and family: I love you. I know an apology cannot undo what I have done. I hope our family will heal and that, over time, I can earn back your trust."

Huang gave no indication he planned to step aside after news emerged of the first affair with the alleged spy, but the company announced he resigned as CEO on Thursday after The New York Times reported that five people who worked at Nvidia claimed he was engaged in a separate affair with Kimberly Powell, Nvidia's vice president of healthcare.

His resignation was effective immediately, according to the company's board of directors.

Executive vice president and chief financial officer of Nvidia, Colette Kress, will serve as interim chief executive officer in addition to her other duties until the company selects a permanent successor.

"Colette has helped lead Nvidia through a period of extraordinary growth and has a deep understanding of our business, customers, operations and financial position," said Harvey Jones, chair of the Nvidia Board of Directors.

"She is supported by an experienced leadership team that has been instrumental in executing Nvidia's strategy and advancing its technology roadmap.

"The board has full confidence in Colette and the leadership team, and we expect the company's operations, customer commitments and product roadmap to continue without interruption."

[ZH: Spy or not, she is clearly deeply involved in the acquisition of Nvidia chips for Chinese companies]

items.content_text:
Futures Rise As Wall Street Moves On From Jensen, Microsoft Outage Drags Into Day Two

US futures are higher as traders move on from the Nvidia leadership shock and shrug off a global Microsoft outage that is now in its second day, while the IEA's call that the oil market is swinging to a surplus and a rebound in short-dated Treasuries take some of the edge off the week's bond rout heading into the PPI report. As of 8:00 am ET, S&P futures are 0.3% higher while Nasdaq futures rise 0.1% and Dow futures add 0.2%. On Thursday the S&P fell 0.4%, the Nasdaq 100 slipped 0.3% and the Russell 2000 tumbled 1.7% after Nvidia plunged as much as 14% at the open on Jensen Huang's ouster before retail dip buyers dragged it back to a 4.3% loss, confirming our post on the record opening retail bid. In premarket trading, Mag 7 stocks are all higher except Microsoft (-2.7%), which is struggling to restore access to Outlook, Teams and Copilot; Nvidia rises 3% and Alphabet 1.1%, while Cerebras jumps 17% on blowout guidance and new deals with Oracle and Microsoft, and Modine soars more than 20% on a report that Samsung is in talks to buy it. The day's driver is inflation (again): October PPI at 8:30am is expected to rise 0.4% m/m after September's 1.3% surge, and comes after a hot CPI and a Treasury selloff that left a December hike fully priced. Treasuries are mixed, with the 2Y yield down 4bps to 4.84% as traders trim hike bets on the dip in oil, while the 10Y is little changed around 5.12% after jumping 13.5bps on Thursday; the combined Tuesday and Thursday jump in 10Y yields was the biggest since April 2025. The Bloomberg dollar index steadies after hitting an 18-month high, USD/JPY hovers just under 160 amid more Japanese jawboning and the Aussie slides to its weakest since January. Brent trades near $96 and WTI slips to $88.42 as the IEA's surplus call offsets Trump saying the US doesn't need a deal with Iran; gold rebounds to around $3,900 but stays well below $4,000, and Bitcoin is down 3% below $70,000. US economic data slate includes October PPI (8:30am). Fed speaker slate includes Goolsbee (8:30am on CNBC), Collins (9:10am and 10:35am), Logan (9:40am), Bowman (10:50am), Daly (12pm) and Jefferson (7pm).

In premarket trading, Mag 7 stocks are mostly higher: (Nvidia (NVDA) +1.9%, Alphabet (GOOGL) +1.1%, Amazon (AMZN) +1%, Tesla (TSLA) +1%, Apple (AAPL) +0.4%, Meta Platforms (META) +0.05%, Microsoft (MSFT) -1.4%)

  • Candel Therapeutics (CADL) tumbles 34% after the biotech delayed its application for aglatimagene in prostate cancer to mid-2027 while talks with the FDA continue.
  • Cerebras Systems (CBRS) gains 15% after the chipmaker gave a sales guidance well above estimates, while unveiling new deals with Oracle and Microsoft.
  • Cisco (CSCO) falls 3% after the networking gear maker’s fiscal first quarter product order growth disappointed. Gross margins are seen coming under pressure in the next few quarters as revenue has become more reliant on AI hyperscalers.
  • Flowers Foods (FLO) falls 9% after the packaged bakery foods producer cut its sales guidance for the full year, which missed the average analyst estimates. Sales for the third-quarter also came below Wall Street’s consensus.
  • Liftoff Mobile (LFTO) gains 21% after the mobile advertising company’s third-quarter adjusted earnings per share beat the average analyst estimate.
  • Lowe’s (LOW) slips 2% after Stifel cut its recommendation on the home improvement retailer to sell and reduced the price target to a Street-low $190 from $195.
  • Nu Holdings (NU) rises 4% after quarterly profit that beat analyst estimates as the Brazilian fintech pushes into new markets.
  • Palo Alto Networks (PANW) gains 4% after the cybersecurity stock received an upgrade by KeyBanc, which sees security budgets on a material acceleration in 2027 due to more threats caused by AI.
  • Sellas Life Sciences (SLS) rises 11% after the drug developer said it expects to report topline results from a late-stage trial of its experimental cancer therapy in November.

In other corporate news, the Nvidia saga keeps giving: a Chinese company founded by Alice Huang, the woman at the center of the scandal, procured smuggled AI chips installed at a Shanghai data center with links to Megaspeed, Bloomberg reports, Commerce Secretary Lutnick has agreed to testify before Congress on Nvidia (NBC), and Singapore charged a fifth person in its Nvidia chip case. Meanwhile, the IPO window could not be wider open: Anthropic's IPO has drawn about six times the orders for the shares available as it seeks to raise as much as $64.4 billion plus $26 billion in a private placement, SpaceX and Tesla are progressing in merger talks that could produce the biggest deal ever as soon as December, and ByteDance plans to buy back up to $6 billion of shares at a valuation of about $400 billion. Samsung Electronics is in talks to acquire data center cooling maker Modine; Keurig Dr Pepper priced 58 million shares at $34.50; Helen of Troy says Empower's bid undervalues the company; and Exxon made a final investment decision on its $12.5 billion Longtail development offshore Guyana.

Traders are ending a rollercoaster week, dominated by the firehose of Nvidia/Jensen news and the AI trade, by contending with a global Microsoft outage that has paralyzed government offices, trading floors and businesses, forcing traders onto phones and knocking out email at exchanges including Euronext; Richemont even had to delay its results. Microsoft says it is not aware of any malicious activity. And yet, markets keep doing what they're not supposed to: Nvidia lost the most famous face of the AI trade, Huang resigned "effective immediately", and the Nasdaq 100 lost just 0.3%. As Bloomberg puts it, the rest of the AI trade is already moving on, with deals still flowing overnight and Europe's soft start owing more to oil and yields than to chips.

Goldman is leaning into the dip: its strategists issued a bullish outlook predicting the S&P 500 will advance 14% over the coming year after the selloff in the biggest tech companies left their valuations historically cheap. Indeed, the Nasdaq 100 now trades at a six-year low on forward earnings after a 25% de-rating this year. At the same time, Goldman's 2027 outlook sees the AI investment impulse peaking early next year, with S&P 500 EPS growth slowing to 11% in 2027 from 36% this year, and a 10Y yield of 4.6% by end-2027.

Calamos co-CIO Nick Niziolek told Bloomberg the AI trade is maturing rather than ending, arguing that the demand and the fundamentals remain intact. Direxion's Bilal Little made a similar point: Nvidia still sits at the center of the AI buildout, and the question is whether the governance shock changes its competitive position or merely the multiple investors are willing to pay.

“Today, I would watch the interaction between producer prices, oil and real yields,” said Florian Ielpo at Lombard Odier Asset Management. “The PPI report will help assess how much of the energy shock is still feeding into prices and squeezing margins, with implications for the amount of tightening the Fed needs to deliver.”

The FX desks are less sanguine. MUFG's Derek Halpenny warned the Microsoft outage could add to already poor tech sentiment and intensify risk aversion, hurting high-beta G10 currencies against the dollar, while ING's Francesco Pesole said the dollar's rally is rooted in hawkish Fed rhetoric and hotter inflation, making a material EUR/USD rebound hard to argue for; he sees a possible test of 1.10.

And BofA's Michael Hartnett is still telling clients to stay risk-off until the dollar drops, the 10Y yield falls below 4.5% and oil drops below $70, even as global equity funds drew $98.3 billion in the week to Nov. 11, the largest inflow since June, led by $63.6 billion into US stocks.

Goldman's Rich Privorotsky did not publish overnight (Goldman's desks are working off backup email due to the outage), but his latest note on Thursday morning remains the best framing of the tape. He found it "quite impressive how much we've managed to rally" in the face of the macro backdrop and Nvidia's increasingly idiosyncratic problems, while noting the move was emphatically not broad based, and that the governance issues are forcing a significant rebalancing of capital within AI. He flagged the SPX vol curve un-inverting, dealer skew flattening and systematic long/short managers posting their best two-day return in nearly three years, and asked whether this is just the mechanical result of light positioning and short covering or the start of something more durable. His list of four tactical AI overhangs (cost of capital, power and permitting, the supply/demand balance going into 2028, and monetization velocity versus capex) leads him to expect episodic, high beta trading rallies rather than pure buy and hold. His bottom line: a durable breakout probably needs lower rates, lower energy and broader leadership, i.e. the market needs oil fixed and rates lower, and the two may well be connected.

JPM's Market Intel desk under Andrew Tyler says the market "feels coil-sprung to go higher, which is seemingly the pain trade": higher yields, Nvidia gapping down and AI headwinds could not stop the next leg of the rally, with retail buying in Nvidia running at roughly 9 standard deviations by 10am and more than 5 standard deviations in the Magnificent Seven, even as institutional participation stayed light. The desk notes 2Y yields are up 33.7bps and 10Y yields 26.7bps week-to-date, making equity resilience all the more surprising. Positioning Intel adds that over the past month most of the move was shorts being covered rather than new longs, with short exposure falling from +2.7z to +0.4z. On Nvidia, JPM credit stays Underweight, warning the bigger implications are for GPU financing and infrastructure deals where Nvidia acts as supplier, investor or provider of contractual support, while Harlan Sur cut his target to $215 after stripping China and other shipments from FY28 estimates. Interim CEO Colette Kress has reportedly pushed back on some of Huang's financing deals, which is exactly the risk we flagged in mapping every circular AI deal that now hangs on Kress.

Goldman's TMT specialist Sean Johnstone makes the same point: Nvidia has acted as "lender of last resort" to the neoclouds, and the key uncertainty is whether a new CEO will have the willingness or authority to deploy the balance sheet; Nebius fell 17% and CoreWeave 7% on Thursday, while AMD, Broadcom and Arista rallied as money rotated within AI. Goldman's EMEA trading desk notes Thursday was the 12-month momentum factor's best day on record relative to 3- and 6-month momentum as the AI trade unwound, with data center basket crowding at the 1st percentile; its high-touch flows were 1.2x better to buy, with long-onlys more than 3x better buyers and hedge funds more than 3x better sellers.
