Assuming there is anyone out there this morning after the global outlook outage, long-time readers of the EMR may remember the whirlwind period when I somehow managed to have three children within two years. Well, in a rather alarming reminder of where the time has gone, Maisie has her first 11+ exam this weekend. Our house is currently impossible to navigate without encountering a mock test paper, rubber or pencil sharpener. To complicate matters, she’s also going for an art scholarship, so the academic debris is now mixed in with paints, charcoal, coloured pens and pencils, and giant sheets of paper. And there’s only another year before we get to do it all again with the twins.

Meanwhile markets are finding their own end of year tests equally challenging. The Santa rally sleigh has been revved up a few times in recent weeks, only for the reindeers to pull up at the last minute, seemingly unconvinced by the aerial conditions. The last 24 hours have seen another aborted attempt, as investors once again grappled with the return of several headwinds. First, energy prices jumped after President Trump said the US didn’t need a deal with Iran. So that meant Brent crude unwound its earlier losses, ultimately ending the day (+3.30%) at $95.82/bbl. And in turn, that inflationary impulse led investors to price in more rate hikes next year, with the 2yr Treasury yield (+14.2bps) surging again to 4.88% (4.45% at the lows towards the end of last week). This backdrop didn’t help equities, with the S&P 500 falling -0.41% as it was also weighed down by Nvidia’s slide (-4.34%), which closed at a 7-month low after Jensen Huang resigned as CEO.

That initial caution yesterday followed President Trump’s post, which said that “We don’t need a deal with Iran. Those days have long since passed. We’ve got their money, Hundreds of Billions of Dollars, and we’ve got their Strait!” So that unwound the optimism since the midterms about some kind of diplomatic resolution. Indeed, it was only the previous evening that the WSJ reported that Trump was open to Vice President Vance restarting talks with Iran. So the post caused an immediate reaction for oil prices, and European natural gas futures (+6.47%) also posted their biggest jump in 3 months, closing at €92.26/MWh.

That backdrop added to the hawkish tone of recent sessions, with fresh concerns about inflation seeing investors price in more rate hikes for the months ahead. For instance, the rate priced in by the Fed’s September 2027 meeting was up +11.7bps on the day, meaning that 91bps of hikes are now priced by then. Bear in mind that stood at just 41bps a week earlier, so it just shows how things have turned thanks to the strong CPI print, the lack of a US-Iran deal, and the pickup in tech stocks from the lows. And with inflation and rate hikes rising up the agenda, that drove a fresh slump for US Treasuries across the curve. Indeed, the 2yr yield (+14.2bps) moved up to a six-week high of 4.88%, having risen by 42bps over the past week. And the 10yr yield (+13.3bps) saw its biggest rise in seven weeks, ending the session at 5.13%.

The US rates repricing supported the US dollar, with the dollar index (+0.25%) rising to its strongest level since April 2025 as the euro fell to 1.1055 against the greenback. By contrast, it weighed on gold (-2.78% to $3,877/oz) and Bitcoin (-3.84%), with the latter falling to its lowest level since August.

The question of Fed hikes will remain in the spotlight today, as the PPI inflation reading is out at 13:30 London time. Normally the PPI print doesn’t get as much attention as the CPI, but it does include several components that feed into the PCE inflation measure that the Fed officially targets. Moreover, Governor Waller’s speech on Tuesday said that a 50bp hike “should be considered” if core CPI was at 0.3% or above. So given that then happened, there’s now a strong focus on any remaining data points that could tip the balance in either direction.

Meanwhile, we had a few further Fed speakers, including Cleveland Fed President Hammack. She dissented in favour of a 25bp hike in October and maintained a hawkish tone yesterday, expecting that the Fed needs to “move to a restrictive stance of policy”. That said, on the question of a bigger hike, she said “I don’t think we’re behind the curve today, but if we get behind the curve, then that might be something that we need to consider”. Later on, while NY Fed President Williams suggested that the Fed will need to take further action as “inflation is far too high”, but that the Fed should also make sure “that we don’t do undue harm to our maximum employment mandate”. Meanwhile, Chicago Fed President Goolsbee said that the Fed was “inching our way into a territory that’s historically a tough spot for any central bank to try to get rid of that inflation”, while San Francisco Fed President Daly said she expected further tightening because of “consistent pressure on inflation”.

Otherwise yesterday, the main market headlines came from the tech space, as Jensen Huang resigned as Nvidia’s CEO. The company said that CFO Colette Kress would be interim CEO until a permanent successor was found. And in separate headlines, the Chairman of the House Foreign Affairs Committee said that Jensen Huang had agreed to testify to lawmakers, whilst Semafor reported that Nvidia faced an antitrust probe from the Department of Justice. In terms of the market reaction, Nvidia’s share price initially slumped over -14% at the open, before recovering the bulk of that to close “only” -4.34% lower. Nevertheless, that was still a 7-month low for its share price and it is now flat over the last 16 months. This also left the company as the worst performer in the Philly semiconductor index both yesterday (-0.54%) and on a YTD basis (-10.89%).

In turn, the NASDAQ (-0.39%) and the S&P 500 (-0.35%) posted similar declines. However, the Mag-7 (-0.05%) saw a slight outperformance in aggregate, in part thanks to Tesla (+1.69%) gaining as Bloomberg reported that it could announce a merger with SpaceX (+0.14%) as soon as December.

Elsewhere, tariffs were back in the spotlight with President Trump saying that tariffs on Mexico would be “immediately doubled” if Mexico did not stop illegal migration into the US. The headlines saw the Mexican Peso hit its intraday low against the US Dollar, although it then recovered to flat on the day by the close, outperforming most EM currencies.

Asian equity markets have largely reversed their early morning gains as tech has seen another reversal. The KOSPI is down -0.70% after rallying more than 3% at the open and the Hang Seng is also -1.22% lower, along with the ASX (-0.71%) and the Shanghai Composite (-0.30%). items.title: The Last Man Defending 'Open' AI Just Left The Building: How Jensen's Fall Clears The Way For A Federal Crackdown...
items.content_text:
The Last Man Defending 'Open' AI Just Left The Building: How Jensen's Fall Clears The Way For A Federal Crackdown...
Four months ago, Jensen Huang was the most powerful voice in Washington arguing that Americans should be allowed to download AI models and run them on their own hardware.

This morning he resigned as Nvidia's CEO, and he gave up his board seat too. A few hours earlier, The Information reported that Alice Huang (no relation), the former Megaspeed executive whom US intelligence believes was recruited by Beijing, had promised Nvidia chips to DeepSeek, the Chinese lab whose open-weight models have been eating American lunch (and tokens) all year.

We summed up what that means in one line:

*ALICE HUANG PROMISED NVIDIA CHIPS TO DEEPSEEK: INFORMATION

If you haven't set up your own open-weight system yet, you soon won't be able to.

— zerohedge (@zerohedge) November 12, 2026

Back in September we laid out the motive in "Here Lies The Motive: AI Leaders' Cunning Plan Exposed": terrify the public, demand emergency regulation, make compliance expensive, crush the competitors, consolidate. What that playbook was missing was a villain the public could actually picture. It now has one, and the villain sits squarely between Nvidia's chips, a Chinese spy and DeepSeek's open weights.

So, a thought experiment, with the same caveat we gave in September: the facts are real, the conclusion is interpretation. Nobody needed to plan the Jensen scandal for it to work as if it had been planned. And the way it works is by making a federal restriction on open models far easier to pass.

The Loudest Voice For Open Weights Just Went Silent

Rewind to July. After Moonshot's Kimi K3 sparked another "DeepSeek moment" for US AI stocks, the administration started weighing restrictions on Chinese open models. Huang responded by organizing the opposition. On July 24, 25 companies including Nvidia, Microsoft, Meta, IBM, Mistral and Hugging Face published "Open Weights and American AI Leadership," and Huang used his first-ever X post to amplify it. OpenAI, Anthropic and Google did not sign.

Four days later he was on Capitol Hill, meeting lawmakers and Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick, then telling reporters that "for the American industry, we need open weight for security, we need open weight for safety." Nvidia launched an industry coalition (the Open Secure AI Alliance) and kept shipping its own open Nemotron models. Washington blinked: the August 4 White House testing framework exempted open-weight models entirely.

That defender now has no role at Nvidia whatsoever. Goldman's Jim Schneider, who cut his price target to $220 from $300 this morning in his note on the management transition (available to pro subs), puts it in terms an analyst can say out loud:

"We believe that going forward, it may be more difficult for the company to negotiate new multi-party investments among ecosystem partners at the same scale it has done up to this point... We believe Nvidia's operations in certain jurisdictions could face more scrutiny going forward."

Translation: the company that bankrolled the open-weight lobby now has to spend every ounce of its political capital proving it isn't a Chinese export-control sieve. Interim CEO Colette Kress, a CFO, is about the last person to go picking fights with Congress over Hugging Face.

From Honeypot To DeepSeek: How A Sex Scandal Became An Open-Weight Story

Until this week, "ban open models" was a hard sell because the harms were abstract: benchmark gaps, jailbreak scores and distillation accusations. The White House's Michael Kratsios alleged in July that Moonshot had distilled Anthropic's Fable, which is not exactly the kind of thing that moves a swing-district voter.

Now look at the chain the scandal has laid out in a single week:

  • Megaspeed, the Singapore firm Alice Huang helped run, reportedly bought over $4.8 billion of Nvidia chips in two years, with nearly $2 billion installed in Malaysian and Indonesian data centers that allegedly serve Chinese customers remotely;
  • Bloomberg reported Monday that Moonshot (the Kimi lab) is renting Nvidia's top AI chips in China, and today that Alibaba rents Nvidia chips through Megaspeed;
  • and this morning, the alleged spy reportedly promised Nvidia chips to DeepSeek.

In other words, the three Chinese labs dominating the open-weight leaderboards are now all, in one way or another, in the same news cycle as smuggled American silicon and a suspected MSS asset. For a hawk, the story writes itself: Chinese open weights are built on stolen chips and distilled American models, then handed back to US startups for free. A year ago you needed a whiteboard to explain that. Now you need a tabloid front page.

And the scandal has already reached the Cabinet. As we reported earlier today, Treasury's Scott Bessent reportedly confronted Lutnick in the Situation Room, asking why Megaspeed still isn't on the Entity List ("I Don't Know"). Per Axios, Trump signed off on action against chip diversion three times this year, and Lutnick held it up each time. The man who was slow-walking the crackdown is now the one under the microscope. That's the kind of pressure that usually ends with somebody being seen to do something, and fast.

The Ladder Is Already Built

Washington doesn't need a new idea here. It only needs to climb a ladder it has been building for two years. As we laid out last month in "DeepSeek Is Now Designing Huawei's AI Chips... Just As DHS Orders It Ripped Out Of Federal Systems", the rungs so far are:

  • state and agency device bans in early 2025;
  • the FY2026 NDAA booting DeepSeek from the Pentagon and its contractors;
  • DHS Exclusion and Removal Order #2026-01, signed on July 24 (the same day as the open-weights letter, funnily enough) and made public in October, which reaches any third-party product "developed using DeepSeek implementations." That's fine-tunes and distillations of the open weights, not just the app;
  • the Senate Armed Services draft of the FY2027 defense bill, which would extend the ban to AI from ten more Chinese companies and their derivative models;
  • and the Gottheimer-Lawler bill, which pairs mandatory federal pre-release review with a ban on Chinese-developed open-weight models across federal systems.

It's the TikTok playbook: government devices first, everyone else later. What was missing was the political urgency to get from rung four to rung five, and that is precisely what the scandal provides. The midterms flipped both chambers, so Democrats take the gavels (and the subpoena power) in January. Elizabeth Warren said today that Huang's resignation "does not absolve him." House chairs want Huang in a closed-door session on November 18, and a bipartisan push is already trying to attach chip export controls to the must-pass defense package. A "no Chinese-derived weights" rider fits in that bill nicely.

Put the two camps on one timeline and the trend is hard to miss. Since early August, nearly every new dot has been red:

Interconnects' Nathan Lambert has warned the White House could restrict open-weight models above roughly the GPT 5.5 / Claude Opus 4.8 / GLM-5.2 tier within about six months. That was before the guy leading the resistance got caught in a honeypot.

Why Now? Because Cheap Tokens Are Winning

Follow the tokens. According to OpenRouter's October data recap, tokens rose 37% in a single month while price per token kept falling, and open weights now take about a quarter of paid spend, up from 11% in January. Chinese-origin models hit a weekly peak of 46% of OpenRouter's enterprise tokens in mid-July, up from under 1.2% in late 2024. Open-weight models handled around 60% of tokens from US-originating requests in August, and OpenRouter's own data team says the Chinese ones typically run 60% to 90% cheaper than flagship US models.

How cheap is cheap? At list prices, DeepSeek's V4.1 Flash charges $1.20 per million output tokens (half that off-peak) versus $10 for Claude Sonnet 5.5 and GPT-6.1 Sol, $20 for Claude Opus 5.5 and $50 for Claude Fable 5.1 and GPT-6 Astra. That's roughly 17x cheaper than Opus and 42x cheaper than the flagships (napkin math, list prices only). Adjust for how smart the models actually are and the gap barely narrows: on the Artificial Analysis index, the frontier closed models cost about 35 times more per point of intelligence than DeepSeek's Flash. The lone exception is Kimi K3, whose first-party API is priced like a closed model. Third-party hosts serving its open weights charge a small fraction of that on input, and Moonshot has since cut its K3.1 Pro to $2/$10. Pay up for the badge, indeed.

And the volume follows the price:

For now, the dollars mostly stayed home. In June, Chinese models pushed roughly 18 trillion tokens a week through OpenRouter versus about 5.5 trillion for US models, yet on the Vercel gateway open weights processed about 29% of tokens while generating less than 4% of spend:

That's the comfortable part for the closed labs. The uncomfortable part is the second panel of the first chart, which shows which way it's heading. Every time token prices halve, more workloads cross over from "premium closed API" to "good enough and nearly free," and the people who sell premium closed APIs can read a chart too. (We noticed the market had read it as well, pointing out that Goldman's momentum basket was up 70% in late June, just before Chinese open weight models flooded AI, and had turned negative on the year by mid-October.)

Which brings us back to cui bono. Lambert argues the restriction push is largely regulatory capture by the closed labs, Anthropic in particular. To be fair, Anthropic says it has never advocated a ban and instead backs mandatory safety testing for all sufficiently capable models, open and closed. But mandatory testing that only a handful of labs can afford gets you to roughly the same place, and nobody who sells tokens at 60-90% premiums is going to lose sleep if DeepSeek becomes a compliance headache for every Fortune 500 procurement desk.

The Case Against Our Own Thesis

We promised a thought experiment, so here's the other side, and some of it is strong:

  • There is no evidence of coordination. US scrutiny of Megaspeed predates the affair by a long way: Sen. Tom Cotton asked Commerce to investigate it in October 2025, and the New York Times flagged the Southeast Asian data centers that year. Spy scandals happen without anybody's help.
  • The administration has been going the other way. It exempted open weights from the August framework, and the NYT reported that a Commerce draft aimed at Chinese open-source models was halted inside government in favor of promoting US open models abroad. Lutnick, the man now under fire, worried that chip controls "will start a trade war with China." He doesn't sound like someone itching to ban Qwen.
  • Enforcement is a nightmare. The weights already sit on Hugging Face and millions of hard drives, and a weights-level ban runs straight into the First Amendment. A ban mostly binds law-abiding American startups, roughly 80% of which reportedly use Chinese open models somewhere in their stack.
  • The open lobby isn't just Jensen. Microsoft, Meta, Palantir and nearly 200 startups are still on record against restrictions, and OpenAI and Google DeepMind later signed an open letter opposing regulation of open-weight models.
  • Beijing may get there first. China's commerce ministry has floated export controls on model weights above certain thresholds. If the next Kimi and DeepSeek flagships never get open-sourced at all, Washington won't need to ban anything.

All fair points. But notice that every single one argues the restriction is harder. None of them argues it's less wanted, and wanting it is the thing this week changed.

Follow The Political Will, Not The Plot

Whether anyone planned it is beside the point; we suspect nobody did, at least not the honeypot part. What matters is what the scandal does to the incentives. The most effective defender of open weights is gone. His company has every reason to keep its head down. The Chinese labs that dominate open-model usage are now tied, in the public mind, to smuggled chips and a suspected spy. And a Democratic Congress arrives in January with subpoenas, a must-pass defense bill and a ready-made villain.

So yes, we think this ends with a lot more political will behind a federal restriction on open models. We doubt it arrives as a clean "ban." More likely it's the de facto version we flagged in October: procurement exclusions that widen from DeepSeek to every Chinese lab, then to anything "derived" from their weights, then to contractors, then "advisories" that let enterprise compliance departments do the rest. No law required. Once "derived from" is in the statute, the distance between "Chinese open weights" and "open weights" is just one lawyer's memo.

And if you want to know how fast the rhetoric is moving, listen to the Treasury Secretary. Speaking at the Heritage Foundation this afternoon, Scott Bessent blamed a Chinese AI model for the recent hacks that disabled refrigerators across French supermarkets (Bloomberg). Those attacks hit about 700 stores and France's public blood bank, and France's own foreign minister has pinned them on Iran's IRGC:

"I don't know who here saw the refrigerators and 150 grocery stores in France that got turned off... That was a Chinese model. Probably the worst of all worlds, the Iranians using a Chinese model. Sums up the world, doesn't it?"

Chinese models, he added, "are dangerous because they don't have guardrails."

Now compare that with where Bessent started. In July, right after Kimi K3, his line was that "this administration supports open source models, but what we do not support is IP theft." In September he told Congress that America needs more open models of its own, so that eventually nobody would use the Chinese ones. By October the talking point had become Chinese models that are "80%, 90% as powerful, without guardrails, that can be imported anywhere in the world." And today, Iranian hackers spoiling French groceries.

That's the arc from trade dispute (IP theft, sanctions) to national security threat (cyberattacks on critical infrastructure), and the second framing is the one where restrictive action tends to follow fastest: official rhetoric first, then an interagency review, then the rule. Bessent didn't say "ban" (and pointedly didn't mention Jensen), and he heads to Shenzhen next week with Trump to talk AI with Xi and He Lifeng. But a Treasury Secretary doesn't name "a Chinese model" as the weapon in an attack on European food supplies by accident. That's how you build the record for an Entity List designation, or something bigger.

As Goldman put it, Nvidia's operations "could face more scrutiny going forward." So could everyone else's Hugging Face downloads. We'll know a lot more next week, when Huang sits for his closed-door session on November 18 and Bessent sits down with the Chinese in Shenzhen. Until then, if you were planning to set up your own open-weight box, maybe don't wait for the Federal Register.

items.title: United Airlines Moves To Ban Use Of AI Agents In Booking Flights For Customers
items.content_text:
United Airlines Moves To Ban Use Of AI Agents In Booking Flights For Customers

Authored by Jacob Burg via The Epoch Times,

United Airlines is moving to ban the use of artificial intelligence (AI) agents to make flight reservations on behalf of customers over concerns of possible security risks and violations of federal regulations.

United warned travelers on Nov. 11 that sharing their account details with AI assistants could expose sensitive information and lead to "unintended purchases, account changes, or use of MileagePlus miles." For an AI agent to book a flight, a customer would have to give the model access to his or her personal account information, including payment credentials.

Allowing an AI agent to complete a flight check-in may also violate Federal Aviation Administration and U.S. Department of Transportation regulations, the airline noted, because flight check-ins require a human acknowledgment that bags "do not contain banned substances like explosives."

"As a result, United is taking steps to restrict access - directly within our digital platforms and indirectly via travel agencies and aggregators - to prohibit use by unauthorized, third-party personal AI agents or assistants. This work includes updates to our booking, ticketing, and distribution policies," the company said in a news release.

AI companies have begun rolling out agents that users can direct to make purchases on their behalf, including Meta's Muse and OpenAI's dots.

Walmart has also unveiled an AI agent dubbed Sparky that can help customers search for product deals, summarize reviews, and assist with ordering.

But some warn that giving AI agents access to payment information could expose customers to risks. Earlier this year, tech start-up founder Sebastian Heyneman asked an AI bot to help him secure a speaking spot at the World Economic Forum in Davos, Switzerland.

The AI agent then violated his original instructions and agreed to pay roughly $31,000 for a corporate sponsorship spot, Heyneman said, adding that he didn't have the money to pay the bill.

These potential problems make it a "reasonable move" for United to ban AI agents booking flights on behalf of travelers while the industry addresses the risks, said Shem Malmquist, aviation safety expert, former pilot, and visiting assistant professor of aeronautics at Florida Institute of Technology.

"An AI agent can make decisions or statements during a booking that the passenger may later plausibly say they did not make or authorize," Malmquist told The Epoch Times.

"That creates uncertainty about what was agreed to and who is responsible if something goes wrong, as well as a potential liability issue for the airline."

The airline is updating its online Digital Trust Center, where customers can see detailed rules and suggestions for using third-party AI agents.

United said safe use of an AI tool may involve asking the agent to search for potential travel destinations in a particular region during a specific time of year to avoid large crowds. However, customers should avoid providing the AI with any MileagePlus account numbers, passwords, or sign-in info.

United also offers a detailed FAQ section where customers can check what AI agent actions are currently permitted.

"As personal AI assistants evolve, United will continue to evaluate how these tools interact with our services, with a focus on protecting our customers," the airline said.

items.title: Mapping Alleged Chinese Spy Network Behind Banned Nvidia Chip Flows To China
items.content_text:
Mapping Alleged Chinese Spy Network Behind Banned Nvidia Chip Flows To China

Jensen Huang spent decades building Nvidia into a multitrillion-dollar AI chip giant. He ends the week out of the top job, with CFO Colette Kress stepping in as interim CEO. But for Jensen, he might have a future elsewhere ... 

Reports of three extramarital relationships, including one with an alleged Chinese spy, have prompted key House Republicans to request a briefing about Jensen's dealings and potential national security risks. 

Alice Huang, the suspected Chinese spy, was a former Megaspeed International executive, and a new Bloomberg News report finds how Alice potentially obtained restricted Nvidia chips that ended up at a Shanghai data center. 

The report traces 22 Dell Technologies servers containing Nvidia H800 chips purchased by Singapore-based Aperia Cloud Services that ended up at Shanghai's Yangtze River Delta Project, despite US restrictions on exporting those chips to China.

Via Bloomberg

A subsidiary of Shanghai Longteng Intelligent Computing, which Alice (also known as Haung Le in corporate filings) founded, listed the Dell equipment among 193 servers pledged as collateral for financing in January 2025. The equipment was valued at about  $73 million, and included 52 Super Micro Computer servers containing restricted Nvidia H100 or H200 chips. 

Via Sayari 

Bloomberg noted, "The filings didn't specify how the Nvidia chips in question were obtained, or whether Alice was personally involved in that transaction." She relinquished her Shanghai Longteng shares in 2017. Huang Yu, identified by The Information as her sister, remained the company's majority owner until January 2026.

Dell told the outlet that it "stopped all sales and support to Aperia International in February 2025 due to unauthorized diversion concerns." That month, Singapore authorities arrested Aperia's chief executive on charges of defrauding server suppliers. He has pleaded not guilty. Aperia has denied wrongdoing.

Via Bloomberg

Bloomberg also noted, "In addition to the Dell servers, it included 52 units manufactured by US-based Super Micro Computer Inc. and containing either Nvidia's H100 or H200 chips — both restricted from sale to China without a US license." 

The Shanghai project also has links to Megaspeed International, another company Alice founded and is under US investigation for alleged chip smuggling. 

"This activity, which surfaced through our analysis of Alice's network, warrants a national security and [technology] counterproliferation investigation," Brian Andersen, Tesari's vice president for national security applications and a former supervisory special agent with Homeland Security Investigations, told CNBC. 

CNBC also said, "Businesses connected to Alice Huang were linked with supplying Nvidia computing power to Huawei, according to documents reviewed by CNBC, around the same time she and Jensen Huang were first publicly seen together, in December 2023."

items.title: Trump's $40 Billion Mineral Push Enters Democrats' Crosshairs: Which Miners To Own, Which To Avoid
items.content_text:
Trump's $40 Billion Mineral Push Enters Democrats' Crosshairs: Which Miners To Own, Which To Avoid

The Trump administration's efforts to break China's grip on critical metals mining and refining span $40 billion across 160 mining and minerals deals, creating massive new targets for Democrats when they take control in January.

That strengthens the case for producing miners that did not take government handouts and have limited ties to the Trump administration, because top Democrats have already signaled plans to unleash lawfare on a scale the country has never seen before, in what appears to be an effort to derail the Trump administration's industrialization agenda.

Since President Trump signed an executive order in March 2025 to boost American mineral production, streamline permitting, and bolster national security, the federal government has entered into equity deals with MP Materials, Lithium Americas, Trilogy Metals, USA Rare Earth, and others.

The investments marked a highly unusual expansion of federal involvement in companies outside wartime or a financial crisis. This suggests the government's urgency to rebuild domestic critical mineral supply chains, including mining and refining, to break China's quasi-monopoly in critical materials.

The Trump administration wants to break China's grip on minerals because Beijing weaponizes trade against the US and has even slowed, or in some cases halted, critical mineral flows to the US and allied countries. 

Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick and Interior Secretary Doug Burgum have defended the federal government's investments in the critical minerals space.

A White House official recently told CNBC that the miner deals allow private capital to flood into these companies and supercharge operations.

With Democrats set to take control of both chambers of Congress early next year, many CEOs of these critical mineral mining companies will likely appear before committees to answer questions about how these deals work. That could draw unwanted attention to their stocks and create volatility for investors.

MP Materials has disclosed those risks to investors. Its Department of War deal, which combines an equity investment with a price floor and an offtake commitment, could face audits, investigations, congressional scrutiny, and litigation, the company warned in a filing.

"We may be subject to heightened scrutiny of our business activities with both government and non-government customers, government audits, investigations, congressional scrutiny, inquiries about conflicts of interest, civil or criminal enforcement by the Department of Justice (including actions under the False Claims Act), exclusion or limitation on future government-funded opportunities, suspension, debarment, and other administrative remedies," MP wrote in the filing.

If you want exposure to miners that did not make deals with the Trump administration and could avoid hearings on Capitol Hill, there are Freeport-McMoRan, Hecla Mining, Coeur Mining, Newmont, and Almonty Industries.

"We've always believed government's place in our business is as a customer, not a shareholder, and look forward to continuing to provide the U.S. and its allies with tungsten to support critical defense and industrial needs," said Lewis Black, CEO of tungsten miner Almonty Industries.

The VanEck Rare Earth and Strategic Metals ETF (REMX) captures the scale of the selloff: the fund, which holds some of the world's leading critical mineral producers, has lost roughly half its value since early summer.

Recall we wrote last month:

  • The Great Rare Earth Disconnect: Prices Up 23%, Miners Down 28%

We continue to favor the "owning the bottlenecks" theme as China restricts critical material supplies to the West. The focus remains on miners with conflict-free supply chains (ex-China) and now entirely independent of US government-backed financing.

items.title: British Universities Push Sharia Loans While Taxpayers Cover The Unpaid Tab
items.content_text:
British Universities Push Sharia Loans While Taxpayers Cover The Unpaid Tab

Authored by Steve Watson via Modernity,

British universities are now openly advertising government-backed "interest-free" student loans designed around Islamic finance rules.

The Alternative Student Finance product, based on the principle of takaful, replaces interest with a mutual "contribution" that is ring-fenced to fund other students on the same scheme rather than flowing back into the Treasury.

Official forecasts already expect nearly half of student debt never to be fully repaid, so British taxpayers will underwrite the shortfall while the ring-fenced pot serves a program primarily aimed at Muslim students, the Telegraph reports.

British universities are preparing to offer interest-free sharia-compliant loans to Muslim students, with repayments used to fund others joining the scheme rather than going to the Treasury. The plans have sparked concerns that they could create a "two-tier system" in higher education. ? https://t.co/pB9wmbam8j

— The Telegraph (@Telegraph) November 10, 2026

The scheme is open to anyone eligible for student finance, yet it exists because Islamic law prohibits interest.

Universities including University College London, Bristol, Leeds, City St George's, Newcastle and De Montfort have begun telling applicants the loans could be available in the 2026-27 academic year, describing them as "compatible with Islamic finance principles," "non-interest bearing" and "sharia-compliant."

The Department for Education paid the Islamic Finance Council UK more than £365,000 in public money to design it and has presented the arrangement as one of the first state-backed sharia-compliant student loan systems in the world.

Suella Braverman, Reform's education spokesman, said: "This outrageous anti-British scheme creates a two-tier education system and divided society. The scheme from Labour proves they are addicted to double standards in all aspects of British life."

She added that offering sharia-compliant loans risked "creating parallel institutions that are incompatible with the British way of life" and that "the whole idea is made even more farcical by the fact that the Treasury, and therefore British taxpayers, will have to foot the bill if they fail to pay."

The UK Government's priorities are absolutely wicked Knowing how graduates struggle with huge monthly repayments, they have decided to offer Muslims interest-free "Islamic finance" loans We really have to stop facilitating this, no wonder we are the Muslim destination of choice https://t.co/uuMeMOsVqM

— NW Nature Lover (@nwnatur) November 10, 2026

A Department for Education spokesman insisted it would be "completely false to assert that Alternative Student Finance arrangements would give favorable treatment to Muslim students."

He further stated that "all graduates will be repaying their loans in full regardless of which system they use, including an equivalent alternative to interest," and that the product "unlocks higher education for thousands more students and means that nobody is excluded from a university education because of their faith."

A 2021 Muslim Census survey of nearly 39,000 British Muslims found that 80 percent of students "feel conflicted" by regular loans, with 71 percent claiming the existing system discriminates against them.

Some Islamic scholars and universities, including Cambridge, have advised that mainstream loans are permissible and are "backed by the UK Fatwa Council."

The new product will be certified by an Islamic Finance Supervisory Board. Contributions are calibrated to match the repayment amount and schedule of ordinary student loans, yet the money stays inside the takaful pool instead of returning to general public funds.

This is not an isolated concession. Braverman's warning of parallel institutions incompatible with the British way of life sits alongside existing public fears of sharia-dominated society.

Public anxiety about parallel legal and social arrangements has already registered in polling. A YouGov survey published by King's College London found that 34 percent of adults believe there are "no-go" areas in London where sharia rules and outsiders stay out.

Separately, the Home Office has granted skilled-worker sponsorship licenses to Islamic bookshops that stock texts by Muslim Brotherhood figures promoting jihad against secular governments and guidance on wife-beating.

The pattern is consistent: institutions and government departments accommodate one set of religious rules inside a common system, ring-fence resources around them, and leave the costs and the social friction with everyone else.

When nearly half the loans are expected to go unpaid, the Treasury - not the takaful fund - absorbs the loss. When universities advertise the product as "sharia-compliant" and "for students who can't take out interest-bearing loans for religious reasons," the two-tier character is not hidden.

Critics see a deliberate expansion of differential treatment that normalizes separate financial, legal and cultural tracks.

The practical result is a higher-education finance system that treats one religious prohibition as a design constraint while the broader public continues to subsidize the unpaid portion.

The direction of travel is clear. The Labour government is not merely tolerating parallel systems; it is building them with public money and official certification. Each step is framed as inclusion or equal access. Each step further entrenches a two-tier arrangement in which British law, British finance, and British norms are bent to accommodate a minority's religious prescriptions while the costs, the unpaid debts, and the social friction fall on everyone else.

This is not accommodation at the margins. It is the deliberate construction of separate tracks inside the state, and it will not stop at student loans.

items.title: After France, Belgium Is Europe's Next Debt Flashpoint
items.content_text:
After France, Belgium Is Europe's Next Debt Flashpoint

Authored by Thomas Kolbe via American Thinker,

In the shadow of France's sovereign debt crisis, other smoldering fires threaten to become a raging blaze. In Belgium, things could come to a flashpoint that sets the entire eurozone alight.

Among the many catastrophic lessons of the great financial and sovereign debt crisis more than a decade ago, one came as a surprise: it is not the size of an economy that determines the outbreak of a sovereign debt crisis. It was tiny Greece, accounting for just 2.5 percent of the eurozone's total economic output, that came within a hair's breadth of blowing the union apart from within. At the time, Greece's sovereign debt reached 170 percent of GDP. Austerity was then the order of the day, and given the country's homogeneous population and undeniable state lethargy, it was ultimately accepted.

But things hung by a thread. For in the eurozone, states are chained together through the bond market. The EU, and above all the eurozone, is simply not a federation like the United States. Debt consolidation under the leadership of the European Commission may be Brussels' goal, but given the growing tensions on the continent, it is likely to remain an illusion.

Brussels has long been using an instrument that points in this direction: through NextGenerationEU, the Commission raises joint funds on the capital markets in order to make them available to member states in the form of grants and loans. Countries such as Spain and Italy in particular benefit from this. The political trick is to increasingly cushion national financing problems through joint debt and EU funds. Joint liability is thus growing not necessarily through an open decision in favor of a debt union, but gradually through new financing instruments.

In Brussels, it has been recognized: in the event of a crisis, a fragmented capital market exacerbates the problem. If one member comes under pressure in the bond market, speculators shift their capital in cascades through the ranks of the fiscally weakest members, setting off a domino effect. Moreover, the construct stands and falls with the creditworthiness of the Federal Republic of Germany - and lately, that is no longer in such good shape either.

Much has recently been said about France's political paralysis and its sovereign debt, growing at an annual rate of more than five percent, which is likely to reach more than 120 percent of economic output by the end of the year. A financial catastrophe is quite obviously brewing here, one that even a doubled Federal Republic of Germany in better years could hardly cope with out of its own economic strength.

France is undoubtedly currently the biggest problem in the euro debt club. And it remains to be seen whether a possible President Marine Le Pen could turn the fiscal tide - or whether the Germans would be drawn more strongly into joint liability in order to steer Europe's second-largest economy into calmer waters after all.

Right next door, to the north, a similar financial catastrophe is brewing in comparatively manageable Belgium.

Belgium's budget deficit this year is well above the long-expired Maastricht criteria and is likely to come in at around 5.2 percent of economic output. The national debt has piled up to more than 110 percent of GDP. Belgium's situation looks fatal. All the more so as Prime Minister Bart De Wever has crashed and burned with his consolidation plans. A savings plan worth billions was planned up to 2029, but it failed because the coalition fell out over which social groups should ultimately foot the bill for the reform policy. While some in the alliance are pushing for spending cuts, others are calling for tax increases and a greater burden on wealth and capital.

For Belgium is not simply a country with a budget hole. It is a state whose federal architecture has splintered fiscal responsibility between Flanders, Wallonia, and Brussels. While thrifty Flanders insists on cuts, the more free-spending Wallonia demands protection from the fiscal axe. Every austerity policy thus quickly becomes a regional power struggle, a test for the entire federal system.

In Belgium, different fiscal policy views collide, further straining the deep fault lines between the regions. De Wever offered his resignation on November 2nd, thereby making the blockade visible. King Philippe initially did not accept the resignation, but instead instructed the prime minister to enter new negotiations. A solution to the fiscal bottleneck still remains up in the air.

It almost seems as if France's budget-policy paralysis is blowing across the border into Belgium. In this way, the crisis is approaching the country in whose capital the center of power of the EU is located. Belgium appears - as the home of the EU institutions - like the fated place of the looming crisis.

What is more, it is strangely ironic that it is precisely in Brussels, with Euroclear, that the custodian for a large proportion of the frozen Russian central bank assets is based. The enemy's state treasure - within reach and yet so far away. No one has yet dared to commit this fatal breach of the law, to access Russian state assets in order to postpone their own financial problems, at least for a time.

Belgium's internal fragmentation and fiscal vulnerability are also reflected in the financial markets. The yield on Belgian ten-year government bonds rose from around 3.5 to 4.25 percent within a few months. This is unmistakable consolidation pressure: the markets, investors, banks and pension funds are demanding that the overstretched state apparatus, with a state share of around 54 percent of GDP, be consolidated, that the welfare state be cut back and that the excessive taxes be reduced to a normal level. In terms of the burden on the average earner through taxes and social security contributions, Belgium is the OECD leader.

If consolidation fails - and at present there is little to suggest that it could succeed - Belgium too will be drawn into a debt vortex of higher interest rates, rising refinancing costs and growing risk premiums, which could ultimately lead to the collapse of public finances.

Like so many European states, Belgium suffers from a postmodern illusion: that an oversized welfare state is indispensable, that the state must take responsibility for the economy and the distributional processes of a society - down to regulating the details of everyday existence. The costs of this policy are now coming to light. And they could ultimately culminate in a major sovereign debt crisis that would burst the illusions of state omnipotence and the belief in the state's ability to shape society.

Tyler Durden Fri, 11/13/2026 - 06:00

items.title: 旅行者 1 号距离地球的距离达到一光日
items.content_text: 北京时间 11 月 18 日 18 时 16 分 07 秒，旅行者 1 号与地球的距离将达到约 259 亿公里，相当于光在真空中传播 24 小时的距离，也就是“一光日”。如果将一光年划分为 365 个刻度，每格代表一个光日，那么 1977 年 9 月 5 日启程的旅行者 1 号，经过近半个世纪的飞行，终于抵达了第一格。今年 10 月，旅行者 1 号曾经历一场短暂的通信中断。NASA JPL 称，18 日和 19 日，NASA 深空网络连续两次未能收到探测器预期发出的信号。直到 20 日，信号才重新出现，异常原因仍在调查中。对于一艘运行近半个世纪的探测器而言，设备老化始终是地面团队面临的挑战。旅行者 1 号依靠三台放射性同位素热电发生器供电，利用钚-238 衰变释放的热量产生电能。随着发电功率逐年下降，电力日益紧张。两艘旅行者探测器的可用电功率每年约减少 4 瓦，工程师必须精打细算地安排每一瓦电。旅行者 1 号发射时搭载了 10 台专用科学仪器，如今仅剩磁强计和等离子体波动仪仍在运行。

items.title: 非洲加速发展太阳能
items.content_text: 在津巴布韦首都哈拉雷（Harare）的一个工业区，如果想要寻找一个新的发电项目，你需要抬起头。Limpopo Way Power 太阳能发电站没有传统的独立厂区，而是将一排排太阳能电池板铺在两座仓库的屋顶上，它通过协议向工厂供电。在非洲和亚洲的很多地区，太阳能革命随处可见。能源智库 Ember 的报告预测，2026 年非洲太阳能新增装机量有望达到 17 GW，同比增长 45%。报告作者之一的 African Tech Futures Lab 研究总监 Joel Nana 表示，我们正见证一场自下而上的革命。多种因素共同推动了非洲太阳能的普及：光伏电池板成本的下降、市电供应的不稳定性、日益加剧的全国性能源危机，发电机所用柴油成本的上涨，以及非洲大部分地区拥有充足且稳定的日照。Deloitte 南非公司的 Jayne Mammatt 表示，非洲很多国家缺乏完善的电网或稳定的电力供应，而太阳能技术已相当成熟，成为一种可在本地直接部署的切实可行的方案。非洲太阳能增长量的 75% 是小型太阳能发电装置，Solar as a Service（缩写 SaaS）就是其中一种活跃的模式。非洲仅有 10%-20% 的家庭实现了通电，其增长空间远未见顶。

items.title: 台积电内部员工数据泄露
items.content_text: 台积电在递交到 SEC 的一份声明中称，部分现任及前任员工的个人数据在未经授权的情况下出现在了一个外网上。相关信息与存储在某云服务提供商系统服务中的数据相吻合。台积电表示，目前尚未发现其自身系统遭到入侵的证据，且这些数据与其业务运营或客户信息无关。公司正通知受影响的员工，与该云服务商、相关调查机构以及一家外部网络安全公司合作，以查明事件真相。据报道，黑客在 DarkForums、BreachForums 等地下论坛上拍卖 6.9GB 容量的台积电员工数据，起标价为 3 BTC。黑客提供的样本显示数据涵盖员工姓名、生日、职称、住址、身分证字号、手机号码、银行帐户等资讯，甚至还有紧急连络人电话。黑客称，如果一周内没有找到买家，将会公开所有数据。

items.title: 地球冰冻圈不再处于安全运行空间内
items.content_text: 地球上的冰冻部分——包括冰盖、冰川、海冰、积雪和永久冻土——在调节地球气候、水资源供应和碳循环等诸多生态系统服务中发挥着至关重要的作用。但根据中外研究人员的一项新分析，冰冻圈的基本功能已不再处于安全运行空间（SOS）之内；其被推越界限的程度将给地球人口带来长期挑战。作为地球界限（planetary boundaries）方法的一部分，安全运行空间（SOS）定义了地球系统保持稳定与韧性、并使人类及生态系统能够繁荣发展的环境界限。研究人员对关键控制变量（包括陆地冰体积、海冰面积、积雪面积和永久冻土温度）进行分析后得出结论：冰冻圈的完整性正在经历“加速且部分不可逆的丧失”。他们指出，这些控制变量的状况已经恶化，或已注定将恶化至超过定义冰冻圈安全运行空间的全新世水平。他们写道：“为了维护和恢复地球系统的韧性，现在需要全球采取紧急行动，停止并逆转温室气体和黑碳排放，并减少人类局部干扰的影响，例如在冰冻圈地区扩张基础设施。”

items.title: 《幻兽帕鲁》开发商给员工五天假期畅玩 GTA 6
items.content_text: 《幻兽帕鲁（Palworld）》开发商 Pocketpair 宣布了五天特别假期，让员工可以畅玩即将发售的 GTA 6。GTA 6 将于 11 月 19 日上市，有望创下游戏销售新记录，预计首周销量将高达数千万份拷贝。Pocketpair 表示，所有想要玩 GTA 6 的员工都可以利用这一特别假期。它同时表示《Palworld》和《Craftopia》的开发顺利，会按计划推进。此前游戏外设制造商罗技也宣布给所有员工放假一天去畅玩 GTA 6。

items.title: 英伟达员工请愿让黄仁勋复职
items.content_text: 英伟达创始人黄仁勋辞职后公司内部员工发起请愿让他复职。一名员工在内部意见系统上写道：我们都是人、都会犯错，黄仁勋办了那么多好事，理应得到第二次机会。黄仁勋担任英伟达 CEO 长达 33 年，领导公司成为世界市值最高的公司之一，很多员工都认为他对公司的贡献巨大，不应因此遭到抹杀。英伟达员工还通过 LinkedIn 公开表达对他的支持，且无人公开支持罢免他。

items.title: 无印良品客户信用卡数据泄露
items.content_text: 运营无印良品的良品计划公司社长清水智 12 日就遭遇非法访问问题在东京都内召开记者会，致歉称：“给大家带来了巨大担忧与困扰，对此由衷道歉。”包括已经解约的在内，信用卡的完整号码等可能已有约 109 万条信息泄露。清水承认信息管理存在疏漏，说明称部分系统存在漏洞，未能阻止非法访问。清水透露说“本应废弃的信用卡信息仍被保存”，表示“将推进建立不持有非必要信息的机制”。对于信息有可能泄露的信用卡，他表态说将承担换发新卡的手续费。良品计划 10 月 30 日发布消息称，官方 APP“MUJI APP”遭到非法访问，最多可能有约 2726 万条客户信息泄露。此后的调查又发现，信用卡的完整号码、货到付款的配送地址等约 44 万条客户信息也可能外泄。除了官方网上商城和官方 APP 的部分功能外，公司已暂停了相关服务，正在推进加强安全对策。

items.title: 美国扣押了从币安盗走的逾 12 亿美元加密货币
items.content_text: FBI 周四宣布扣押了价值逾 12 亿美元的加密货币。这些加密货币是黑客组织 TraderTraitor 此前从全球最大加密货币交易所币安盗走的。币安在这次事件中被盗走了价值 63 亿美元的加密货币，其中约半数的被盗加密货币——全部是稳定币，稳定币发行方能通过智能合约冻结交易——被成功冻结，但另外一半是难以被冻结的比特币、以太币和 XRP。美国政府表示它通过法庭授权扣押或冻结了逾 12 亿美元的加密货币。它没有透露更多细节。

items.title: 微软云服务全球宕机
items.content_text: 微软云服务全球宕机，受影响服务包括了 Outlook、Teams 和 OneDrive 等办公工具以及 AI 工具 Copilot。微软通过其社交媒体账号表示正全力解决该问题。根据 Downdetector 的报告，截至周四 18:00 GMT，全球报告的 Outlook 故障数量接近 14 万。目前无迹象表明此次大范围宕机是由网络攻击引起的。微软表示，受影响的用户可能无法查看部分文件，或无法在日历应用中查看详细信息。Copilot 也可能无法正常运行。即时通讯和在线会议功能基本保持正常。微软称此次事故是由部分服务器意外不可用导致的，这给其余系统造成了沉重负担。与微软有合作的 AI 巨头 Anthropic 和 OpenAI 也报告了故障。

items.title: 用户抱怨难以在流媒体服务上找到想看的内容
items.content_text: 根据尼尔森的 Gracenote 对美国、巴西、法国、德国、墨西哥和英国的 3000 名 18 岁及以上的流媒体用户进行的调查：虽然流媒体平台内容无比丰富，但用户经常找不到想要看的内容。逾 51% 的受访者表示：内容和流媒体服务的极度丰富，反而让人更难找到想看的东西。19.2% 的受访者表示，他们总是或经常遇到这种情况：不知道该看什么，也找不到想看的内容，最终只能去做别的事。27.4% 的受访者表示，他们总是或经常在试图观看特定节目时却因无法在流媒体平台上找到它，最终只好放弃。47% 的受访者表示，他们花在寻找观看内容上的时间比一年前更多了，平均耗时 12 分钟。72.3% 的受访者表示，他们希望拥有一份整合所有已订阅流媒体平台中可用节目的完整指南。

items.title: 印度苹果代工厂发生三名合同工死亡事故
items.content_text: 塔塔电子位于泰米尔纳德邦、为苹果公司 iPhone 生产零部件的工厂发生三名处理废水处理设施的合同工死亡事故。事故发生于周一晚间，地点位于 Krishnagiri 的 Hosur。工人在检查一个外部纳滤罐时吸入了气体导致了悲剧的发生。三名工人被送往一家私立医院，医生在他们抵达时确认其已经死亡。塔塔电子承担了印度约 40% 的 iPhone 组装工作，其余由富士康负责。近几个月塔塔电子的 iPhone 业务面临诸多挑战，包括遭遇勒索软件攻击，以及引发了水污染的担忧。随着苹果将生产扩大到中国之外地区，印度已成为一个关键的制造枢纽，目前全球约四分之一的 iPhone 产自印度。

items.title: 黄仁勋辞职
items.content_text: 英伟达宣布，黄仁勋即日起辞去公司总裁、CEO 及董事会成员职务；Colette Kress 被任命为临时 CEO。在确定正式继任者之前，Colette Kress 将继续担任执行副总裁兼首席财务官。董事会已启动继任者遴选程序，将同时考虑内部和外部候选人。Harvey C. Jones 被任命为董事会首任主席。

items.title: BMI 误判数百万人肥胖
items.content_text: 中外研究团队基于中国、英国、美国、西班牙4国、超 84 万人的数据研究证实，肥胖诊断不能只看体重，更不能单凭BMI(体重除以身高的平方)“一刀切”。长期以来，全球普遍以 BMI 作为筛查和判定肥胖的核心指标。但论文第一作者及共同通讯作者、华中科技大学同济医学院公共卫生学院教授潘安指出，BMI 存在天然缺陷——它只能算出体重与身高的关系，却无法区分增加的究竟是肌肉还是脂肪，更无法判断积累的脂肪是否已伤害到内脏器官。此项研究中，潘安团队与合作者通过研究超 84 万人的跨国数据发现，5.2%—8.6% 参与者的肥胖程度被 BMI低估，1.2%—3.1% 被高估。在体脂过多者中，仅 22.7%—31.3% 出现归因于肥胖的器官功能受损或身体功能受限(“临床肥胖”)，绝大多数仍处于器官及身体功能未因肥胖而导致受损的“临床前肥胖”阶段。在超过 10 年追踪随访中，研究团队还发现，与健康人群相比，处于“临床前肥胖”阶段的人全因死亡风险增加19%，而一旦恶化为“临床肥胖”，死亡风险将陡增至 69%。此外，约 77%—91% 的“临床前肥胖”者并没有进展为“临床肥胖”，这意味着只要在器官未受损的早中期阶段及时进行科学干预和生活方式重塑，绝大多数人有望守住健康底线，阻断病情发展。

items.title: 天文学家发现一个恒星系统每八分钟发射一次射电信号
items.content_text: 天文学家发现一个不同寻常的双星系统 GPM J071507−114153，由一颗白矮星——一颗恒星死亡后留下的致密核心——和一颗类太阳 G 型恒星组成。白矮星自转一周八分钟，它每八分钟发射一次射电信号。这是首次在绕类太阳恒星运行的白矮星中探测到射电脉冲。此类双星属于被称为长周期瞬变天体（long-period transients，LPT）的天体。天文学家至今共探测到十多个 LPT 天体。天文学家表示，通过白矮星发射出的射电脉冲，研究团队探测到了类太阳恒星上的恒星耀斑。

items.title: 《Big Walk》开发商利用 AI 修 Bug 引起争议
items.content_text: 热门独游《Big Walk》开发商 House House 承认在生成式 AI 帮助下修 bug，结果在独立游戏节（Independent Games Festival，IGF）上引发了激烈争议。IGF 评委团的多名成员周一发表联合声明，强烈反对使用生成式 AI 的游戏，并督促官方制定强有力的反 AI 政策。《Big Walk》是一款非常受欢迎的合作冒险游戏，使用了 Unity 引擎开发，开发商发现游戏存在一个拖慢游戏速度的 bug，联络 Unity 工程师后被告知无法解决，于是询问了生成式 AI 工具，大模型提供了一种修复思路，House House 在此基础上写出了用于最终产品的 10 行代码。这种利用 AI 工具加速开发和辅助修 bug 的做法在行业已经非常普遍。但 House House 的做法引发了争议，游戏在 Steam 平台还遭遇了差评轰炸。游戏开发者 Brendan Keogh 认为这种对生成式 AI 零容忍的立场其效果可能会适得其反，可能会促使其它游戏开发商不披露使用 AI 的信息，而未来要避开完全不使用 AI 工具的游戏几乎是不可能的。

items.title: M87 星系黑洞存在甜甜圈结构
items.content_text: 作为人类首张黑洞照片，距地球约 5500 万光年、质量超太阳 60 亿倍的 M87 星系中心超大质量黑洞(M87*黑洞)被形象称为“甜甜圈”的图像，自 7 年多前发布以来广受关注，学界对其独特环状结构是否存在也有争议。一项研究独立验证了M87*黑洞经典重建图像中的独特环状结构，确认“甜甜圈”图像无误，最新的重建结果利用一款新开发的独立成像算法，其生成的新图像与原始图像高度重合。研究人员将 M87* 黑洞数据集输入一个成像算法，以验证之前的图像重建结果。该算法将望远镜按闭合三站而不是两两配对进行划分，再综合个体望远镜的测量结果，这么做能计算校准误差，最后得到了一组符合这些标准的重建图像。

items.title: 《Python 之禅》作者 Tim Peters 去世
items.content_text: Python 语言作者 Guido van Rossum 发表文章悼念了 2026 年 7 月 15 日去世的 Tim Peters（享年 74 岁）。他写道：Tim Peters 最为人熟知的贡献是撰写了《Python 之禅》，“但对我而言他是我的良师益友，也是这门语言的共同设计者之一。”Tim Peters 很早就接触了 Python 语言，说服 Guido 让 Pytho 支持整数（int）与浮点数（float）之间的混合运算，他在邮件列表上非常活跃，总是细致耐心回答用户的各种问题，以至于获得了 Timbot 这一绰号。他在 2002 年带来 一种全新的排序算法 Timsort，它后来被 Java 和 Android 采用。如果没有 Tim Peters，Python 绝不会有今天的模样。

items.title: 电视厂商回应有关监视的提问
items.content_text: 在 LG 电视监视用户的报道引发广泛关注之后，The Verge 联系了亚马逊、苹果、Google、海信、LG、松下、Roku、三星、索尼、TCL 和 Vizio 等机顶盒和电视厂商，询问了相同的问题，其中海信、松下等无任何回应，TCL 等厂商很多问题也没有直接回应，而 LG 即便被发现监视用户但其代表在回应时基本上完全予以否认。举例来说，电视是否会在用户观看内容时收集屏幕截图、录制视频或音频——即使用自动内容识别（Automatic Content Recognition）技术：亚马逊、Google 和苹果都否认使用 ACR 技术，而 LG 声称它的 ACR 功能不会收集或存储电视上的屏幕截图、屏幕图像、屏幕录制内容或视频录制内容，而是利用电视音频处理组件从播放内容的音频中生成音频指纹去识别当前正在观看的内容。

items.title: 腾讯计划将半数员工部署到 AI 原生业务
items.content_text: 腾讯创始人马化腾称，他愿意将半数员工投入到 AI 原生业务，并敦促公司逾 10 万名员工拥抱这项定义时代的技术。 马化腾本周在年度演讲中告诉员工，行业已进入“大航海时代”，他将腾讯的核心业务比作陆军，将新的 AI 业务比作海军。马化腾称，50% 的人要像陆军一样，守土有责，通过提效去做好现有的核心业务；另外 50% 的人像海军一样，拥抱浪潮，探索 AI Native、拓展新的发展空间。近期有传言称腾讯计划裁员50%，对此知情人士称，公司资源适应 AI 时代的重新调度，可能是所谓“裁员 50%”的谣言出处，该说法完全不属实。

items.title: MAGA Rep. Freaks Out at His Own Party After Election Bloodbath
items.content_text:
Texas Representative Chip Roy ripped into his own party during a half-hour rant on the House floor Thursday, slamming Republicans for failing to prioritize the American public over their own political interests.

“Somebody tell me why Republicans lost last Tuesday? I’ll say it’s because they were focused on themselves and the ruling class and not the people,” Roy declared.

Roy rejected the idea that conservative candidates lost because of the ongoing war in Iran, instead insisting that voters are tired of “corporate crony government interests” and Republican-led redistricting efforts that ran roughshod over local electorates. He celebrated the fact that Republicans passed Donald Trump’s “Big, Beautiful Bill” in 2025, but lamented that they “didn’t campaign on it.”

“Spent our time trying to focus on political power rather than focusing on the people who sent us here to represent them,” he said, noting that the culmination of his party’s midterm failures “pisses [him] off.”

“The arrogance! The arrogance of the powers that be, the masters of the universe, who tell you that that’s what you have to do,” Roy continued. “And when you pursue political power over the people, you lose, and that’s what happened. That’s what happened.”

The 54-year-old Texas lawmaker did not run for re-election during the 2026 midterm cycle. Instead, he cast his hat in the race for Texas attorney general and lost. He will leave Congress on January 3.

Republicans suffered historic losses last week, losing control of both the House and the Senate by a spectacular margin. Even historically deep-red states such as Kansas, Iowa, and Texas ideologically flipped, ushering in a new wave of Democratic leadership.

In Texas, the conservative caucus even lost four of the five supposedly GOP-friendly seats they had created through recent gerrymandering efforts, initiated at the president’s behest.

items.title: Alito Goes After Lower Court Judges Who Dare to Rule Against Trump
items.content_text:
Conservative Supreme Court Justice Samuel Alito thinks that many of the lower court judges were “unjustified” in blocking President Trump’s policies.

Alito made the comments at a Federalist Society panel on Thursday.

“They are dedicated and they are skillful, but they’re not perfect and they make mistakes,” Alito said. “And in some instances, I think they have gone far astray in abuse of their powers.”

Alito made no mention of Trump’s attacks on the judges who rule against him or which rulings exactly he believed were an abuse of power.

Lower courts have blocked Trump’s attempts to limit mail-in voting, end birthright citizenship, build his White House ballroom, among other things. For Alito to suggest that those orders were “unjustified” is highly questionable, but unsurprising from one of the court’s most right-leaning justices.

Alito also warned that a new Democratic congress could “defund” or “turn off the lights” at the Supreme Court—a claim that seems hyperbolic on its face.

items.title: Full List of Senators Who Back Chris Van Hollen Over Chuck Schumer
items.content_text:
The race for Senate majority leader is heating up.

Maryland Senator Chris Van Hollen has emerged as the leading alternative to New York Senator Chuck Schumer in a sign of the incoming Democratic majority’s preference for change and an aversion to establishment politics.

So far, 16 lawmakers have staked their claim behind Schumer, while just four have explicitly expressed support for Van Hollen. The coalition behind Van Hollen is still developing, however: five other senators and senators-elect have expressed interest in a potential change, even if they haven’t mentioned Van Hollen by name.

Lawmakers supporting Schumer:

  • New York Senator Chuck Schumer
  • Virginia Senator Tim Kaine
  • Maryland Senator Angela Alsobrooks
  • Rhode Island Senator Sheldon Whitehouse
  • Arizona Senator Ruben Gallego
  • Arizona Senator Mark Kelly
  • Ohio Senator-elect Sherrod Brown
  • New York Senator Kirsten Gillibrand
  • Pennsylvania Senator John Fetterman
  • Connecticut Senator Richard Blumenthal
  • Hawaii Senator Brian Schatz
  • Maine Senator Angus King
  • Nevada Senator Catherine Cortez Masto
  • Nevada Senator Jacky Rosen
  • Wisconsin Senator Tammy Baldwin
  • Rhode Island Senator Jack Reed

Lawmakers supporting Van Hollen:

  • Maryland Senator Chris Van Hollen
  • Vermont Senator Bernie Sanders
  • Michigan Senator-elect Abdul El-Sayed
  • Minnesota Senator-elect Peggy Flanagan

Other lawmakers not supporting Schumer or who want new leadership:

  • Illinois Senator Juliana Stratton
  • Kansas Senator Adam Hamilton
  • Maine Senator-elect Troy Jackson
  • New Hampshire Senator-elect Chris Pappas
  • Texas Senator-elect James Talarico

Another 16 senators or senators-elect have not yet committed as to whether or not they will support Schumer, according to an analysis published Friday by Primary Democrats. Fifteen have yet to take a public stance on the issue. Altogether, 25 Democrats have veered away from Schumer—nearly half of the at least 55 Democratic seats that will dominate the upper chamber come January.

items.title: The Real Reason Chris Van Hollen’s Challenge to Schumer Is a Big Deal
items.content_text:
Senator Chris Van Hollen—a lawmaker who thinks creatively about deploying congressional processes toward progressive ends—announced Thursday night on MS NOW that he’s challenging Chuck Schumer for the post of Senate majority leader. Listen to the interview carefully, and you’ll notice that around half a dozen times, Van Hollen consciously emphasized the word “power.”

Here’s why that matters. Van Hollen is unlikely to prevail against the deeply connected Schumer. But his bid could still accomplish something important. It could force a serious discussion in the Democratic caucus about how far to go in wielding congressional power—and which authorities they’re willing to fully deploy—to check Trump’s lawlessness and derail his efforts at authoritarian consolidation, which are very much ongoing despite last week’s electoral bloodbath.

That’s the big public argument among Democrats we need right now. Because on this particular question, the party is all over the place.

Van Hollen wants his leadership bid to be understood in such terms. “I believe that we should use our full power in the United States Senate to respond to the calls of the American people,” he told MS NOW’s Jen Psaki. He cited the need to defund Trump’s Iran war as an example, saying Democrats should end it “now” because it’s “illegal and senseless.”

Van Hollen’s intended message is clear: The next Democratic leader should be willing to use maximal power to check Trump’s illegal and lawless conduct. So what should a big public argument over how to do this look like?

This week, Brian Beutler and I published a long TNR piece on exactly this topic. The threshold issue, we argued, is as follows. It’s nice that Democrats are vowing aggressive oversight and accountability efforts. But what will they be willing to do when Trump and his co-conspirators contemptuously decline cooperation with congressional demands, by throwing subpoenas in the garbage, laughing at letters requesting information and documents, and possibly even refusing to appear at hearings?

How will Democrats respond at that point? As Beutler and I argued, the most potent recourse might be a willingness to aggressively wield the power of the purse as a weapon, by, say, being willing to defund parts of agencies that refuse to comply with legitimate oversight demands. Will Democrats be willing to do this? That’s the critical question. It will help decide—far more than boilerplate promises of “accountability” will—how successful Democratic efforts to stop Trump’s corruption and lawlessness will actually prove to be.

On that topic, Van Hollen’s interview with MS NOW’s Psaki—which was otherwise good and illuminating—didn’t shed much light. Indeed, it raised some causes for concern.

For instance, while Van Hollen did strongly support impeaching Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, he was oddly resistant to impeaching Trump himself. Van Hollen also opposed impeaching Attorney General Todd Blanche, who has enthusiastically carried out Trump’s staggeringly corrupt orders for prosecutions of Democratic critics, including sitting members of Congress. Van Hollen asserted that they do merit impeachment but insisted it might take time from “kitchen-table issues,” which should be a “priority.”

Yet this answer revealed a strange disconnect. Van Hollen did stress that Blanche’s Justice Department shenanigans should face intense oversight. But left undiscussed was the fact that impeachment boosts congressional authorities and tends to produce more insider witnesses of malfeasance. This would make it easier for Democrats to overcome inevitable DOJ resistance to that oversight. Impeaching Trump might do the same more broadly.

In fairness, one might argue that even though impeachment does maximize congressional investigative authorities, it still detracts too much from addressing voters’ affordability concerns and signals lack of concern over them. (Beutler and I offered our own rebuttal to this in our piece.) But even if so, the likelihood that impeachment would put more teeth in accountability must at least be engaged with. Van Hollen should say why he’s willing to forgo that additional oversight advantage.

A leadership battle is exactly where such debates can be fleshed out.

On MS NOW, Van Hollen did strongly argue for Democrats to stand firmly for defunding the Iran war as the December 11 deadline for new government funding looms. He said Democrats should be willing to shut down the government to force an end to the war. That bodes well, suggesting he’d be willing to wield the power of the purse aggressively to force oversight compliance. But we need more clarity. Shutting down chunks of agencies to compel cooperation will create awkward political moments. We need to hear Van Hollen and Schumer debate how far to go in this regard.

Similarly, Representative Jamie Raskin has said Democrats should use the spending power to defund corrupt and baseless prosecutions ordered by Trump. That will also create politically challenging moments. We need Van Hollen and Schumer to debate this too.

The big defunding question will become a fault line in Democratic politics soon enough. The progressive group Indivisible—which backs Van Hollen’s bid—has sent a memo to Democrats on Capitol Hill arguing that real accountability must include the following:

Deploying the power of the purse: refusing to appropriate an agency or department, or even specifically the salary of the executive branch member who is being subpoenaed until information is supplied.

As Leah Greenberg, a co-founder of Indivisible, told me, the next Senate leader must charge Democrats with being “creative in using every tool they can to hold the Trump administration accountable.”

It seems self-evident that Van Hollen is more likely to carry out this mission than Schumer. That said, Schumer can now surprise everyone by signaling newfound aggressiveness himself. The key threshold question is: Will Democrats be willing to deploy all the congressional authorities at their disposal to stop Trump’s lawlessness and thwart his ongoing effort to consolidate an authoritarian state? On this urgent matter, a leadership battle could prove illuminating indeed.

items.title: Scott Colom Pushes Back on Schumer After Historic Mississippi Win
items.content_text:
Newly elected Democratic Senator Scott Colom is pushing back after Senator Chuck Schumer took credit for his win, refusing to commit to backing him for Senate majority leader next year.

Colom told MS NOW’s Symone Sanders-Townsend Thursday that he spoke to Schumer after his victory the day before and “thanked him for his part in making this happen.” Colom made sure to stress that it was the people of Mississippi who chose him to be a senator, not Schumer.

“He did initially understand that our party has to look south for future leadership. It’s not accurate to say he recruited me, though, because the people of Mississippi recruited me,” Colom said. “You think I was listening to somebody that lives in Brooklyn when I was deciding to run for United States Senate? No, I listened to the people of Mississippi.”

In a New York Times interview last week, Schumer said he recruited Colom to take on Mississippi’s incumbent Republican, Senator Cindy-Hyde Smith. When Townsend asked Colom if he would support Schumer to lead the Senate next year, Colom wouldn’t commit.

“I gotta know my options, and I’m not trying to be cute,” Colom said. He said he didn’t think it was “a good thing” that Schumer and Representative Hakeem Jeffries, who is currently in line to be the next speaker of the House, “both live in the same borough” of New York City.

“I’m looking for a person that’s going to be committed to Mississippi and rural voices,” Colom added. “If you’re able to listen to those voices and make sure that you understand their needs and putting them in position to be successful, then that’s the type of leadership I want.”

It’s telling that arguably the most surprising Senate victor from the midterms won’t immediately back Schumer. Colom joins several other senators and senators-elect in refusing to support Schumer becoming majority leader, and Senator Chris Van Hollen announced Thursday that he will be challenging him for the position.

Major labor unions, Senators-elect Abdul El-Sayed and Peggy Flanagan, and Senator Bernie Sanders are now throwing their support behind Van Hollen. Who will Colom support when the choice comes to a vote?

items.title: Walmart Holiday Meal Basket Is Sadder Than Ever as Trump Tanks Economy
items.content_text:
A year ago, President Donald Trump lied to Americans about how much Thanksgiving dinner would cost them—now the prices have only gotten worse.

Last holiday season, Trump plugged Walmart’s yearly Holiday Meal promotion as proof he’d beaten the Democrats on low prices. Spoiler alert: That wasn’t true at all. Fast-forward a year, and Walmart has unveiled its newest holiday promotion, which offers a snapshot of Trump’s crumbling economy.

Walmart’s newly unveiled 2026 Holiday Meal contains 17 products and can feed a crowd of 10 for a record-low price of $3.50 per person. Walmart claims that this year, shoppers will receive 18 percent more items than last year, and a 12 percent lower price for the same items compared with last year.

A quick trip to Walmart’s website, however, reveals that the price of the company’s Holiday Meal has decreased by swapping the items for cheaper options, and forgoing cooking and holiday staples.

While this year’s basket has more products than the 2025 Holiday Meal, which contained only 15 products and boasted feeding 10 people for less than $4 per person, the newer iteration scraps carrots and macaroni and cheese, adding corn muffin mix, sweet potatoes, mini marshmallows, and whipped topping instead.

These changes can’t hide the fact that the items from last year’s basket have only gotten more expensive. A year ago, the items included in Walmart’s 2025 Holiday Meal Basket cost a total of $35.51. Now they cost a total of roughly $39.72.

By comparison, the company’s original Holiday Meal, launched in 2024, included 29 items and served eight people for less than $7 per person. The items in that holiday basket now cost roughly $63.45, increasing drastically from the $55 price tag at its debut. The 2026 basket does not include certain items from the original, including onions, carrots, celery, seasoning, pecan pie, or cranberry sauce.

Increasing prices are a direct result of spiking energy costs from Trump’s war against Iran, as well as his disastrous tariff policies. As of October 2026, the estimated year-over-year headline inflation rate has risen to 4 percent. The producer price index rose 0.3 percent in October, putting the annual rate at 6.5 percent, the highest rate in four years. Policymakers are beginning to worry that inflation is so widespread that it’s even starting to affect categories that are not driven by oil prices or tariffs, CNBC reported Thursday.

Clearly, Americans have no illusions about how Trump’s policies have affected prices. Last week, voters issued a stunning rebuke of Republican leadership by flipping both the House and Senate blue in the midterm elections. American voters continue to be interested in affordability. At Walmart, they might get it, but with Trump, they certainly won’t.

items.title: Trump Tries to Control Nvidia Leadership as Scandal Blows Up
items.content_text:
Donald Trump tried to keep Jensen Huang atop Nvidia. It didn’t work.

The president called Huang earlier this week, encouraging the ex–artificial intelligence chief to resist internal pressure to remove him, The New York Times reported Thursday.

Huang resigned as Nvidia’s CEO, president, and board member Thursday morning, after he was caught in two scandalous affairs with direct reports, and another with a Chinese businesswoman that U.S. intelligence agencies had identified as a Chinese spy.

Trump reportedly knew about Huang’s affair—and his spying partner—for months. State Secretary Marco Rubio informed Trump about the alarming relationship moments before Huang joined the presidential trip to Beijing at the president’s request. It was at least the second time that Trump had been informed of Huang’s ties to the Chinese government, inside sources told the Times.

But Trump did not act on the information.

Instead, the president has repeatedly denied that he had any knowledge of the illicit affair before it was unearthed by U.S. news organizations. On Tuesday, Trump refuted the Times’ report, telling a reporter in the White House press room that he “didn’t hear about” the scandal in May. Trump added that he spoke with the Nvidia leader earlier that day, sharing that Huang insisted he had “absolutely no idea that the person in question was a spy.”

The president did not mention that he had also attempted to influence Nvidia’s leadership during that phone call.

Nvidia emerged in recent years as the largest semiconductor company in the world, and a precious American asset in the burgeoning AI tech wave. In January 2025, Nvidia was announced as one of the “key” technology partners in the Trump administration’s $500 billion public-private initiative to jump-start AI-focused data center development, dubbed the Stargate Project. Months later, Trump allowed the company to export previously banned chips to China, loosening trade restrictions on tech that Washington feared could be used against U.S. national security interests.

Yet Huang’s intimate relationship with an alleged foreign asset didn’t seem to bother the president. Instead, Trump was more focused on dollar signs, concerned about the potential financial consequences if Huang was forced out of the company he co-founded in 1993. (Trump’s interest stems beyond the broad scope of the economy, however: The president’s 2026 financial disclosures revealed that he purchased between $1 million and $5 million of Nvidia stock earlier this year.)

Trump isn’t done meddling in Nvidia’s corporate decisions now that Huang is gone, either. On Thursday, the president blasted his opinion about the company’s potential succession plan on Truth Social, writing that “there is only one man to take” Huang’s place: “TIM COOK of Apple. A Legend replaces a Legend!”

items.title: Two Unions Representing 700,000 Members Back Van Hollen Over Schumer
items.content_text:
Two unions with a collective 700,000 members have endorsed Maryland Senator Chris Van Hollen for Senate majority leader. Both also explicitly called for Senator Chuck Schumer not to run.

On Friday the more than 90,000-member Office and Professional Employees International Union, or OPEIU, and the 600,000-member International Association of Machinists and Aerospace Workers Union, or IAM, both made their support for Van Hollen known in separate press statements.

“The overwhelming support for congressional Democrats at this time in history cannot be squandered. After careful deliberation in consultation with the OPIEU Executive Board, consisting of union leaders from coast to coast, we are respectfully asking you to decline to seek to become the next Senate Majority Leader,” the OPEIU wrote in its letter addressed directly to Schumer. “The American people are desperate for change, and for a new generation of political leaders to deliver that change. We are grateful for the decades of support you’ve shown for organized labor throughout your career, but we must empower the next generation of political leaders at this pivotal time in our nation’s history.”

“The IAM Union proudly supports Senator Chris Van Hollen for Senate Majority Leader. He’s a proven champion of working people who will fight to unrig an economy stacked against working families,” the union wrote in a press release.

“Senator Van Hollen understands this is a fight of Workers vs. Billionaires and has the courage to deliver the change voters demanded. Workers did their part on election night. Now it’s Senate Democrats’ turn. Senator Van Hollen is the right choice.”

Protest against Schumer’s leadership, which was once considered an inevitability, has grown substantially. The longtime New York senator has been criticized by the left wing of the Democratic Party for his beholdenness to Israel, the American Israel Public Affairs Committee, crypto, artificial intelligence, and corporations in general, as well as a lack of progressive vision on issues of affordability and health care. He has also been criticized for failing to adequately support the campaign of Florida Senate candidate Angie Nixon and backing moderates who failed to win Democratic primaries in Michigan and Maine. On Friday, Mississippi Senator-elect Scott Colom pushed back on Schumer’s claim that he “recruited” him.

At least 10 senators or senators-elect—from Bernie Sanders to Elissa Slotkin—have refused to endorse Schumer’s leadership. That animus has also trickled down to Representative Hakeem Jeffries’s candidacy for speaker of the House, and for nearly identical reasons.

Schumer still thinks he has an excellent chance at winning the leadership position.

“I welcome any discussion about the future of our caucus and the important work ahead,” Schumer wrote Thursday night. “I’m proud of what we’ve accomplished together—55 seats and counting is an amazing result—and I have the votes to continue serving as Democratic Leader.”

That statement was not well received, getting ratioed badly on X. Most of the comments called for him to step down.

This story has been updated.

items.title: Dems Have a Plan to End the Iran War. It’s Risky, Though.
items.content_text:
You’re reading The TNR Blue Book. Get daily scoops, strategy, and developments inside the liberal ideas factory delivered right to your inbox. Sign up for free.


Inside Washington

Democrats won in November in no small part because of their opposition to the war in Iran. Now they have an opportunity to stop that war even before new members of Congress take office. The catch? It could hurt federal workers and the people who depend on them—and burn a lot of political capital.

Representative Ro Khanna and Senator Chris Van Hollen have suggested using the December 11 government funding deadline to push for an end to the war. In this scenario, Dems would withhold votes from a continuing resolution (CR) to keep the government funded, demanding that Congress attach restrictions to war funding if it wants the CR to pass. That, of course, could lead to a government shutdown, and many lawmakers aren’t eager to go down that path just ahead of the holiday season.

“I understand the impulse,” Representative Becca Balint said about the plan to use the CR as leverage. But, she added, “we want to make sure that we are not continuing to—I want to use the right word here—terrorize our federal workforce. They have been through hell and back again.”

The two Democratic appropriations leaders, Senator Patty Murray and Representative Rosa DeLauro, have remained noncommittal on whether they want the CR to include restrictions on war funding. “We’re looking at all options,” Murray told reporters on Thursday. Meanwhile, DeLauro signaled that she’d like to pass a short-term CR to avoid a shutdown and work on a more substantial funding bill in the new Congress. “I want to make it as short as possible,” she told reporters.

House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries likewise declined to endorse a particular strategy and instead deferred to DeLauro. “I don’t want to get out ahead of Congresswoman DeLauro, but House Democrats have uniformly opposed providing any additional money to Donald Trump’s war machine, to Pete Hegseth’s war machine, over in the Middle East,” he said in a press conference on Thursday.

“I think that we should be looking for every way in which not to have a shutdown,” DeLauro told me when I asked for clarification on her position. “But I understand the view that there shouldn’t be the billions of dollars that are being requested, you know, for Iran, and we need to move to end that war. So we’ll look for the various ways in which that might be accomplished.”

Congress has used a continuing resolution this way before. In 1973, legislators successfully used a funding package to force President Richard Nixon to stop bombing Cambodia. Last week, a group of 40 civil society organizations sent a letter to Congress pushing lawmakers to adopt this CR strategy. “We don’t think we should spend one more minute, spend one more penny, to fund this illegal war,” said Cavan Kharrazian, senior policy adviser at Demand Progress, which was a signatory of the letter.

Democrats could also use the National Defense Authorization Act to restrict the war, either by inserting provisions to stop the flow of funding or by withholding votes. The CR is a stronger bet, Kharrazian explained. “The NDAA is considered must-pass, but continuing government funding has much more leverage to it,” he said.

On Thursday, several lawmakers remained tight-lipped on whether they want to use the CR to restrict war funding. “We’re going to do everything we can to bring this war to an end. It’s illegal, a war of choice, and we’re going to do everything we can to keep the government funded,” said Senator Tammy Baldwin. When I asked if she’d prefer not to attach war funding to the CR, she just repeated the same sentence.
