Senator Mazie Hirono seemed open to using the CR as leverage. “I think we should make it very clear that the war needs to end, and whatever vehicle we’re going to use for that, I will support,” she said. At the same time, she said she hoped to avoid a government shutdown.

Progressives in the Senate insist that the plan is to keep the government running and say that they need to take the risk regardless. “When we vote on appropriations, we intend to fund the government and stop funds for this war. It is what the American people demand, and what they deserve,” wrote Senators Chris Van Hollen, Michael Bennet, Tammy Duckworth, and Bernie Sanders in a statement.

Van Hollen’s advocacy for ending the war comes as he is considering a challenge to Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer for the majority leader job next year. “I think this is a really important moment for Democratic leadership,” he told The Washington Sun last week. “Are the Democrats, including the Democratic leadership, going to listen to the verdict of the American people and vote to end this war?”

Even if Democrats could theoretically pass a stopgap CR and return to the funding issue again in January, some think that would be an early capitulation for the party, fresh off their November wins. “We should have that fight now,” Kharrazian said. “We shouldn’t allow the money spigot to continue, for even a month.”

—Emma Janssen


Outside Washington

A story to watch, semi-buried in a Washington Post piece about Dems’ new power in state legislatures and governorships: Texas state Representative Brian Harrison, the outlet notes, “has called for a special session to limit the governor’s executive powers while Republicans still control the legislature.” He tells the Post: “If we don’t limit those, [Hinojosa] may well be able to advance her priorities without passing almost any legislation.”

Harrison is not the only lawmaker thinking along these lines. In Ohio this week, anticipating not just Amy Acton’s first days in office but the loss of a GOP supermajority, Republican state Representative Ron Ferguson introduced a joint resolution to amend the state constitution to require only a simple majority to override a gubernatorial veto. Other proposals on the table, according to the Ohio Capital Journal, include one to “expand the General Assembly’s ability to rescind state Department of Health orders”—which Republican House Speaker Matt Huffman called a “good thought.” None of this is new: GOP legislatures in Wisconsin in 2018 and North Carolina in 2024, for example, moved to curtail gubernatorial power in lame-duck sessions before a Democratic governor was set to take over.

Elsewhere:

  • NBC reporter Sahil Kapur noted on Thursday, following the news of Democrat Scott Colom’s stunning victory in Mississippi, that Republican Senator Cindy Hyde-Smith’s official website continues to feature “a 2023 article about how she single-handedly blocked Colom’s nomination to be a federal judge.” For more on this remarkable race, check out The New York Times’s story from last week about Angela Lewis, whose father, James Chaney, was murdered by Klansmen in Mississippi days after her birth. The article describes how Lewis, a nurse, drove straight after an overnight shift to her polling place in Meridian to vote for the candidate who will now become the state’s first Black senator since Reconstruction.
  • The Guardian’s Sam Wolfson explores the phenomenon of the manosphere turning on Donald Trump. The “gay jokes, casual racism, and rape apologia” remain the same, and many of the key players still want immigrants deported. But now they’ve decided that “MAGA is gay.”

—Heather Souvaine Horn


The Ideas Factory

Paparo about “deterrence in the Pacific,” exploring the complexities of U.S. competition with China in the region. Bruce Jones will offer opening remarks, and Lynn Kuok and Michael E. O’Hanlon will moderate.In case you missed it: The World Resources Institute published a useful analysis this week, as Democrats pivoted to thinking about how to deliver on affordability promises, and global policymakers convened in Antalya, Turkey, for COP31 (the United Nations’ annual climate conference). Can electrification help with the affordability crisis? Yes, it can, WRI’s Clem Perry and Nick Wayth write in their explainer. But in order to harness the potential affordability benefits, governments need to make the switch “affordable up front” for households and businesses, “reduce the financing costs for clean power,” and ensure—among other things—that the cheaper price of producing renewable energy is actually reflected in the price passed on to consumers. While that may sound complicated, consider this striking scenario they outline to show the potential benefits:
Take home heating. Electricity can deliver cheaper warmth even when it costs more per unit than gas. A heat pump moves heat rather than generating it by burning fuel, delivering three to four units of heat for every unit of electricity purchased — an effective efficiency of 300-400%. Even at the lower end of that range, a heat pump uses 70% less purchased energy than a modern gas boiler operating at 90% efficiency. That efficiency advantage means that even if electricity costs three times as much per unit as gas, the energy cost of heating is still 10% lower.

—Heather Souvaine Horn


In Closing

Good Week: Scott Colom

While the Democrats have been celebrating their midterm wave for more than a week, the party’s nominee for Senate in Mississippi had to wait until Wednesday for his victory to be declared. And it’s the most historic of all of them this election season: Colom will be the state’s first Democratic senator since segregationist John C. Stennis left office in 1989, and the state’s first Black senator since Reconstruction.

Bad Week: Jensen Huang

The drip-drip of bad news finally swamped the co-founder and CEO of AI chipmaker Nvidia, who resigned on Thursday after The New York Times reported on a second affair—this one with a subordinate, as opposed to a suspected Chinese spy. That proved too much to withstand, even for the head of the $4 trillion company at the heart of the AI investment boom.

—Ryan Kearney


Political Trivia Question of the Day  

Who was the legendary Senate majority leader in the 1960s and ’70s who shepherded through all the major Great Society legislation, and what state was he from? (Sign up for The TNR Blue Book to find the answer in tomorrow’s newsletter.)

—Michael Tomasky

items.title: Leaked Texts Reveal How Much Power Kristi Noem’s Rumored Boyfriend Had
items.content_text:
Former Secretary of Homeland Security Kristi Noem’s relationship with senior adviser and rumored boyfriend Corey Lewandowski crossed both professional and personal lines.

Leaked emails and Signal messages reveal that Lewandowski was directly involved in responsibilities beyond that of an unpaid “special government employee,” as the Trump administration classified him, directly planning third-country deportations and weighing in on the high-profile deportation of Kilmar Ábrego García to El Salvador.

The messages were obtained from the Department of Homeland Security by the nonprofit American Oversight through a Freedom of Information Act request, before they were shared with Politico. Many of them were redacted, but from what was visible, it was clear that Noem’s DHS treated Lewandowski as a high-ranking official, equal to Noem herself, rather than as a special adviser.

Deputy Homeland Security Secretary Troy Edgar once sent an email to his top aide with a list of items to report to “S1 and Corey,” where “S1” referred to Noem. Lewandowski also received many of the same briefings as Noem and Edgar, including ones about deportation cases and operations in Djibouti.

In some high-level email and Signal chat exchanges, Lewandowski was taking full charge with Noem absent. He wrote to other high-ranking officials such as DHS spokesperson Tricia McLaughlin, Immigration and Customs Enforcement deputy director Madison Sheahan, and DHS senior official Joseph Mazzara, who gave him updates on department projects.

Lewandowski took particular delight in news of deportations. “Praise Jesus,” he wrote in one message after an immigrant was deported to South Sudan, despite having no ties to the country. “I love deportations,” he wrote in another message a week later.

Lewandowski’s tenure in DHS was marked with rampant corruption, and now there is further proof he was practically running the department along with Noem, whom he was more than likely in a relationship with despite both of them being married. Months ago, Democrats sought to preserve all of the department records related to Lewandowski. Now that they have recaptured Congress, Lewandowski, and Noem will have a lot more to worry about thanks to these new revelations.

items.title: Another Big Job for Democrats: Make Jim Jordan Toxic Across America
items.content_text:
Earlier this week, I wrote a piece taking aim at the ridiculous “affordability vs. accountability” debate among Democrats, arguing that they obviously have to do both—and more. Such is the nature of our continuing crisis that, even after these amazing midterms, the Democrats will need to do four, five, six things at once.

For example, they must not train their investigative sights only on the Trump administration. They need to go after bad corporate actors whose misdeeds have nothing to do with Donald Trump: banks and companies imposing junk fees, private equity buying up everything that isn’t nailed down (volunteer fire departments?), health care and farming monopolies, the Nerd Reich tech companies, businesses that are using algorithms to rip people off and laughing about it. Life isn’t unaffordable only because of Trump’s war. It’s unaffordable because too many corporations are nickel-and-diming people to death, because they know they can get away with it. Elizabeth Warren gets this, and I hope other Democrats do.

So that’s a third thing. Here’s a fourth: Hakeem Jeffries (assuming he’s the House speaker, which we should assume for now) ought to identify several House members from safe districts who know how to attack and assign them one task and one task only: Make the name Jim Jordan a toxic one across this great land.

Jordan is now the House Republicans’ leader, having won election to the post this week, and he’s one of the most thoroughly odious figures in—well, certainly in Congress today. Is it too much to say in recent American political history?

As we shall see, I think not. The House GOP caucus is a true Murderers’ Row of crypto-fascists who hate every good thing this country stands for. But for wall-to-wall awfulness, it’s hard to top Jordan. It stands to reason that the Republicans decided that he is the man to lead them, because he embodies everything that’s appalling about them.

Specifically, he embodies three traits that have always surrounded corrupt and decadent political movements. The first and plainest is that he hates democracy. We know this because he was up to his eyeballs in the January 6 insurrection. He attended meetings at the White House in late 2020 with administration figures like Mark Meadows and Stephen Miller, devoted to discussions of how to challenge the election results. On January 5, he forwarded to Meadows a text message from a right-wing lawyer describing how Vice President Mike Pence could refuse to certify certain electoral votes.

There’s surely more, but we don’t know a lot of it, and we may never know. Jordan initially cooperated with the House January 6 committee chaired by Democrat Bennie Thompson, then he stopped. The committee subpoenaed him—which, as a lawyer and duly elected member of Congress, he had to know was a legal and valid thing for them to do. He defied it. This, despite having issued 91 subpoenas on his own when he was chairing the House Judiciary Committee. It all led Liz Cheney to remark: “Jim Jordan knew more about what Donald Trump had planned for January 6 than any other member of the House of Representatives.”

And it led Sarah Longwell, the former Republican who broke ranks and left the party to found Defending Democracy Together and now leads the important anti-Trump website The Bulwark, to tell The Atlantic’s Ron Brownstein in 2023, when Jordan ran for House speaker: “Nominating Jim Jordan to be speaker is not them acquiescing to antidemocratic forces; it is them fully embracing antidemocratic forces.”

The second trait is his utter aversion to substance. The job of a legislator is to legislate. But the job of a bloviator is to bloviate, and that’s wholly what Jordan has spent the last 19 years doing. As Steve Benen noted in his righteous smackdown of Jordan this week, the man has “quite literally never passed bill.” Look for yourself.

Here is his official Congress.gov page, which lists all legislation each member has under their belt. He’s sponsored four pieces of legislation in his entire two-decade career that have passed the House; none have become law.

Did these efforts revolve around, oh, energy policy or national security or tax policy? Of course not. They concerned appointing a committee on the “weaponization” of the federal government by the Biden administration; demanding that Attorney General Eric Holder investigate alleged targeting of conservative groups by the IRS (a phony Obama-era scandal); holding Attorney General Merrick Garland in contempt for defying a House subpoena (!); and expressing the support of the people of the United States for flood victims in Ohio. At least the last one is the normal meaningless stuff that members of Congress do.

That’s it. Nearly 20 years. Even if you relax your standards, eliminate the search filter “agreed to in House,” and just look at the number of bills he’s introduced, that number is 55. In two decades. Compare that record to Jamie Raskin, his Democratic counterpart on the Judiciary Committee. In a mere nine years, Raskin has introduced 149 bills. Three times the number in less than half the time. Jordan’s pathetic record is a hallmark of corrupt, fascist parties. The people who rise to the top are pointedly not the people who make some vague attempt to do their jobs. They go on propaganda “news” networks and lie about the opposition.

Jordan’s implacable resistance to doing the actual work of a legislator caught former GOP Speaker John Boehner’s eye, who wrote of Jordan—his fellow Ohioan—in his memoir: “I just never saw a guy who spent more time tearing things apart—never building anything, never putting anything together.”

Finally, the third characteristic of decaying political movements is scandal, and on this front, Jordan faces allegations that are just this side of sickening. Ohio State University wrestling team doctor Richard Strauss abused—as determined by the university—at least 177 male athletes in his tenure. Some of those athletes were wrestlers. Jordan was an assistant coach during part of Strauss’s tenure. He has denied vehemently for years that he had any knowledge of Strauss’s abuse. A pretty large number of wrestlers say otherwise. As Newsweek reminded its readers this week, with reference to a 2025 documentary about the scandal: “Former wrestler Dan Ritchie said in the film that Jordan’s assertion that he knew nothing was ‘a flat-out lie.’”

It’s quite astonishing that a party that had a House leader this century who was literally enmeshed in a wrestling scandal—Dennis Hastert pleaded guilty in 2015 to paying hush money to cover up his own abuse of high school wrestlers, admitting to a judge that he abused an unspecified number of boys—would choose as its leader a man who has such similar charges hanging over him (not of committing abuse himself but of knowing about it and doing nothing). But then, denial of this type is yet another trait of decadent movements.

So there it is. There’s plenty of material. Come January, Jordan will be, after Trump and Vice President JD Vance, the most prominent Republican in America. In the trench warfare that will characterize the next Congress, Democrats are going to have to play hardball. If John Boehner can call Jordan a “political terrorist,” one would hope that the Democrats can. And if Jordan’s approval rating isn’t south of 20 percent in a year’s time, the Democrats haven’t done their job.

This article first appeared in Fighting Words, a weekly TNR newsletter authored by editor Michael Tomasky. Sign up here.

items.title: Republican Senator Blasted for Breaking Federal Financial Law
items.content_text:
Billionaire Senator Jim Justice broke the law by failing to file his annual financial disclosure report on time. Now he’s facing a reckoning on Capitol Hill.

The Senate Select Committee on Ethics issued a letter of admonition to the West Virginia Republican this week, slamming him for effectively hiding his finances from the public.

“The public must feel confident that Members never place personal financial interests ahead of the best interests of the United States,” committee Chair James Lankford and Vice Chair Chris Coons wrote in the letter. “Your actions failed to uphold that standard, resulting in harm to the public trust and confidence in the United States Senate and a violation of federal law.”

The Ethics in Government Act of 1978 stipulates that all federal officials—including lawmakers, senior executive branch officials, and candidates for national office—disclose their annual finances. The law was drafted after Richard Nixon’s Watergate scandal, and was intended to combat corruption and restore faith in Washington.

By law, officials must submit their financial reports by May 15. Justice asked for and received two extensions, pushing the deadline to August 13, but he didn’t heed that deadline either. His filing assistant acknowledged the deadline in six separate communications, according to the letter. A week and a half after the latest deadline passed, the committee ordered Justice to submit his report by August 28, a date he also ignored before ultimately filing on September 8.

Justice is unique in his noncompliance. The letter noted that “in the 47 years since the governing statute was enacted, the Committee has no record of any other Member failing to file a timely annual financial disclosure report.”

The committee acknowledged Justice’s rationale for the delay—which was apparently affected by his filing assistant’s “significant family hardship”—but nonetheless argued that “this does not abrogate your personal responsibility as a U.S. Senator to comply with governing federal law.”

The letter is an unprecedented wrist slap for a misbehaving lawmaker, but it is not actually tantamount to a formal punishment. Whether or not the Senate takes the issue a step further remains to be seen.

items.title: Bessent Publicly Throws Lutnick Under the Bus as Nvidia Scandal Grows
items.content_text:
Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent placed blame for the Trump administration’s inaction regarding Megaspeed, the Chinese firm at the center of the Nvidia spying scandal, solely on Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick.

“There’ve been reports that there was some tension between you and Secretary Lutnick about why Megaspeed was not placed on the Entity List,” Bessent was asked on Friday morning on CNBC. “Could Treasury have done that? Was it only Lutnick that could’ve done that?”

“I can tell you there was coordination. It was Treasury, War, [the U.S. trade representative], and State. They were in favor of putting Megaspeed on the entity list for months. But Commerce has the pen,” Bessent replied. “You will have to ask [Lutnick] about their internal process.”

WOW -- Bessent throws Lutnick under the bus: "Treasury, War, USTR, and State were in favor of putting Megaspeed on the entity list for months, but Commerce has the pen. You will have to ask them about their internal processes." https://t.co/vJEegPggTa

— Aaron Rupar (@atrupar) November 13, 2026

Questions are swirling about Lutnick’s close relationship with former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, who recently stepped down over reports of his affair with Megaspeed executive (and suspected Chinese intelligence asset) Alice Huang. The Commerce Department did not list Megaspeed on its Entity List, which restricts U.S. technology from foreign businesses believed to pose a national security risk. In fact, the department has added no businesses to the list since October 2025, despite Megaspeed long being under investigation.

The Trump administration was aware for at least a year that Alice Huang was likely working on behalf of the Chinese government. And yet, according to Bessent and multiple other sources, Lutnick actually spent the year going out of his way not to target Megaspeed and stop it from sending Nvidia chips to China. Lutnick has finally agreed to testify in Congress about the scandal.

“The obvious question is why did [Lutnick] choose to sell advanced chips?” Republican Senator John Kennedy told Politico Wednesday. “Secretary Lutnick needs to answer that in front of God and country. If I were he, I’d call a press conference this afternoon and explain what happened and why he agreed to sell them chips, and I would stop doing it.”

items.title: Todd Blanche Forced to Admit Free Speech Is Not a Crime
items.content_text:
Attorney General Todd Blanche has admitted that there was absolutely nothing illegal about Democratic Senator Elissa Slotkin’s supposedly “extortionist” remark about working for Donald Trump.

During an interview on SiriusXM’s The Dan Abrams Show Thursday, Abrams cornered Blanche about Trump’s demand that Slotkin be investigated by the Department of Justice over comments she made at the University of Chicago last week. Slotkin said at the time that she wanted to send a message of “deterrence” to young people who might consider working for the Trump administration.

“I want them to be like, ‘Lord, that might be buying myself a ton of problems that I don’t want. And so let me avoid participating in that,’” she said.

In a post on Truth Social shortly after, Trump claimed that Slotkin was “saying that she is going to go after all young people that believe in Republican Values, and that give even the slightest inclination to be a Republican.”

“The imprisonment should be against these EXTORTIONISTS, and Republicans should get smart, fast!” Trump wrote, adding: “By copy of this statement, I am ordering the Department of Justice to look into this criminal act, immediately!”

But in the radio interview Thursday, Blanche couldn’t explain what crime Slotkin had supposedly committed. “Whether that’s a smart thing to say or not a smart thing to say, how is that even potentially criminal?” Abrams asked.

Initially, Blanche was extremely defensive, but eventually admitted: “Of course what the senator said in and of itself is absolutely not a crime.”

“However, if leadership in the Senate are working together to try to stop young people from going to work in the administration by basically threatening them, saying you should be worried that you’re going to be open to investigations,” Blanche said, “that is totally wrong, and again, there’s no evidence that people are threatening young people, right? And again, maybe not criminal, but we should be worried if that’s happening.”

“Right, but there’s no evidence that people are threatening young people,” Abrams said. “She’s talking about trying to have accountability, and it serving as a deterrent. I don’t even see, when the president is referring to her as an extortionist, and you’ve cited it as well, it just doesn’t seem to me to even be in the ballpark for crime.”

“The difference between something being OK and being criminal is huge, right?” Abrams added. Blanche nodded silently.

Abrams then pressed Blanche on whether Slotkin had actually committed extortion, as the president had claimed.

“Her comments alone are absolutely not a crime. There is no criminal investigation here, and I’ve never said that there is,” Blanche eventually admitted.

Let’s hope this lesson sticks. Earlier this week, Blanche claimed that it was his role to defend the Trump administration from the “vile rhetoric” of Democratic lawmakers. Following sweeping Democratic victories in the midterms, lawmakers have warned the Trump administration to “lawyer up,” and clearly, its lawyer has responded by threatening free speech.

items.title: Democrats Flip Two More Governor’s Offices in Massive Win
items.content_text:
The midterms may have been more than a week ago, but the Democrats are still racking up wins.

Democrats won the governorships of Kansas and Alaska Thursday night, holding onto the seat in the normally GOP-dominated prairie and flipping a Republican position up north. Cindy Holscher defeated Republican Ty Masterson in Kansas on a narrow 50.3 percent to 49.7 percent margin with 98 percent of votes counted, according to the Associated Press, to take over from fellow Democrat Laura Kelly, who is term-limited.

In Alaska, CNN called the race for Democrat Jonathan Kreiss-Tompkins, who has 50.2 percent of the vote in his favor in a crowded field. He dwarfed Republican Bernadette Wilson, who only had 28.7 percent with 88 percent of the votes counted. With these two victories, more than 75 percent of Americans will live in states with Democratic governors.

Democrats also control the majority of state legislatures, and have trifectas (control of state legislatures and governorships) in 22 states. That opens the door to progressive legislation including joining the National Popular Vote Interstate Compact, which could nullify the Electoral College.

The 2026 midterms have proven to be a sea change in American politics, with Democrats gaining power not just in Congress but also at the state level with majorities they haven’t seen in decades. The question is how they will exercise this power and whether they will seek to undo entrenched conservative policies across the country.

items.title: JD Vance Mulls Stunning 2028 Move as He Scrambles to Save His Future
items.content_text:
Vice President JD Vance is seriously considering shelving his dreams of a 2028 presidential campaign, as GOP hopefuls are rushing to distance themselves from President Donald Trump.

Vance was once considered the GOP frontrunner for 2028, but people close to him told CNN Friday that the Ohio Republican has become less than convinced of his own candidacy, following sweeping Republican losses in the midterm elections last week.

“The question isn’t if JD can do it. It’s: If the Iran war is still happening, can any Republican do it?” one Vance ally told CNN. “If they don’t end the war in Iran, no Republican has a shot at 2028.”

Republicans are already turning on Vance’s nascent presidential run. As Election Day results rolled in last week, Vance received a text from one of his confidants advising him to consider sitting out of the next presidential race.

Another Vance ally noted that a lot could change in two years: “Just look at how far Trump has fallen since his win.”

Meanwhile, Rich Baris, a pollster closely connected to the MAGA movement, had a more dreadful analysis: “MAGA is dead.”

“The problem the vice president is going to have is that he has to motivate [MAGA voters] and make them believe again, because the Republican brand has completely lost credibility with them,” he said.

Vance’s soul-searching comes as he and Secretary of State Marco Rubio have rushed to distance themselves from the Trump administration. After Trump suffered a stunning rebuke in the midterm elections, Rubio and Vance have begun leaking to publications “like crazy,” according to Majority Report podcast host Emma Vigeland on X.

Vigeland observed that The New York Times coverage of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s reported affair with a Chinese spy “emphasized that Rubio told Trump about Huang and the spy, but Trump let him on the plane anyway.”

Meanwhile, Vance had stepped out of line to criticize Trump’s war in Iran in the wake of the midterms, citing it as a major reason for Republican losses. “Vance’s alleged resistance to the Iran War is repeatedly noted,” Vigeland added.

items.title: Nvidia’s Jensen Huang and the Troubling Rise of the Imperial CEO
items.content_text:
Jensen Huang resigned Thursday as chief executive of Nvidia, a company that he co-founded in 1993 with the modest goal of creating 3D graphics for video games, but which now dominates the global market for the advanced graphic processing units that power AI. Nvidia’s shares were, according to one September calculation, 8 percent of the entire S&P 500. Lately, they’ve slipped below 6 percent, but that’s still gargantuan. Under the best of circumstances, it’s very difficult to force out the chairman of a company making this kind of money for its shareholders. Huang made it even harder by eliminating potential sources of accountability.

Some will conclude Huang’s resignation shows that America’s system of corporate governance works, but that’s the wrong lesson. Huang kept his job long after it became evident to pretty much everyone working at Nvidia that he was abusing his executive power. What his story really illustrates is that big-shot tech chiefs—Huang, Mark Zuckerberg, Elon Musk, and Anthropic’s Dario Amodei come most readily to mind—tend to amass so much wealth and power that they make themselves almost impossible to fire. These corporations are, in effect, hostage to the merchant princes who run them.

Huang’s resignation wouldn’t have occurred, or anyway wouldn’t have occurred this week, without The New York Times reporting Thursday that he was caught on video last March canoodling during a company meeting with Nvidia’s vice president of health care. This came after Huang confessed Sunday to conducting an extramarital affair with Alice Huang (no relation), who, as the Times revealed last week, is a suspected Chinese spy. Conceivably Huang didn’t know this about her, but as the corporate governance expert Nell Minow pointed out to me, Huang was certainly aware that the company Alice ran, Megaspeed, was Nvidia’s biggest customer in Southeast Asia, making any such relationship, even if consensual, a violation of corporate ethics and potentially a violation of securities law. It would not astonish me to learn that Huang turned a blind eye to, or even collaborated with, his paramour’s alleged diversion of Nvidia AI chips to China, which the Times reported on more than a year ago. (Huang denies the diversion took place). The filing of class-action lawsuits has already begun.

“If involved in a situation that could present a perceived or actual conflict of interest,” the Nvidia ethics manual advises, “contact Employment Legal for guidance.” Had Huang followed his own company’s policies and confessed to Employment Legal that he was bumping uglies with a Nvidia customer and snogging with a Nvidia employee, he undoubtedly would have been told not to fish off the company pier. 

Insinuations that Nvidia’s chief executive had an affair with Alice Huang have been public for more than a year. If Nvidia’s board never asked Huang about it, then the company was hostage to Huang to a greater degree than I think. More likely, it did ask; Huang lied; and the board pretended to believe him because to do otherwise would tank Nvidia’s stock. Which is exactly what happened after the Financial Times confirmed the affair. As I write, Nvidia has lost about $1 trillion in value, lending weight to Bloomberg’s Matt Levine’s observation that this is “the most expensive extramarital affair in human history.” We know that Huang lied about Alice last month to Bloomberg, saying, “Our relationship, our interactions, have been related to Megaspeed, and it was all completely normal and not unusual.” For at least as long, Nvidia company spokespeople have denied that Jensen and Alice were knocking boots.

We don’t know whether the board knew that Huang also got caught spooning with Nvidia’s Kimberly Powell (the Times used the term “being affectionate”) at a San Jose hotel where Nvidia employees stayed while attending Nvidia’s annual developer conference. A bystander recorded this on a cell phone; Huang’s security team observed the surveillance; and the security team then “sequestered the person,” the Times reported, and “asked the person to sign a nondisclosure agreement.” 

The Times doesn’t relate whether this person signed the agreement. But assuming they were a Nvidia employee (I don’t see how Huang’s security team could “sequester” somebody who wasn’t), merely asking that person to remain silent would violate California’s 2021 Silenced No More Act. In any event, the video’s existence did not remain confidential, and the Times got confirmation of the smooch from no fewer than five Nvidia employees, suggesting that Huang’s brazen behavior was common knowledge at Nvidia, even perhaps to the board. Suppressing such information might also constitute securities fraud. In addition, Reuters reported yesterday a third “intimate relationship” with yet another Nvidia employee, this one unnamed. It isn’t clear how many people knew about that.

Why was Huang allowed to misbehave for so long, and why did so many people risk legal reprisals to protect him? Board members fearing a drop in the company’s stock price is only part of the story. Nvidia’s governance structure is a nightmare. Until Thursday, the company never had a board chair. Huang made sure there was no succession plan, and three years ago Huang said he expected to run Nvidia three or four more decades, by which time he would be age 90 or 100. More than 60 Nvidia employees reported directly to Huang, and last year Huang claimed, “I probably read several thousand emails a day.” If you go to Nvidia’s website and click on “management team,” you’re shown a grand total of four company officers, one of whom, Colette Kress, was just named interim chief executive. What until recently was the world’s wealthiest company was managed like the corner drugstore. 

The financial world rushed to defend Huang after he admitted his affair with Alice. “I believe Jensen is irreplaceable for America’s AI leadership,” Shaun Maguire, a venture capitalist at Sequoia Capital, posted on X on November 8. “We should all support him and his family,” Bill Ackman posted. Ackman later added, “If indeed this is more than an affair, then it is an [sic] obviously a real problem,” failing to grasp that even without the espionage angle, Huang’s affair with a leading Nvidia customer was a firing offense. Gavin Baker, managing partner of the investment firm Atreides Management, tweeted, “It would be a disaster for America—and a gift to China—if Jensen goes down.” After Huang resigned on Thursday, Musk tweeted that it “would be an honor” to hire him. 

If nothing else, Huang’s resignation should serve to educate Wall Street that the planet doesn’t explode when the chief executive of a company valued at more than $5 trillion is forced to resign. But Huang is not the only chief executive to assume excessive control over a corporation by selling his board on his infallibility. 

Mark Zuckerberg, as I explained last month, turned California’s billionaire wealth-tax ballot initiative, which failed last week, into an opportunity to extort a raise from his board. The raise was not an increase in compensation per se but rather an increase in liquidity; Meta created a new class of nonvoting stock that had the effect of maintaining Zuckerberg’s control of 61 percent of all voting shares even if he were required to pay the state of California 5 percent of his net worth, which he won’t be. Zuckerberg persuaded the board not to condition this change on Proposition 40’s passage, which already seemed a pretty bad bet when Zuckerberg cut the deal. The arrangement had the effect of diluting Meta’s accountability to shareholders who weren’t Mark Zuckerberg.

Zuckerberg got what he wanted by threatening to move out of the state to avoid the tax. This was a transparently nonsensical scenario because the wealth tax was structured in such a way that it was already  too late for Zuckerberg to avoid it. But the threat so jangled Meta’s board that it gave away the store. Never mind that Zuckerberg’s stewardship of Meta in recent years has been less than stellar; his infatuation with the virtual reality “metaverse” cost his company $85 billion.

Elon Musk famously extracted a $139 billion pay package from Tesla’s board outrageous enough to prompt a Delaware judge to throw it out on the grounds that it didn’t represent a good-faith negotiation, largely because Musk packed the board with personal friends. The ruling was overturned in December 2025. By then it was evident that Musk’s participation in DOGE had damaged Tesla sales. Tesla’s board nonetheless granted Musk that year another pay increase potentially valued at $1 trillion that could give him 25 percent voting control at the company. Musk had previously threatened to develop AI technology outside Tesla if he didn’t get it, which I find difficult to reconcile with a chief executive’s fiduciary duty to the company he runs.

“We live in the Age of the Imperial CEO,” The Wall Street Journal’s Tim Higgins wrote last month, citing Zuckerberg’s shakedown and Musk’s 85 percent voting control of yet another company, SpaceX. Higgins also cited the structure of Anthropic’s forthcoming initial public offering, which gives founders Dario and Daniela Amodei, along with five other investors, majority control so long as three of the seven remain. It’s a sort of tontine that could last for decades, provided AI doesn’t kill us all before then. (For an exegesis of the tontine, I refer you to Robert Louis Stevenson’s 1889 novel The Wrong Box and the hilarious 1966 movie that Bryan Forbes made from it with Peter Cook and Dudley Moore.) 

Huang’s departure won’t likely destroy Nvidia because no matter who runs the company, it still controls somewhere around 80 percent of its market. Even if Huang is a genius, it would take someone at least as dumb as Huang is smart to run this company into the ground. One hopes the lesson will be that it’s a very big mistake for corporate boards to yield so much power to chief executives. But don’t count on them noticing.

items.title: The Democrats’ First Move After Their Big Win? A Giveaway to Big Oil.
items.content_text:
Last week, Democrats won historic majorities in the House and Senate, receiving an extraordinary mandate to take on the bad actors they campaigned against: President Donald Trump, the Republican Party, data centers, and Big Tech. This week, in their first major action since then, Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer and 21 other Democratic senators voted to fast-track a Republican bill that would eviscerate America’s bedrock environmental laws in order to, in Trump’s words, “codify our America First Energy Agenda” of building “Pipelines, Mines, and Power Plants faster than ever before” so that America remains “Number One” in data center construction. 

So what can explain this almost unimaginable betrayal—and can it be stopped? 

The Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act, or BAAJA, which the Senate is expected to vote on next week, has been framed as a compromise to make it easier to build both clean energy and fossil fuel infrastructure. It was developed behind closed doors by Senate Republicans and two Democrats, Sheldon Whitehouse and Martin Heinrich. But there was a fundamental mismatch in this secretive drafting process. The fossil fuel industry has been all in for permitting reform—indeed, it has long been the top priority of the American Petroleum Institute, the lobbying arm and political face of major oil and gas corporations. So Big Oil was involved in BAAJA’s drafting. 

Whitehouse and Heinrich, by contrast, kept Democrats’ traditional allies in the dark—not just environmental groups, which are uniformly opposed to the legislation, but tribal organizations (many of which released a joint statement condemning BAAJA provisions that “fundamentally undermine Tribal sovereignty” and “threaten sacred sites and cultural resources”); racial justice organizations like NAACP (which warned that BAAJA “directly threatens the health, safety, and future of Black and frontline communities”); and anti-ICE groups like Detention Watch Network (which condemned how BAAJA will “pave a path for detention expansion by making immigration detention facilities easier to build and much harder to stop”). 

The upshot is that the staff of two Democratic senatorial offices were alone at the negotiating table, while Republicans had the full lobbying, analyzing, and bill-drafting capacity of the entire fossil fuel industry. So of course the Democrats got rolled. And BAAJA reflects this asymmetry in the severe lopsidedness of its ostensible “compromise.” 

The positive pitch from BAAJA’s Democratic-leaning cheerleaders, like Democratic strategist Adam Jentleson’s Searchlight Institute, is that the legislation will be a huge boon to Democrats’ affordability and climate goals by lowering energy costs and supercharging the build-out of renewables. These claims are dubious at best. It’s essentially impossible to confidently model the full climate effects of a legislative package like BAAJA, but current analyses include predictions out of Purdue University that BAAJA will actually increase both “domestic energy-related greenhouse gas emissions” and “domestic mortality attributable to air pollution from fossil fuels.” The most optimistic modeling, from Rhodium Group, predicts a range: from BAAJA having zero effect on greenhouse gas emissions to a best-case scenario of reducing U.S. emissions by a negligible 4 percent by 2040. Rhodium’s modeling on affordability is similarly laughable, with a best-case scenario reduction of energy bills by $4–$7 a month by 2040.

So that’s what Democrats stand to gain from supporting this Republican bill. What are they giving up? From an environmental perspective, the costs are almost unimaginable. BAAJA severely weakens the Clean Water Act, robbing states and tribes of their ability to protect water quality and require adequate safeguards for activities that pollute or destroy water resources. It practically nullifies the Endangered Species Act by delegating its core responsibilities to the states, most of which either oppose the act’s wildlife protections or lack the expertise and resources to adequately fulfill these obligations. And it essentially repeals the National Environmental Policy Act, the bedrock environmental law that gives the public a voice in decisions that impact the environment, by prohibiting the enforcement of NEPA violations. These three legal frameworks are responsible for most the improvements in water quality, green space, and wildlife recovery in our country over the last half-century.

And that’s just the beginning. Other provisions of BAAJA go to even greater lengths to radically lock in fossil fuel development far into the future. The “disparate treatment” section of the bill effectively makes the permitting decisions of the Trump administration permanent. In the words of David Bookbinder, an environmental lawyer who has worked for both the left-leaning Sierra Club and the libertarian Niskanen Center, “The result of making these energy permitting policies permanent is that future administrations will be unable to effectively reduce GHG emissions.” BAAJA also guarantees  not just the construction of fossil fuel projects but also their “operation at full capacity,” permanently blocking any future administration from regulating energy infrastructure.

If you’re thinking this legislative assault on the environment sounds like it was pulled straight out of Project 2025, well, you’re right—and the authors of Project 2025 are strong supporters of the bill. BAAJA is also the top legislative priority of API, ExxonMobil, Chevron, Shell, BP, ConocoPhillips, and other fossil fuel giants. So no wonder climate advocates have been sounding the alarm—and not just progressive leaders like Bill McKibben, but moderate climate advocates like Jody Freeman, John Podesta, and Al Gore, who recently warned that “now is not the time to give the Trump administration freer rein to double down on fossil fuels—which is what President Trump would surely do.” This point is crucial: Trump will be implementing BAAJA if it passes, and he very clearly has no intention of allowing the “supercharge clean energy” side of the bargain to move forward. Indeed, just this week Trump reiterated that he is not going to approve any wind turbines, even if Democrats submit to his desire to “codify our America First Energy Agenda” by passing BAAJA. 

Of course, Big Oil companies aren’t the only villains that want to see this Republican legislation pass. Big Tech is also all in, from Marc Andreessen’s tech venture firm to ITI, the trade association for OpenAI, Nvidia, Meta, Amazon, Google, and other tech giants, which praised BAAJA as “essential to America’s ability to build, compete, and lead—especially in the AI era.” Advocates of BAAJA, including Trump, have tried to obscure this support by pointing to provisions in the legislation that would require data center developers to pay for the grid and transmission upgrades their projects require. But Americans have made overwhelmingly clear—not least through the massive victories they just handed to Democrats who pledged to support data center bans and moratoriums—that they don’t just want AI data centers to help pay for some of their own costs. More than anything, they want the ability to say “no” to these monstrosities coming into their communities. They want to be able to decide their own futures, rather than having Big Tech billionaires make those decisions for them.

BAAJA is a direct response to this democratic backlash. AI corporations want to cut the public out of these decision-making processes, and BAAJA is laser-focused on overcoming the two most important roadblocks the public can use to check the explosion of Big Tech’s data center build-out: permitting and easy access to fossil gas. (Abigail Dillen, the president of Earthjustice, recently explained exactly how BAAJA enables “the dirtiest version of the data center build-out to move even faster.”) 

The antidemocratic betrayal here really cannot be overstated. Democrats just won their biggest congressional majorities in 50 years—to say nothing of victories in places like Texas, where Democrats swept every single statewide office and flipped the state House—in large part by promising to respond to the massive voter backlash against the AI industry’s out-of-control expansion of hyperscale data centers. Just a week later, Democrats’ Senate leadership team—not just Schumer but incoming Majority Whip Brian Schatz and DSCC chair Kirsten Gillibrand—joined Trump and the GOP to pass a catastrophic giveaway to the Big Tech billionaires who spent hundreds of millions of dollars trying to defeat their incoming colleagues, directly rebuking the massive voter mandate their party just received to stand up to those billionaires.

And that, maybe more than anything, helps explain the timing of this push. It’s not just that BAAJA was developed without hearings or any of the other review procedures that a bill of this magnitude would normally go through. It’s that Democrats like Whitehouse, Heinrich, Schumer, and Schatz are trying to ram this Project 2025 atrocity through a GOP-controlled lame-duck session weeks before Democrats take control. BAAJA advocates have argued that the legislation needs to move now because Trump would never sign a bill passed by a Democratic Congress, but that’s an absurd claim. We have no idea how Trump will respond to the Democratic majority. There are myriad ways he could be brought to the table on a clean transmission bill—name the legislation after him, insert some shady Trump Organization business opportunity in the text, send in Zohran Mamdani to sell it ... 

The reason top Senate Democrats are working to pass BAAJA now, before their majority is seated, is that this rotten handout to Big Oil and Big Tech—and massive “screw you” to the voters who just gave Democrats their majority—would never pass in a Democratic Congress. BAAJA is a radical MAGA bill that takes a sledgehammer to America’s most important environmental laws, permanently locks us into an expansion of fossil fuels, disempowers local communities’ ability to decide their own futures, and opens the door to a radical expansion of methane-powered hyperscale data centers. It needs to pass now because it is fundamentally a Republican bill. 

BAAJA is on a fast track through the Senate, with a final vote only days away. But we must not accept this as a done deal. The Congressional Progressive Caucus, which represents more than 100 members of Congress, just announced its opposition to the legislation. So did the Democratic attorneys general from California, Colorado, Delaware, Hawaii, Illinois, Maine, Maryland, Massachusetts, Michigan, Minnesota, Nevada, New York, Oregon, Vermont, Virginia, Washington, and Washington, D.C., who sent a letter asking Senate leadership to halt the upcoming votes on BAAJA in order to “protect our natural resources, historic and tribal sites, and state regulatory prerogatives.” And it’s not just elected officials who can weigh in. Everyone can make a difference by calling and emailing their representatives and senators and looking out for further mobilization opportunities. If all else fails, at the very least, we must make sure that Democrats understand that their voters are paying attention to who is selling out our futures to Big Oil and Big Tech—and that 2028 is not so far away.

items.title: A Mediocre, Miserable Man
items.content_text:
In the course in international relations I took with him as a Harvard undergraduate in the early 1960s, when he was still a mere professor of government, Henry Kissinger had certain personal observations that he would frequently reiterate, a main one of which was, “In retrospect, everything looks inevitable.” President Donald Trump, halfway through his second term in office, suddenly—and, I would guess, to a certain extent unexpectedly, to him—finds his political power severely circumscribed. Was this midterm election outcome, more extreme in its repudiation of his government than virtually anyone anticipated, foreordained by Trump’s egomaniacal approach to business, politics, and other people in general?

An argument could be made that the undoing of his presidency was bound to happen. Another concept I picked up in my undergraduate studies was that of “omnipotence of thought.” This is the conviction that one’s thoughts or beliefs can not only influence the external world but control it. Trump came into the business world and later political office with a set of misguided and inflexible beliefs and habits, instilled in him first by a stern and un-loving father, which were extended and fortified by the man who became not only his attorney but his political mentor, the notoriously ruthless and unprincipled Roy Cohn, chief counsel to Senator Joseph McCarthy’s communist witch-hunt hearings in the 1950s. In the three books that his niece, Mary L. Trump, has written about him, she has made clear that her uncle was raised by a cold, ruthless, mercenary father and a largely absent and sickly mother. The lack of love in the household, to Mary, is the most telling aspect of Donald’s upbringing. The film The Apprentice (2024), which highlights Cohn’s mentorship of him, makes clear the essence of Cohn’s tutelage of Donald: No matter what, no matter how wrong you might be or turn out to be about a given matter or issue, you must never bend, never give up your adherence to a position, no matter how misguided it might turn out to be. And incidentally, the film also highlights the instance in which “The Donald,” as his first wife, Ivana, called him, allegedly raped her as she was spurning his unwanted conjugal advances.

It should come as no surprise, therefore, that Trump would stake out positions that are autarkic in nature, for himself as an individual as well as for the country. Autarky is a state of self-sufficiency and self-absorption that is as complete as possible. Trump does not brook advice from other people as to what he should or should not do in a given circumstance. Therefore, in his first term as president, when anyone in the government or the White House of high caliber—say, for instance, his first chief of staff, retired Marine General John Kelly—tried to offer advice contrary to his own inclination, he would chafe against it in annoyance. In his second term, he stacked his Cabinet with pliant, mediocre individuals who would never dare challenge his inclinations, no matter how wayward or bizarre they might be. Over his entire adult life, he had nurtured the notion that tariffs were paid by businesses exporting goods rather than by the consumers in importing countries purchasing them, a delusion I ascribe to a belief instilled in him early on that other people are invariably out to undermine or savage you. Having managed to kidnap the president of Venezuela, which has an estimated population of 28.6 million and no more than 150,000 military personnel, he then fantasized that he could similarly subdue the vastly larger nation of Iran, with its estimated population of 93.4 million and approximately 610,000 military personnel, including its notoriously brutal Revolutionary Guard. In this latter case, U.S. bombardment killed the nation’s supreme leader, Ayatollah Ali Khamenei, and subsequent strikes did away with many of the country’s top leaders, including, it is believed, many of the identified moderate leaders, those who U.S. analysts believed would have been open to striking a reasonable deal with the United States over the issue of nuclear weapons.

But now let’s look at the positive side of Trump—and yes, there is perhaps a positive side to focus on. During his 2024 campaign, this magazine ran a picture of him with a faint mustache and short haircut that suggested he might be an American Hitler. We were far from alone in making such a comparison. But as it has turned out, he was not such. He is a tyrant, no doubt, but one whose nefarious program has been to attenuate America’s most commendable aspects without turning the country upside down and destroying it. He did not cancel the 2026 political elections, or make any serious moves to undermine them, much to the surprise of many. His reaction to the election results, so far, has been muted, and it appears that he may content himself with pursuing his various construction projects during the rest of his second term. Which is not to say that he won’t get up to some forms of mischief. His top priority, clearly—and one doomed to failure—is and has been trying to turn the United States back into an overwhelmingly white country; hence his attacks on all programs involving affirmative action and his relentless efforts to deport as many noncitizen residents of color in the country as possible as rapidly as possible (which may well amp up with Stephen Miller now elevated to chief of staff).

Beyond that, I think he aspires to reduce every aspect of excellence in the country to a level of mediocrity, which is to say, down to his very own level. And at this, I confidently predict, he will woefully fail, as he has failed so often at his major endeavors throughout his miserable life.

items.title: Did the Midterms Kill Climate Politics?
items.content_text:
Climate change was not a hot topic during this year’s midterm elections. Candidates who’d previously championed climate action walked those positions back this cycle. Abdul El-Sayed supported the Green New Deal when he ran for governor in 2018; he said he wouldn’t defend it now. James Talarico sponsored climate legislation as a state legislator in Texas and once said that “fossil fuels are destroying the planet.” In his Senate run, Talarico embraced an “all of the above” energy strategy as part of a platform to protect jobs in the oil and gas industry while encouraging cleaner sources like solar and wind, which already proliferate in the Lone Star State. Looking at these shifts, Axios declared, “Democrats’ blue wave leaves climate behind.”

So are Democrats really done with climate politics? Not exactly. An analysis from the Climate and Community Institute points out that candidates in deep blue districts and swing states alike touted their support for clean energy investment and taking on polluting utilities. While these planks weren’t necessarily central, Republicans didn’t manage to sink campaigns by attacking Democrats’ past or present support for a “Green New Scam,” either. Climate politics may not be dead, then, but its future is going to look very different.

During the first years of the Biden administration, climate change was both a consistent White House talking point and treated primarily as an investment opportunity that would allow the United States to accomplish a range of goals for various factions within the Democratic Party: outcompete China in the twenty-first century’s most important growth industries; bring well-paid, potentially even unionized jobs back to deindustrialized areas, and thus win voters in critical swing states back for Democrats; rehabilitate the country’s global reputation after Trump; and reduce greenhouse gas emissions. Debates still rage over how successfully the Inflation Reduction Act—the Biden era’s highest-profile legislative achievement—was at accomplishing these aims. A year after its passage, polls showed that seven in 10 Americans had heard only “a little” or “nothing” about it.

Whatever the next era of climate politics holds, it will likely revolve less around the United States becoming some sort of global climate champion and pledging to reach “net-zero” emissions by some point far off into the future. Given the sheer force of the climate disasters now regularly battering the U.S.—from heat waves to wildfires, floods, and droughts—it should probably also engage with climate change as a force that is actively upending life here rather than as a problem still primarily hurting poorer parts of the world. It is difficult, that is, to imagine an affordability agenda that ignores how soaring energy costs make monthly bills unaffordable in scorching summer heat; how the skyrocketing cost of home insurance is driving up housing costs; or how persistent droughts have driven the U.S. cattle herd down to its lowest levels in 75 years and sent beef prices soaring. Addressing these sorts of climate-induced cost-of-living concerns might also mean turning away from treating climate change as a distinct issue, and infusing it into a broader-based economic populism.

Will Lawrence—the Sunrise Movement co-founder who flipped his Michigan House seat last week—told The New York Times this week that climate is one of many “cascading crises” facing the country, on top of wars and rising costs: “Figuring out how to wrap that all up into one neat story is not easy for any of us.” His message, he added, was about security “in the sense of being able to look forward to the future and be secure at night knowing that we and our kids are going to be taken care of, that we’re going to be OK. Climate is as important to that as it’s ever been.”

Such an approach could entail broadening the focus of climate politics beyond the energy sector, where most climate policy and messaging in the U.S. has tended to focus. Although people care quite a lot about how much electricity costs, how those electrons are generated—and how they make their way to homes and businesses—isn’t an especially pressing questions for most Americans. Decarbonizing the power sector is both a vital goal and a virtually incomprehensible statement. Fortunately for would-be green populists, some of the same companies that are profiting off of wildly unprofitable data centers are also responsible for rising electricity bills and excess carbon emissions. If greening a utility’s energy mixture doesn’t excite voters, holding its CEO’s feet to the fire might. Candidates for public utility regulators in Georgia and Arizona focused on expanding renewable energy and reining in utility bosses’ attempts to raise rates for the sake of powering data centers.

The disturbing reality of the climate crisis is that it affects virtually every facet of life. For Democrats who want to help the country navigate a hotter and pricier century, the sheer scope of that crisis can be the grounds for a new climate politics that responds to voters’ concerns with more than abstract pledges.

items.title: America Has Entered a New Age of Propaganda
items.content_text:
On July 16, Donald Trump went on prime-time television to repeat to Americans that an election he had lost nearly six years earlier had been stolen. Four months before the midterms, Trump turned a presidential address into another recital of the conspiracy theories that have sustained him since 2020. In an ominous and unhinged speech, he claimed that China’s attempts to acquire voter data were evidence of a plot to corrupt the vote, then returned to his familiar claims about widespread fraud.

ABC and NBC declined to carry the speech on their main broadcast channels. CBS aired it, then broke away after about 15 minutes to debunk Trump’s assertions. Trump answered that the networks were engaged in a “plot” and said those that did not air the speech should lose their licenses. Six days later, Federal Communications Commission Chair Brendan Carr said ABC’s snub would be considered in an unusually early review of licenses for eight Disney-owned stations. ABC and Disney have since sued the FCC, alleging retaliation.

America has entered a new era of truth manipulation and censorship in which journalists are faced with a self-sealing trap. Carry the speech and help spread the election lie, or refuse and be cast as part of the conspiracy supposedly suppressing it. Either response could be recruited into the government’s propaganda campaign.

The prospect of a society in which truth and falsehood are indistinguishable—one in which the difference doesn’t even seem to matter—troubles philosophers Avishai Margalit and Assaf Sharon in their book Captive Minds: A Study of Manipulation. Sharon is a political theorist who specializes in democratic legitimacy and the conditions under which citizens can genuinely govern themselves. Margalit is a preeminent philosopher best known for The Decent Society (1996), The Ethics of Memory (2002), On Compromise and Rotten Compromises (2010), and On Betrayal (2017). He has spent his career asking what degrades human dignity—humiliation, forgetting, rotten compromise, betrayal—and now, with Sharon, turns to the capture and domination of judgment itself.

Margalit and Sharon explain their personal stakes in the preface. Living in Jerusalem, they began writing Captive Minds while watching demagogues exploit the threat of terrorism to justify occupation and the horrors of occupation to excuse further brutality. “As more blood flows between the River and the Sea, the two peoples living on this punished land become easier prey to manipulators who exploit fear, hatred, and confusion,” they write. That blood is “the fuel of manipulation,” which then precipitates further violence. And the resurgence of authoritarianism in Europe and the United States threatens a similar vicious cycle on a global scale. Donald Trump, in their view, is more a symptom than a cause. Their subject is the set of conditions that makes such a figure possible.

The book is neither a conventional work of media criticism nor a narrowly academic philosophical treatise. It reads instead as an urgent work of late democratic anxiety. What if the greatest political danger of our time is no longer that governments force their subjects to obey, but that they induce citizens to surrender their judgment willingly? How did that become possible?


American propaganda has a long lineage, from the partisan press of the early republic to wartime mobilization and modern public relations. During World War I, the federal Committee on Public Information promoted the war through official news, posters, films, and more than 75,000 “Four Minute Men,” who delivered vetted speeches in movie theaters and other venues. After the war, veterans of such campaigns brought those techniques into commercial persuasion. One of the field’s principal theorists was Edward Bernays, who treated public opinion as something trained experts could engineer.

Bernays regarded the manufacture of public opinion as both legitimate and necessary. In his 1928 book Propaganda, he argued that democratic society was too complex for citizens to navigate unaided, and therefore required the “conscious and intelligent manipulation” of the habits and opinions of the masses by an “invisible government.” The following year, working for the American Tobacco Company, he arranged for fashionable young women to smoke cigarettes during New York’s Easter parade, while alerting the press that women’s rights marchers would light “torches of freedom.” A campaign to sell Lucky Strikes appeared as a spontaneous protest against a sexist taboo. Bernays’s method was to identify an existing desire, attach it to a product or policy, and make the desired behavior appear to originate with the public rather than the sponsor.

The darker connotations of propaganda are clear in its history in Fascist Italy, Nazi Germany, and the Soviet Union, where mass persuasion worked alongside censorship, surveillance, terror, and political violence. Nazi propaganda exploited prejudice, fear, humiliation, resentment, and the desire for restored greatness, supplying a story in which Germany’s defeats were caused by internal enemies and traitors. Soviet agitprop likewise defended the state, sanctified its leaders, manufactured heroic myths, and attributed failures to saboteurs and class enemies. In both systems, propaganda did more than circulate falsehoods. It organized a way of seeing the world. “If everyone always lies to you, the consequence is not that you believe the lies, but that no one believes anything at all anymore,” Hannah Arendt said in her final interview in 1973. “That means that the people are deprived not only of their capacity to act, but also of their capacity to think and to judge. And with such a people you can then do what you please.”

Church and state were once the main manipulators; now the giants of the attention economy join them as full partners.

This subtlety is a theme of Margalit and Sharon’s book. One of their recurring contrasts, drawn from Cicero and Machiavelli, is between the lion and the fox: The lion rules by force; the fox by cunning, seduction, flattery, deception, and psychological leverage. Another text to which they repeatedly return is Shakespeare’s Othello. For the authors, Iago is the archetypal manipulator. He does not command Othello or threaten him. Instead, he asks insinuating questions, claims that Cassio spoke of a secret affair with Desdemona in his sleep, and arranges for her handkerchief to turn up in Cassio’s room. Othello’s love makes him vulnerable, and Iago converts that vulnerability into jealousy and self-destruction. By the time Othello murders Desdemona, he believes he is acting on evidence and exercising his own will, but he is carrying out another man’s design. “Instead of binding you in chains,” Margalit and Sharon write, “the manipulator pulls your strings.”

Iago’s art is ancient, but the scale on which it is being practiced is new. What used to be individual cunning has become commercialized by Silicon Valley, a transformation described in Franklin Foer’s World Without Mind: The Existential Threat of Big Tech, and most recently in Jill Lepore’s The Rise and Fall of the Artificial State. Church and state were once the main manipulators; now the giants of the attention economy join them as full partners.

What concerns Margalit and Sharon is that the liberal ideal of the open society, with free expression, a free press, and open exchange, may now function less as a safeguard than as “quicksand,” because under laissez-faire conditions it can enable “mind-numbing nonsense” to overwhelm the public sphere. More speech is not the answer, not when citizens are saturated with media to the point that the distinction between truth and falsehood begins to collapse. A public sphere flooded with conspiracies, grievance-optimized messages, fabrications, and artificial productions may remain formally open while leaving citizens increasingly vulnerable to domination. An open society permits expression, but a free society protects each person’s capacity to form a judgment genuinely their own.

The present danger is subtler and harder for liberal democracy to recognize and fight against, because the United States may remain formally democratic while losing the conditions necessary for meaningful self-government. Citizens may still vote, the press may remain legally free, and political speech may be abundant, yet public opinion may no longer be independently formed. Disinformation and conspiracy theories can shatter common factual ground into rival realities, while generative AI makes the fracture endlessly scalable.

Disinformation and conspiracy theories can shatter common factual ground into rival realities, while generative AI makes the fracture endlessly scalable.

Because manipulation has become so pervasive and profitable, resisting it requires more than correcting lies one by one. Margalit and Sharon argue that public discourse should be treated as democratic infrastructure, as essential as fair elections and independent courts, and cannot be left to an unregulated market for attention. Society cannot eliminate manipulation any more than it can eliminate friction, they argue; it can only keep manipulation from becoming an organizing principle. That means reducing the emotional and economic dependencies that make people easy to control, fortifying institutions that earn epistemic authority, respecting genuine expertise, and cultivating a public culture that rewards rigor and punishes quackery.

Their argument points toward a useful principle for more specific reform: Regulate the business rather than political opinion itself. Specific efforts are already underway. Google restricts how election advertisers can target voters, while Google and Meta have stopped accepting political advertising in the European Union. Those measures should go further. Congress should ban behavioral political microtargeting, phase out surveillance advertising, make engagement-driven ranking opt-in, and tax digital advertising to fund independent local and public media. Regulators should be able to audit platforms and hold companies liable for the harms they cause. Courts should treat internet giants not as speech platforms but as corporations subject to consumer-protection, negligence, and product-liability law. Recent lawsuits against Open AI and Meta’s landmark $18 billion settlement with nearly every U.S. state are just a start. These reforms rest on the premise that a democracy is entitled to govern its information environment and reduce the incentives that make manipulation so ubiquitous and lucrative.

Finally, the survival of American democracy depends on citizens rediscovering the power to uncover manipulation and change their minds. Margalit and Sharon find a model in 427 BCE, when the city of Mytilene rebelled against Athens. In a fit of rage, the Athenians voted to kill every Mytilenaen man and enslave its women and children. When they reconsidered the next day, the demagogue Cleon chastised those having second thoughts and pandered to the people’s urge for revenge. His opponent Diodotus instead implored the Athenians to restore their sense of reason and compassion, and thankfully narrowly prevailed. A second trireme raced after the ship carrying the original order, arriving just as the decree was being read and averting the massacre.

For Margalit and Sharon, Mytilene’s escape offers hope for democracy, after all. Even when it seems too late—even after the ship has sailed—a free society might, just in time, still be able to send a second.

items.title: Transcript: Trump Shivs Vance as Election Meltdown Takes Unhinged Turn
items.content_text:
The following is a lightly edited transcript of the November 13 episode of The Daily Blast podcast. Listen to it here.


Greg Sargent: This is The Daily Blast from The New Republic, produced and presented by the DSR Network. I’m your host, Greg Sargent.

Donald Trump unraveled in a series of crazed Truth Social posts on Thursday, and one thing stood out. Trump instructed JD Vance to stop seeking a deal with Iran, instead telling him to focus on investigating alleged corruption in blue states. This really shivs Vance. It also illustrates that Trump and MAGA will never come to terms with why they just suffered the massive electoral rebuke they did, which Vance badly needs them to. And all of this creates major openings for Democrats and liberals to make a new kind of case to voters.

We’re talking about all of it with Zack Beauchamp, who has a great new Substack called Public Reason that’s all about how to restate the liberal case after these Democratic victories. Zack, thanks for coming on.

Zack Beauchamp: Hey, happy to be here, Greg. It’s always fun, especially after a big launch like this.

Sargent: Congrats on the launch, Zack. So Trump erupted on social media, declaring that he’s asked JD Vance to focus entirely on largely invented blue-state “CORRUPTION.” He said this: “Corruption is in the Democrat leadership’s blood. We don’t need a deal with Iran. Those days have long since passed. We’ve got their money, hundreds of billions of dollars, and we’ve got their strait.”

Zack, none of this is real. Iran remains a total catastrophe for us. But note how Trump won’t allow Vance, who’s eyeing a 2028 run, to become the guy who fixes Trump’s Iran fiasco. It’s telling, isn’t it?

Beauchamp: Yeah, look, I want to say two things. First, I love how your intonation changes when you’re reading a Trump quote. Like, it sounds like Trump when you’re talking, right?

Sargent: Thank you.

Beauchamp: See the hands moving back and forth. Second, obviously a lot of what you quoted is nonsense blather, right? It’s like the president just saying what he feels like he needs to say to make it sound like he’s succeeding in Iran.

The Vance stuff, that’s real, and it’s fascinating. Because if you read the post very carefully, when Trump says he’s moving Vance off of the Iran portfolio—he doesn’t quite say that.

But what he does say is we don’t need to make a deal with Iran, and JD, I’m moving you full time to be focusing on fraud at home. That is essentially saying you’re off the case.

Which, in light of Vance’s comments right after the election, right, where he said basically the election was lost because of Iran—it’s clear to me, anyway, from the totality of this messaging, that Vance is being punished for the way that he talked about Iran after the election, blaming the entire election on Iran, and for stepping out from the company and party line on what you’re supposed to say about Iran, and basically blaming Trump for the election loss.

Sargent: That’s really fascinating. I agree that it really, really puts Vance in a box as a kind of punishment. It’s like a penalty box or something.

So Trump also angrily reopened his threat to prosecute Democratic members of Congress. He also raged that the GOP’s failure to pass the so-called Save America Act was “devastating” to Republicans in the midterms.

Zack, Trump suffers the biggest GOP defeat in a half-century, and his answer is to threaten to ramp up the authoritarian lawlessness and the voter suppression. What do you make of that?

Beauchamp: I mean, a leopard can’t change its spots, right? It’s like Trump has one playbook. It’s not that this electoral defeat happened by accident, right? It happened largely, but not entirely, because of Iran. Largely, but not entirely, because of tariffs. And largely, but not entirely, because of Trump’s immigration policy, and specifically the crackdown in Minneapolis, that seems to have been incredibly self-defeating.

But it’s all of those things. And it’s all the other things, too. It’s the constant chaos of the administration. It’s the way in which he betrayed elements of his base on Epstein. It’s who he is, right, as a person. It is his character asserting itself in office.

And what he’s done—I wrote about this actually in the first piece for Public Reason—is removed all the guardrails that prevent policymaking from being checked by anyone other than the president. That was, like, the number one authoritarian priority early in the administration. And what it’s meant is that there’s no transmission layer blocking Trump’s impulses from turning into policy.

And it means that just, like, the craziest things that he thinks and feels and that he believes as a person, the most aggressive things that he thinks, they just go straight into action a lot of the time. And so he just does what he’s going to do. And I don’t think he’s capable of rethinking premises at a deep and fundamental level. It’s just not who he is.

Sargent: Well, all this seems symptomatic of a broader problem gripping MAGA right now. You had a very good piece on this for your Substack—folks, check it out, it’s called Public Reason, it’s very good. MAGA thinkers are saying, essentially, that the real MAGA agenda has been failed by poor execution.

The war was handled incompetently, the tariffs were poorly done, Trump failed to communicate effectively about the reasons for the ICE invasions of Minneapolis and other places. That’s their emerging argument. You wrote very well on this. Can you talk about it?

Beauchamp: Yeah. The thing that’s interesting about this line that is emerging for Trump’s empathetic right is that they’re framing what happened as, like, a combination of a stabbed-in-the-back narrative and a real-Trumpism-has-never-been-tried. It’s, like, kind of both of those blended together, right?

The argument is that Trump did a really bad job implementing the things they care about. And in addition to that, he then betrayed one of the core MAGA principles, which was no new wars. Allegedly—I’ll come back to the allegedly, right?

But that was, in these commentators’ views—and in some ways this is implicit, I think, very clearly, in the way that Vance wrote about the election afterwards—that they think that they’ve strayed from what Trump won on in 2024.

But the problem here is that there’s, like, a fundamental misconstrual of what Trump and Trumpism was, what his supporters want from them, and what the ideology they were standing for was.

There just wasn’t really any kind of principled no-new-wars plank in MAGA ideology, for the simple reason that Trump has been a hawk for his entire life. Trumpism is just Trump. It’s not something separate. There’s no MAGA set of principles you can appeal to, to say Trump has gone wrong.

And so the right now is in this predicament where the one stable thing that sort of determined what it was about, and that papered over these deep divisions in the conservative coalition—Trump himself—is now obviously weakened and on the outs.

And so these people are trying to set up a narrative in which they’re the true heirs of the movement that brought Trump to power. But it’s not at all obvious that they’re going to be able to win that.
