And I think Vance personally will lose it, for the simple fact that, as Kamala Harris showed us, it’s very difficult to run against an administration when you were part of it.

Sargent: Right. And I think this idea that MAGA was betrayed, that true MAGA principles weren’t brought to fruition or whatever, and that’s the reason for the loss, also misses the immigration story in a big way. In other words, it misses what actually happened in this election with immigration. I think, by the way, a lot of liberals miss this as well.

The failure here isn’t just that Trump’s immigration agenda was unpopular. It’s that the underlying ideological goal of ethnically purging the country was also roundly rejected. And that’s core MAGA.

The exit polls showed a huge majority think immigrants are good for our country. People like James Talarico made an extremely powerful pro-immigrant argument. He won the debate on this issue in the polling with Ken Paxton.

Zack, I think liberals—and this connects to your new project—I think liberals were too quick to conclude that Trump’s 2024 win signaled a durable anti-immigrant shift in the country.

Now that we know this didn’t really happen, is there an opening for liberals to make a more robust case for immigration as a positive good, using the type of liberal language that you’re advocating be brought forth?

Beauchamp: Yes. Yes. I think, absolutely. I feel like it kind of sort of dovetails with trade. And people don’t always admit this, but what you’ll see is that Trump’s tariff policy has led to a total 180 in polls on how Americans view free trade.

Right now, Americans are free traders all of a sudden again. And it turns out that what people thought was this durable protectionist backlash in American politics was really just the fact that a bunch of people didn’t like the status quo, and they blamed free trade for some things that were happening in the status quo. Once they saw the alternative, they swung back.

And so there’s now a question of how to redefine not just, like, how you talk about it as a liberal and what your specific policy stance is, but the terms of the conversation. Like, for a long time, the background theory of American politics has been, American voters have turned against, quote-unquote, globalism, right?

They don’t like more people coming in here. They don’t like interfacing with other countries. And they want to shut the door in a variety of different ways. And I just don’t think that is true on a values level. I think that was a fundamental misread.

But there’s an opening now to give people a new set of concepts, right? To be able to say, well, actually, sure, I get it, you didn’t like the chaos in the Biden administration. And sure, I get it, there were problems with integrating China into the global trade order. But guess what? The United States benefits when we open the doors to cooperation with other countries.

We benefit, as we always have throughout our entire history, when we let in people who contribute to the United States, and keep our population growing, and keep our economy humming, and bring in new kinds of people with new ideas, who end up winning Nobel Prizes in the United States.

Like, this is the classic self-interested case for immigration, but it also is, at a deeper level, a liberal case. It’s an argument that openness is good for people. And I think you saw that a lot in—you pointed to Talarico. You saw it a lot in his campaign rhetoric.

Sargent: Very much so. And I think if you step back even a little bit more, you can sort of frame the whole thing this way. If you think about the three main pillars of MAGA, right—tariffs, mass deportations, America First foreign policy—those kind of make up, I think, basically the entirety of what was rejected in this election by a very, very broad majority of people.

And with the tariffs, I think it’s self-explanatory why Trump is kind of getting people to take another look at global trade as a positive for the country. The mass deportations are getting people to take another look at the fact that they like immigrants.

And America First, which you’ve been very eloquent on—I think you were ahead of the curve on this, in fact. America First is probably best understood not as isolationism, but more American unchecked militarism and utter contempt for international commitments and human rights norms and alliances.

That, I think, is what gives, you know, liberals an opening to restate the case for a more interconnected world, liberal international human rights norms, and so forth. Don’t you think there’s, like, a very big argument to be made right now?

Beauchamp: Yeah, yeah, there is. The way that I think about this is, after 2016, the United States entered a period of ideological rupture, where it’s clear that the old settlement that we had—which was, like, a competition between a sort of center-left Democratic Party and a center-right Republican Party that were both, I think, broadly and in their main contours, liberal politically—that was broken, right? That old consensus was broken. And there was a need for new ideological innovation.

And for a long time, part of the reason why the debate was happening on the terms that it was is that liberals felt very defensive and were having a lot of trouble coming up with new ideas to fill this vacuum. And the right felt not only emboldened by Trump, but also, I think, there was a lot of imagination, a lot of effort going into ideological reimagining on that side of the aisle.

And also, I would think, among a certain set of anti-liberal socialists. So that’s why liberalism has seemed so defensive, in large part. It was intellectually defensive and wasn’t coming up with these new ways of reacting to the collapse of the old liberal settlement.

And what you saw in this election—I don’t want to overread it, right, the same way that Trump people overread things in 2024 on their side. But I do think that the scale of this defeat—like, 2024 was a very narrow victory for Trump; 2026 is the biggest midterm landslide since Watergate, right?

It really is historic, and maybe we should start thinking about it in these historic terms. I think what it suggests is that people aren’t satisfied with the narrative that was on offer from the MAGA types as an explanation for what happened in the world and what it is now.

There’s a tremendous opportunity if someone like Talarico or Jon Ossoff, who I think maybe is the most plausible political actor to do this, can rebuild a new vocabulary for describing what it is people don’t like about the political status quo. Because they don’t like it.

Sargent: Right. And I think we really need to be clear that when people talk about this election as being about affordability, they’re hamstringing us from making this case. They’re hamstringing liberals from making this case. What we need to be saying, I think, is that the core ideas of right-wing populist nationalism, right-wing authoritarian nationalism, have all kind of fallen apart: tariffs, mass deportations, “America First.”

This wasn’t just a reaction to costs. The data is very clear that the public rejects the idea of imposing tariffs. The public is now much more pro-trade, as a positive good for the country. The data is also very clear that the public is rejecting the idea that the way to restore proper American identity, or a purified American identity, is to ethnically purge the country of non-white immigrants and their descendants.

And the data’s clear that nobody seems to really like the way Trump is treating our allies. And nobody seems to like Trump’s unilateral war in Iran. So America First, also rejected. The core pillars of right-wing populist nationalism have collapsed. I’d like to see that understood as the basis for our case going forward. Does that make sense?

Beauchamp: Yeah. I don’t want to dismiss the affordability point, because it is sort of objectively true, right, that the reason that voters voted against Trump is because of affordability.

But I think what you’re saying points to is that sometimes, in people’s minds, affordability was a proxy for some other concerns that they had. When they said things weren’t affordable, yeah, they blamed those policies for the fact that they had trouble affording things. And not unreasonably, by the way. The Iran war really did drive up gas prices. Tariffs really did make some things more expensive.

And immigration, I think, is a kind of different case, because it also played out unevenly. Immigration wasn’t as important in, I don’t know, let’s say, the Michigan Senate race as it was in Texas, or in House races in Texas in particular, because the impact was uneven.

In some places, there was a real sense that the federal government was snatching their friends and neighbors. And that had this very concentrated effect. And you can see—if I have the data right in my head—you can see pretty clear shifts, disproportionate shifts, in high-immigrant, high-ICE-targeted communities, or areas that have large populations that might have been really punished by Trump. And so there’s a backlash. It’s just a different thing that wouldn’t show up in the same way in the aggregate national data.

And so, yes—like, this is a roundabout way, Greg, of saying, well, I have some issues with the way that you framed it and phrased it. Like, I agree with the underlying point 100 percent.

Sargent: And I want to return to something you said earlier, because I think it gets at the stakes of all this. Which is this idea that I think a lot of liberals have in their heads, that they have to tiptoe around Trumpian populism, that they have to say to themselves, well, the reason Trump won in 2024 is voters decided that Trump was in some sense right about trade, about immigration, and about the liberal international order.

Now, I don’t want to dismiss entirely the idea that voters did think that there was something to Trump’s case. But a lot of liberals really overread that, especially after 2024. And we’ve got to stop doing that. To get to the point where we correct our own ideology and make a good case for our own, we have to be not afraid to say that right-wing populist nationalism has failed and is very unpopular. And there’s a starting point there, I think. What do you think of that?

Beauchamp: Yeah. The way I conceptualize it is that the public hasn’t made up its mind on what it wants to be affirmatively. The American public doesn’t have a sense of what—maybe no public has an ideological sense, but the American public is unusually unsettled as to where it stands right now.

And so what it suggests to me is that they’re open to persuasion, because they’re not happy with the way things are going, and they haven’t seen anyone come up with a way to channel what they think is wrong with the status quo into a political agenda that seems to address their concerns.

I think one advantage Democrats have here, particularly, is that their agenda is not inherently inflationary. Whereas getting rid of immigrants, and, you know, putting big tariffs on other countries, and starting expensive foreign wars in the name of, like, seizing stuff for America—that makes things more expensive. That is just what it does. And there’s no way to avoid that with tariffs and immigration crackdowns.

Sargent: Yeah. In a sense, there’s a political economy of Trumpism. I think we need to rehabilitate the concept of political economy. And maybe this is the place to end this. It connects everything together. This idea that the election was about affordability takes the political out of political economy.

People decided that trade is good, people decided that they like immigrants, people decided that they like our international alliances and human rights norms and so forth. Yes, as you pointed out, the starting point for that, or the entry point, the tip of that spear, was the high costs. 

But they connected those high costs to a set of values that they thought was off. And so liberals, I think, can now step forward and do what you’re calling for, which is a refocusing on what worked for Democrats in this election, connecting liberalism to everyday politics by saying, these are the values that make an economy that will be fairer for all of us. Is that sort of where you want this to go?

Beauchamp: Yeah. My view of it is that there was a baby step in the right direction when Democrats started picking up on some of the themes in Abundance. I don’t think it’s the whole solution. But  that package of beliefs and ideas said, hey, there’s this ambient concern people have about things not really working, and things being too expensive, and government not operating in the smooth way that corporations do sometimes when you interface with them. And those are everyday complaints people have about the state.

And there’s a liberal way to to surface these problems and to bring them into the ordinary political agenda, through very specific policies like permitting reform—that was an act of ideological innovation that seems to have actually worked pretty well in a lot of cases.

I don’t think that swung the election for Democrats. I think it has led to some good policy changes in blue states particularly, that may end up helping build power long term, or, like, sustain a blue-state model. And what you need to do is do that kind of work on a grander scale. Tell not just a story about fixing government and making more things. Tell a story about building a society that people want to live in—a society, not just an economy. A place in which we feel like we have purpose, meaning, connection, and value.

Sargent: In a way, the simplest way to put it might be that we need people to start really making the case for a liberal political economy. Zack Beauchamp, your website is really starting us off on this thing. Public Reason, it’s called. It’s a Substack. Check it out, folks. Zack, awesome to talk to you. Thanks so much for coming on.

Beauchamp: Hey, Greg, I’m always happy to be here. Public-reason.com. I just have to do that at the end of every episode. I was going to say my agent makes me do that, but that was for my book. I don’t have an agent. I just have me, for a Substack.

Sargent: Cool, man. Well, I’m glad you got it in. Zack, thanks for coming on, man.

Beauchamp: Thanks.

items.title: Trump Shivs JD Vance as Meltdown Over GOP Losses Takes Unhinged Turn
items.content_text: Donald Trump, fuming over the midterms, just unleashed a new series of crazed Truth Social posts. He again threatened to prosecute Democrats. He raged that Republicans only lost because they failed to pass voter suppression. And critically, he bizarrely decreed that JD Vance will only be assigned to fighting supposed blue-state corruption from now on. Trump ordered Vance to forget about negotiating an end to the war, delusionally insisting we’ve already won so much that “we don’t need a deal with Iran.” That totally shivs Vance. It punishes him for blaming the war for GOP losses. And it prevents him from repositioning for 2028 by getting on the right side of the Iran fiasco. We talked to Zack Beauchamp, author of the excellent new Public Reason Substack, which is devoted to rehabilitating liberalism. We discuss how Trump kneecapped Vance, why this shows MAGA can’t accept that its worldview unleashed the electoral debacle, how it reveals the deeper failings of right-wing nationalism, and how liberals can seize this moment to make a new case for their ideas. Listen to this episode here. A transcript is here.

items.title: DOJ Says Maybe She Wasn’t a Spy as It Tries to Clean Up Nvidia Mess
items.content_text:
U.S. intelligence officials reportedly concluded Alice Huang—the woman whom Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang had an affair with—is a Chinese government spy one year ago. But now, when pressed for further answers, the Justice Department is suggesting that she might not have been a spy at all.

“When did the Justice Department learn, with regard to Nvidia, that Alice Huang might be a suspected Chinese asset?” a reporter asked Attorney General Todd Blanche at a Thursday press conference. “There’s been concerns raised that the Commerce Department was giving favoritism to Nvidia and Megaspeed, which was Alice Huang’s company. Do you share the concerns that maybe the Commerce Department was impeding the ability to uncover the smuggling network that Alice Huang was involved in?”

“Well, your first question assumes something that I have never said, and that I don’t know to be true,” Blanche replied. “So you assume that DOJ learns that she is in fact a spy—I have not, nobody said that, I certainly haven’t said that. All I said … is that of course DOJ’s investigators are looking at it. There’s no conclusions reached … around who she is or is not.”

Todd Blanche suggests that perhaps Alice Huang isn't really a spy after all and says he has no concerns about Lutnick's alleged involvement in the Nvidia scandal

(they are circling the wagons!) pic.twitter.com/1DsJB0zrzi

— Aaron Rupar (@atrupar) November 12, 2026

This raises further questions about the Trump administration’s handling of the scandal. According to The New York Times, President Trump reportedly knew about the intelligence reports on Huang’s affair—and the fact that she was an alleged honeypot—for months. U.S. intelligence had had Alice Huang under surveillance for more than a year, and State Secretary Marco Rubio personally informed Trump about it again after the president invited Huang to join him on his trip to Beijing. The two traveled together to China anyway. Meanwhile, Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick has reportedly spent the last year trying to avoid targeting Megaspeed.

Nvidia is the most powerful artificial intelligence company in the world, with 90 percent of the market share of the chips that power the vast majority of AI. The Trump administration knew that U.S. intelligence was reporting that Jensen Huang was likely compromised by the Chinese government. But Blanche’s answers suggest that the Trump administration is moving to protect Huang, who is a good friend of Trump—even as he resigned from his post at Nvidia on Thursday as his third cheating scandal was exposed.

items.title: Top Republican Calls for Ilhan Omar to Be Removed From Congress
items.content_text:
Republican Representative Tom Emmer, who was just reelected to lead House Republicans as the party’s whip, a member of the GOP leadership in the House, appears to be doubling down on bigotry and racism following his party’s massive midterm defeat.

On Thursday, Emmer, who represents Minnesota’s 6th congressional district, called on the House sergeant-at-arms to remove his fellow Minnesota Representative Ilhan Omar, who is of Somali origin, saying that she should be removed from Congress after ranting about all the Somalis in his state. Emmer was speaking to conservative podcaster Benny Johnson, who asked him if Omar was an American citizen.

“I don’t think she should be. I think it’s gonna be proven that her birthdate—she has lied about it repeatedly. I think that’s documented,” Emmer said.

Emmer added that “once it is confirmed that she was not under the age of 18 when her father was naturalized, regardless of whether he was rightly naturalized or not, she was over the age of 18. Guess what, Benny? That is an administrative process. She is immediately no longer a citizen, and she has to reapply for citizenship. And by the way, I’ll just remind you that at that point, she’s no longer a member of Congress anymore, either.”

Emmer called Omar “one of the dumbest people you could be” and “completely anti-American.” When Johnson asked him if the military or Capitol Police should remove Omar from Congress if she’s determined not to be a legal citizen, Emmer replied, “Yes! The sergeant at arms, she is no longer allowed on the House floor.”

BENNY JOHNSON: Does the military and go and remove Ilhan Omar from Congress?

TOM EMMER: Yes! Yes! She is no longer allowed on the House floor pic.twitter.com/qzPm1N6HPv

— Aaron Rupar (@atrupar) November 12, 2026

The rest of Emmer’s interview with Johnson contained more slurs against Somali Americans, as he made up stories and echoed President Trump’s accusations of fraud. When Johnson called Somalis a “scar” on the face of Minnesota, Emmer readily agreed.

Now the second-highest ranking Republican in the House, Emmer isn’t changing his ways, just like the rest of his party. In the past, he wasn’t so outwardly racist, even co-founding the Somali American Caucus in 2015 with Democratic Representative Keith Ellison, who is now Minnesota’s attorney general.

In 2016, Emmer defended Somalis in a town hall with his constituents, calling them “some of the fastest-assimilating populations that we’ve had.”

“If you’re asking me how I feel about immigrant populations who are in this country legally, and who are actually trying to find a better way for themselves and their families, I support it wholeheartedly,” Emmer said a decade ago. “I mean, the Germans had the same problem when they came over. The Polish had the problem. The Chinese had the problem.”

How times have changed.

The story has been updated to correct a mischaracterization of Emmer’s quote.

items.title: Donald Trump Says He Wants to “Get Cuba Done” Before 2028
items.content_text:
Donald Trump would like to “get Cuba done” before his second term is out.

The president positively responded to a question about potential U.S. military intervention in Cuba during an interview with Salem News Channel on Thursday.

“If freeing Cuba requires military force before you leave office, will you order that military force?” asked host Hugh Hewitt.

“I want to get Cuba done before I leave, yeah, and we have a very good, talented guy for Cuba named Marco,” Trump said, referring to State Secretary Marco Rubio, whose family hails from the Caribbean island nation.

“He would love to do that,” Trump added, before referring to Cuba as a “failed place.”

It’s far from the first time that the administration has made a target out of America’s Communist neighbor.

Trump told reporters at the White House in March—while Cuba was struggling with an unprecedented economic crisis made worse by America’s Venezuelan oil blockade—that he expected to have the “honor” of “taking Cuba in some form.”

“I do believe I’ll be ... having the honor ​of taking Cuba. That’s a big honor. Taking Cuba in some form,” Trump said at the time. “I ​mean, whether I free it, take it. Think I can do anything I want with it. You want to know the truth.”

Months later in May, White House officials told Politico that what had originated as mild musings had since morphed into a genuine interest inside the Oval Office.

“The mood has definitely changed,” the person familiar with the White House’s discussions said. “The initial idea on Cuba was that the leadership was weak and that the combination of stepped-up sanctions enforcement, really an oil blockade, and clear U.S. military wins in Venezuela and Iran would scare the Cubans into making a deal. Now Iran has gone sideways, and the Cubans are proving much tougher than originally thought. So now military action is on the table in a way that it wasn’t before.”

Rubio then refused to say he wouldn’t invade Cuba while testifying in front of Congress in June, sparking deeper concerns about the administration’s machinations.

items.title: Massie Trolls Mike Johnson for “Crashing Out” Over Epstein Files Act
items.content_text:
Republican House Speaker Mike Johnson is clearly bothered after fellow Republican Representative Thomas Massie forced a vote on the second Epstein Files Transparency Act, accusing Massie of staging a “political stunt.”

Johnson’s rebuke came one day after Massie secured enough signatures via discharge petition to force a vote on the Epstein Files Transparency Act II—which would allow members of Congress, attorneys general, and survivors to sue the Department of Justice for failing to comply with the original EFTA.

“Mr. Massie got 218 signatures for this Epstein bill to come to the floor.... Are you gonna try to fight this at all?” CNN’s Manu Raju asked Johnson.

“I have never fought getting the Epstein files out—” Johnson replied.

“But you fought that bill, the last bill.”

“What we tried to do all along is maintain principle and balance to protect the victims. I was concerned with their original gambit, which by the way, Thomas Massie did for attention,” Johnson said, arguing that Massie could have brought up the files while Biden was president. “All those files sat completely dormant … for the entire Biden administration.... They did this to go after President Trump.”

“Do you support this bill?” Raju asked.

“I haven’t seen this discharge, this is Thomas Massie trying to get attention again.... He’s just trying to cause chaos on the way out. We have always, I have always been for full transparency of the Epstein files,” Johnson said, refusing to answer the question.

Speaker Johnson accuses Thomas Massie of a “political stunt” after Massie gets 218 signatures to force a vote on another Epstein bill — this to make it easier to sue DOJ for withholding docs.

“We always handled this with care to protect victims and to get all the information out… pic.twitter.com/P3f1kU9f8l

— Manu Raju (@mkraju) November 12, 2026

Johnson’s diatribe caught Massie’s attention.

“Speaker of the House crashing out when asked about our new EFTA-II bill that will allow State Attorneys General to prosecute Epstein’s coconspirators, give survivors access to their files, and force the DOJ to release files they’re illegally withholding,” he commented on Raju’s interview with Johnson.

While the Justice Department claims to have withheld about three million files to protect victims, there are still questions about missing files and whose names were on them.

items.title: Mike Pence Tears Into Trump and Vance for Midterm “Reckoning”
items.content_text:
Former Vice President Mike Pence issued a scathing indictment of Donald Trump’s presidency and waning political influence Thursday, charging Trump to return to traditional conservative principles in light of what he described as a midterm “reckoning.”

The former MAGA co-chief slammed many of Trump’s second-term policies, during an interview with Fox News Thursday, railing the president’s tariffs and the “air of corruption” that has consumed the White House.

“I believe our voters rejected President Trump’s redirection of our movement toward protectionist tariffs, towards policies of appeasement towards Russia and even Iran, toward marginalizing the right to life,” Pence said. “And I think that the air of corruption around the Trump administration was very concerning to millions of Americans.”

Pence then moved his target toward Vice President JD Vance’s election postmortem. In the immediate aftermath of the election, Vance said GOP-aligned pollsters had identified four issues that overwhelmingly influenced voters: affordability, the Iran war, “America First,” and the current U.S.-Israel relationship.

Pence emphasized that the reasons underlying the election results were “much more complex than gasoline prices or the war in Iran.”

“There’s no question that the war in Iran became a frustration for millions of Americans, but it wasn’t because President Trump started the war or took on Iran,” Pence said. “It’s because we stopped short and didn’t finish it.”

“As Americans saw the politics of appeasement that the administration embraced, one negotiation after another, I think people became ... frustrated with the lack of progress, frustrated with the price of fuel at the pump,” he added.

Pence also chewed Vance out for highlighting a growing national interest in divesting from Israel.

“If the world knows nothing else, the world should know that America stands with Israel. Israel is our most cherished ally. It is the only democracy in the Arab world,” said Pence, an ardent Christian Zionist who has spent much of his political career defending Israel.

items.title: Democrats Launch Investigation Into Trump’s “Princess of Darkness”
items.content_text:
Democrats in Congress are launching a probe into one of President Trump’s fundraising chiefs, whom he calls his “princess of darkness.”

Senator Elizabeth Warren, Representative Robert Garcia, and Senator Richard Blumenthal are seeking information from Meredith O’Rourke about her role in Trump’s pet projects, saying that her fundraising “reeks of potential corruption,” according to The Wall Street Journal. Warren and Garcia are the incoming chairs of the Senate Subcommittee on Investigations and the House Oversight Committee, respectively.

The letter addresses donations made from corporations including Capital One, SoftBank Group, and Lockheed Martin to Trump’s projects, and how the companies got favorable treatment from the White House afterward. It’s asking for a list of every company and donor O’Rourke reached out to for money, how they responded, and how much she is paid.

O’Rourke has been the main point of contact for companies donating to Trump’s White House ballroom, his presidential library, and the political committees connected to him. Trump generally refers names to her to solicit donations from. The Journal reports that she asks donors for anywhere between $5 million and $50 million, telling them that “this is very important to the president” and “the boss wants this money.”

“You facilitate an operation that raises serious questions about quid pro quo politics,” the letter says to O’Rourke, asking that she respond by November 25.

A spokesperson for O’Rourke and Trump dismissed the letter.

“President Trump is the most successful fundraiser in political history, and he is deeply grateful to his donors, but one thing has never changed: He can’t be bought,” the spokesperson said. “Democrats’ accusations are absurd, baseless, and full of hypocrisy.”

The White House has warned against any investigations into the president and his actions, claiming that such probes constitute crimes. Trump and his cronies seem to think that anything they do is above reproach.

items.title: Pete Hegseth Pins Medal on Soldier Who Yelled At Him
items.content_text:
Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth has awarded the soldier who loudly scolded him and his entourage for disturbing the peace at the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier on Veteran’s Day.

“We love soldiers. We love standards. Well done, Specialist. Carry on Patriots,” Hegseth wrote in a post Thursday, sharing photographs of himself and several members of the 3rd Infantry Regiment, known as the Old Guard, taken during an impromptu award ceremony at the Pentagon.

That included Specialist Thomas Iglesias, who reprimanded Hegseth and his retinue on Wednesday as they chatted and laughed after snapping pictures on the stairs in front of the sacred war memorial.

“All visitors will maintain an atmosphere of silence and respect at all times,”
yelled Iglesias, who was guarding the tomb at the time.

Iglesias was awarded the Joint Service Commendation Medal Thursday for carrying out his duties.

But it is not clear if Iglesias was actually eligible to receive the commemoration. The Defense Department’s awards manual stipulates that only service members on joint duty assignments can be awarded the joint service medal, according to a review by Military.com. Iglesias, meanwhile, was assigned to an Army regiment, according to Arlington National Cemetery.

Members of service-specific units “are not eligible for DoD Joint [personal military decorations],” according to the manual.

Although exceptions are allowed (and such exceptions are at the discretion of the awarding body or, in this case, the Defense Secretary) it has not been publicly disclosed if such an exception was approved, as a citation was not mentioned in the Pentagon’s statement provided to CNN.

In the aftermath of the interaction on Wednesday, chief Pentagon spokesman Sean Parnell said that Iglesias “correctly and respectfully reminded everyone to maintain decorum.”

items.title: California Billionaires Got a Tax Break for Fighting the Wealth Tax
items.content_text:
Last week, the Democrats resoundingly won control of Congress in part by tapping into populist anger at an economy rigged for billionaires. And in Washington and Colorado, voters approved tax hikes on the rich. In California, though, the billionaires managed to defeat a proposed wealth tax—and did so not simply by tapping their deep pockets, but by exploiting an unfair tax break that is effectively subsidized by American taxpayers like you.

Proposition 40 would have enacted a one-time 5 percent tax on California’s roughly 200 billionaires, mainly to backfill the federal funding cuts to Medicaid in President Trump’s One Big Beautiful Bill Act. But the billionaires weren’t feeling charitable—at least, not in the typical sense. Building a Better California, the nonprofit organization created to oppose the tax, raised more than $333 million, much of it from Big Tech billionaires: Google co-founder Sergey Brin gave $102 million and Google’s former CEO Eric Schmidt gave $40 million.

Whatever you think of Prop 40 in particular or wealth taxes in general, there’s a wrinkle that should make every working taxpayer furious: The billionaires who spent unfathomable sums of money to keep their taxes from going up actually got a tax break for doing so. As The New York Times reported, Building a Better California’s fundraisers encouraged donors to give appreciated stock instead of cash, because, thanks to a loophole in federal law, gifts of appreciated stock are not subject to capital gains tax. That made for an appealing fundraising pitch to billionaires: Donate your shares, and you will never have to pay capital gains tax on the increase in their value. It worked. More than two-thirds of what the group raised over the campaign’s final six weeks came in as stock.

So how does this loophole work? Billionaires do not make their money the same way that working people do. Their income mostly doesn’t come from a paycheck or even a bonus at the end of the year; they make their money from owning things and having those things increase in value. If they sell those things, they owe capital gains tax—i.e., tax on the amount that the asset’s value increased since it was purchased. But if they donate their ownership stakes to a charity, they owe nothing on the gain, and of course the charity doesn’t pay taxes on the donation, either. That may be defensible if the donation is to a food bank. It’s much less defensible for political donations.

In fact, Congress already addressed exactly that. Section 84 of the tax code says that if you give appreciated property (including stock) to a political organization, you are treated as if you sold it, and you pay tax on the gain. That makes sense—but there’s a catch. Section 84 borrows the definition of “political organization” from another part of the code that covers only groups working to elect candidates. So billionaires like Building a Better California’s donors, who give to an organization fighting a ballot measure, aren’t covered.

The stakes are not small. If a billionaire gives cash to an advocacy group or a ballot initiative, they will have paid taxes on the income that created that cash. But if they give stock or an asset, they won’t. That means the public is essentially subsidizing their advocacy giving. For example, for a founder whose shares cost him or her next to nothing to acquire, every $100 million donated in stock rather than cash can mean as much as $37 million in avoided federal and state capital gains tax. That is a significant public subsidy, paid by everyone else, for the most powerful people in the country to outspend the voters.

This loophole is particularly concerning because the whole point of establishing ballot referenda as a pathway for policymaking was to enable ordinary people to go around legislatures that don’t act in the people’s interest. Indeed, as the Ninth Circuit Court of Appeals has explained, California originally adopted the initiative system in 1911 under the leadership of a Progressive Reform Movement governor as an antidote to capture of the legislature by the Southern Pacific Railroad—that it is, “at its core, a mechanism to ensure that the people, rather than corporations or special interests, maintain control of their government.” And across the country, voters have used initiatives to raise the minimum wage, enact paid leave, expand Medicaid, protect reproductive rights, and more, often over the objections of the politicians and the donors who fund them. That is precisely why the ultrawealthy target these initiatives.

The good news is that the fix is simple. Congress could amend Section 84 to provide that “political organization” means any group organized and operated primarily to accept contributions or make expenditures for the purpose of (1) advocating for or against any candidate for public office; (2) advocating for or against the qualification for the ballot, or the passage of any ballot measure in any election; or (3) federal lobbying activities.

That’s it. Donating appreciated stock to fight a ballot measure would be treated exactly like donating it to fight a candidate: as a sale, with tax owed on the gain. Donors would still be free to spend whatever the law allows. They just wouldn’t get a tax break for doing it.

Granted, passing this fix is not quite as simple. With control of Congress next year, the Democrats could pass this tax-reform measure with a simple majority vote, since tax measures are eligible for the reconciliation process. Trump could veto it. But even if the Democrats have to wait two years to get such a bill over the line, now is the time to start laying the groundwork for it.

Our tax code is in need of many other reforms, of course. There are simply too many ways for billionaires to legally avoid paying their fair share. But it will be immensely more difficult to reform our tax policy if billionaires get tax breaks for fighting to keep their tax breaks.

items.title: What Is Going On With Melania Trump’s “Exclusive Senior Adviser”?
items.content_text:
First lady Melania Trump’s “exclusive senior adviser” is a movie producer who has no security clearance, no political expertise, and no actual boss in the White House. He’s also reportedly been speaking with Ukrainian and Russian officials on the first lady’s behalf.

Marc Beckman, who first worked as a lifestyle consultant to the first lady and produced Amazon’s poorly received Melania documentary, has been advising Melania diplomatically for at least a year. He was specifically credited as a primary connector in the most recent humanitarian ceasefire declaration between Russia and Ukraine, although his role in that process is also unclear. He even posted a picture of himself, Russian envoy Kirill Dmitriev, and Ukrainian official David Arakhamia at the White House on Sunday to celebrate the ceasefire.

Not even the first lady’s former staffers seem to know who Beckman is. First-term adviser Stephanie Grisham told MS NOW that she “never heard [Melania] utter his name for the whole time I was around her.” One current administration member couldn’t seem to remember Beckman’s name when asked. “Is that the guy who looks like Fabio?” he said, referring to Beckman’s shoulder-length hair.

“He’s like the shadow first lady,” Grisham continued. “She does want to do meaningful things, but she lets you bring them to her in a bow. The whole thing is bizarre. I’ve thought, ‘Who the fuck is this guy?’ I remember her saying she felt like she was losing her voice because I was putting so many statements out.… She doesn’t like people speaking on her behalf yet he keeps speaking.”

This is one of many instances in which the Trump administration has ignored the proper rules of engagement for politics and diplomacy, allowing private citizens with potential conflicts of interest—like Elon Musk and Jared Kushner—to have a massively outsize impact on the administration’s decisions.

items.title: DOJ to Democratic Senator: Stop Your Ballroom Investigation or Else!
items.content_text:
The Trump administration is levying legal threats at any Democrat attempting to investigate it.

On Thursday, the Justice Department accused Connecticut Senator Richard Blumenthal of harassment for his probe into the wealthy private donors who funded President Trump’s $400 million White House vanity ballroom. U.S. Attorney Aaron Reitz ordered Blumenthal to lock away any of his findings or face “significant legal consequences.”

“After the election, [Senator Blumenthal] & his allies think they can intimidate Americans for their constitutionally protected associations w/ President Trump,” Reitz wrote online on Wednesday. “Congress is not a weapon to be wielded against the American people. I’m taking the first step to stop this abuse of power.”

Last month, The Washington Post reported that 57 companies donated $100,000 or more to the vanity project. Some of those companies are headed by people who have already donated to Trump in other ways—and have been rewarded in return, in the form of business contracts and dropped investigations. It’s unclear how Blumenthal looking into that constitutes using Congress “against the American people,” as Reitz argues. It’s also unclear why Reitz, the U.S. attorney for Texas, is threatening a senator from Connecticut in the first place—especially given that Blumenthal’s probe is well within the confines of the Constitution.

“Why is a Houston-based US Attorney threatening a Connecticut-based Senator over constitutionally-mandated oversight of DC figures? Because the DOJ is hemorrhaging staff, who don’t want to do this dirty work, and this US Attorney is a trained seal for Trump,” wrote Adam Klasfield, All Rise News editor in chief, “No other reason.”

Blumenthal later responded.

“This investigation into me for conducting a congressional inquiry is just the latest in a series of unlawful actions on the part of the Trump Admin attempting to intimidate Members of Congress for engaging in constitutionally protected activity,” he wrote Thursday night. “The implied threat of an investigation is baseless. As incoming Chair of the Permanent Subcommittee on Investigations, I will not be intimidated.”

items.title: New Nevada Governor Calls to Join Pact to Overthrow Electoral College
items.content_text:
Nevada’s incoming Democratic governor wants to negate the Electoral College.

Aaron Ford said Wednesday that he thinks the state should join the National Popular Vote Interstate Compact, an agreement where member states give their electoral votes in every presidential election to whoever wins the national popular vote.

“I didn’t initially support it frankly because I hadn’t done enough research on it, but I have researched it and, looking at the Electoral College, understanding the, frankly, racist underpinnings of it in the first place leads me to believe that we need to get rid of it,” Ford told Nevada TV station KOLO regarding the compact. “Not only for that reason, but because we’ve seen several times now the person who wins the popular vote not win because of the Electoral College.”

After last week’s midterm elections, Democrats have taken over control of state legislatures and governorships not just in Nevada but also Pennsylvania, Michigan, Arizona, and Wisconsin, which haven’t agreed to the compact. If all five states agree to join the compact, their electoral votes combined with the states that have already agreed to it would be enough to effectively nullify the Electoral College.

Ford’s comments give the idea more weight, especially considering that he’s one of the country’s five Black governors who won their elections last week. But the idea faces constitutional hurdles. In Article 2, Section 1, Clauses 2 and 3, the Constitution says that states can appoint electors “in such Manner as the Legislature thereof may direct.” But in Article 1, Section 10, Clause 3, it also prohibits interstate compacts without the consent of Congress.

The current Supreme Court has six conservative justices who are more than likely to take a narrow interpretation and shoot down the compact, and require Congress and the president’s consent on any deal. That means even if enough states agree to the compact now, it could be years before it takes effect, if ever. Still, for now, Democratic-led states could set up that legal challenge.

items.title: Trump’s Nvidia Problem Just Got Worse
items.content_text:
Former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang has responded to Republican Representative John Moolenaar’s request for a closed-door meeting, and he is reportedly in talks to coordinate a date.

Moolenaar told NBC News’s Brennan Leach that he expects Huang to appear before Congress while the GOP is still in the majority.

“I would hope he would want to come in and have that discussion with us,” Moolenaar told NBC News.

Huang resigned as Nvidia’s CEO, president, and board member Thursday morning, after The New York Times caught Huang in another scandalous affair with one of his direct reports: Kimberly Powell, the company’s vice president of health care.

Huang was already facing fire for a different affair he had with a Chinese businesswoman, former Megaspeed executive Alice Huang (no relation of Jensen’s), who U.S. intelligence agencies identified as a spy and a state asset.

Nvidia emerged in recent years as the largest semiconductor company in the world, and a precious American asset in the burgeoning AI tech wave.

In January 2025, Nvidia was announced as one of the “key” technology partners in the Trump administration’s $500 billion public-private initiative to jump-start AI-focused data center development, dubbed the Stargate Project. Months later, Donald Trump allowed the company to export previously banned chips to China, loosening trade restrictions on tech that Washington feared could be used against U.S. national security interests.

Trump reportedly knew about Huang’s affair—and his spying partner—for months. State Secretary Marco Rubio informed Trump about the alarming relationship moments before Huang joined the presidential trip to Beijing at the president’s request. It was at least the second time that Trump had been informed of Huang’s ties to the Chinese government, inside sources told The New York Times.

But Trump did not act on the information.

Instead, Trump has denied any knowledge of the illicit affair. On Tuesday, Trump refuted the Times’ report, telling a reporter in the White House press room that he “didn’t hear about” the scandal in May. Trump added that he spoke with the Nvidia leader earlier that day, when Huang claimed he had “absolutely no idea that the person in question was a spy.”

“And I really believe him,” Trump added.

But not everyone is convinced by the Trump administration’s blind eye. Connecticut Representative Jim Himes, who is expected to become chair of the House Intelligence Committee in the new year, expressed alarm that the FBI had not opened an investigation into the apparently suspicious relationship, despite the internal circulation of a memo detailing the Megaspeed executive’s myriad links to the Chinese government.

“I would hope that the FBI would launch a major counterintelligence investigation. I haven’t heard that they did,” Himes told Politico, noting that Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton and CIA Director John Ratcliffe apparently “didn’t know” whether the FBI had opened an investigation either.

items.title: Oil Exec Who Got Nice Contract on Venezuelan Oil was Top Vance Donor
items.content_text:
Vice President JD Vance secretly met with one of his top donors days before the Trump administration invaded Venezuela and cut a deal that would make his company millions from selling the country’s stolen crude oil.

A week before the U.S. military invaded Venezuela and kidnapped its leader, Nicolás Maduro, Vance traveled to Bozeman, Montana, where he secretly met with John Addison, a U.S. gasoline trader at Vitol, the world’s largest energy and commodity trading company, Reuters reported Wednesday.

In 2022, Addison poured $300,000 into Vance’s successful bid for one of Ohio’s U.S. Senate seats. He and his wife later gave a combined $7 million to groups supporting Donald Trump’s presidential campaign in 2024.

At the meeting, the two men spoke about Venezuela, and the vice president expressed a particular interest in how fast Venezuelan crude oil could be sold in the case that the U.S. gained control of the country’s energy supplies, a person who was given an account of the meeting from Addison told Reuters. Addison assured Vance that Vitol was more than able to get the job done.

Addison’s private Embraer jet and Vance’s government plane sat together on the tarmac at Bozeman Yellowstone International Airport on December 27, according to flight records reviewed by Reuters.

This meeting was previously unreported, but gives insight to the backroom deals to enrich allies of the Trump administration. Both Addison and Vance denied the meeting took place.

On January 5, just two days after the operation to kidnap Maduro, Addison got a call from Energy Secretary Chris Wright, who asked whether Vitol would be interested in selling Venezuelan crude oil.

Addison wasn’t a natural choice to receive a call from Wright. He wasn’t a regional CEO, or an expert in Latin American gasoline, but rather, a senior trader involved in sales of U.S. oil. But Vance had told Wright that he was the right person for the job, Addison told Reuters.

The Department of Energy, however, claims that Vance and Wright never discussed the sales of Venezuelan oil, and Vitol was chosen solely because of the firm’s scale.

By January 9, Vitol and Trafigura, its direct competitor, had obtained special licenses to sell Venezuelan crude oil. Since then, the companies have raked in hundreds of millions of dollars in profit from selling stolen supplies.

Typically, large U.S. government contracts are awarded through a competitive bidding process—a standard that has seemingly gone out the window during Trump 2.0.

Representative Robert Garcia, ranking Democrat on the House Oversight Committee and its incoming chair, sent a letter to the heads of Vitol and Tafigura demanding answers about how exactly they received these licenses, and voicing concern that the companies may have been given advance notice about U.S. military action in Venezuela. Both Vitol and Trafigura declined to answer Garcia’s letter, but the companies told Reuters that they did not receive any advanced knowledge.

items.title: MAGA Streamer Nick Shirley Just Issued an Embarrassing Correction
items.content_text:
Last month, right-wing conspiracy theorist and YouTuber Nick Shirley followed an old woman around Lam’s Seafood, a Vietnamese grocery store in Seattle. He observed her buying spring rolls and tuna, which he incorrectly called spam and sushi. Shirley claims in a video voiceover that the items were “magically $120.”

“How come you sold this spam and sushi for $120?” he says to the cashier, who gives him a confused look. He eventually demands to speak to the manager and asks any worker in sight why they’re “letting people commit food stamp fraud.”

“You all are committing fraud, this entire block is committing fraud,” he says in the video, which can still be seen on TikTok.

Lam’s denied Shirley’s allegations more than a month ago, with its operations manager saying that Lam’s had never participated in any EBT fraud. They pointed out that because Shirley does not speak Vietnamese, he missed the woman clearly asking for an entire case of tuna—which she was correctly charged.

A month later, Shirley fully retracted his story.

“I have an important correction to make,” Shirley said in a video posted Wednesday. “I stated [the woman at Lam’s] purchased one can of spam and one order of sushi for $120. That was incorrect, as Lam’s has later now clarified that the lady was attempting to purchase a case of spam, which is why the transaction was $120. I have not uncovered any evidence that Lam’s itself engaged in EBT fraud or that Lam’s colluded with the woman in the video who was attempting to use her EBT card.”

So Shirley harassed an old Vietnamese woman just trying to buy tuna for nothing. Many online noted that the GOP operative’s apology and retraction sounded like they had been written by a lawyer.

“Did he get a cease and desist letter? This sounds very lawyered,” The New York Times’s Ken Bensinger wrote.

Shirley has made a career out of harassing minority-owned businesses and baselessly accusing them of financial crimes. In April, more than a dozen federal agents showed up at the Mini Childcare Center in Minneapolis. It was one of the many daycares that Shirley harassed while attempting to prove that Somali Americans were running an elaborate fraud scheme. None of the daycares that Shirley targeted have been found to have committed fraud.

items.title: Trump Wants to Forget About the Disastrous Iran War
items.content_text:
Donald Trump no longer seems concerned about brokering a deal with Iran after the midterms.

In a layered Truth Social post Thursday, the president declared that “we don’t need a deal with Iran.”

“Those days have long since passed,” Trump continued. “We’ve got their money, Hundreds of Billions of Dollars, and we’ve got their Strait!”

Hours earlier, Trump declared victory against Iran during a Veteran’s Day speech at Arlington National Cemetery in Virginia, even though he acknowledged the war is not yet over.

“Under this administration, and it was about time, somebody fought back,” Trump said. “All of us fought back. We fought back. And we seriously fought back. And we won. Just a question of when we want to end it.”

“We want to make sure we have a total victory, not a 93 percent victory,” he added. “It’s going to be total. It’ll take them 25 years to rebuild back what we have destroyed, and hopefully we won’t have to destroy any more of that country.”

Trump on Iran War: We won. We want to make sure we have a total victory, not a 93% victory. https://t.co/d4DTeWZZls

— Clash Report (@clashreport) November 11, 2026

For weeks, Trump teased a full-scale bombardment of Iran after the midterm elections. That has not yet happened. Instead, the Pentagon launched Task Force Iron Gate to choke off the country’s trade routes and limit its advanced weapons shipments, according to Reuters.

But Iran has not backed down. Instead, Iranian security chief Mohsen Rezaei escalated the country’s threats on Wednesday, pledging that Tehran would also attack European military bases if they were used by American forces for renewed warfaring purposes.

“If American aircraft take off from an American military base, even one located in a European country or some other distant region, to bomb Iran, we will strike those bases as well,” Rezaei told Lebanese broadcaster Al Mayadeen TV.

In another portion of the interview, Rezaei vaguely warned that Iran might also attack more distant U.S. military installations, as well as “certain islands that they assume are beyond the reach of our missiles.”

items.title: ICE Caught Deleting Posts After Being Sued for Arrest of U.S. Citizen
items.content_text:
Immigration and Customs Enforcement appears to be trying to cover its tracks after the agency was sued on Tuesday by a woman it violently arrested and detained. 

HuffPost reports that ICE deleted at least two posts from its X account defending the arrest of Minneapolis resident Aliya Rahman, who was heading to a medical appointment in January when agents smashed her car window and dragged her from the vehicle. Rahman sued the agency, accusing agents of false arrest and imprisonment, negligent supervision, negligence, assault, and battery.

The first deleted post, from February, included a video of the incident. ICE captioned the video: “Unfortunately, we have the receipts. As shown in our video, Aliya Rahman clearly had enough room to move herself and her vehicle out of the way. Officers even walked away from the vehicle, thinking that she was going to leave the scene. Instead, she remained at the location, continued to impede our officers, and found out the hard way.”  

The second deleted post criticized Democratic Representative Zoe Lofgren, who brought up Rahman’s violent arrest at a congressional hearing in March with then Homeland Security Secretary Kristi Noem. 

“Rep. Lofgren is pushing a lie that’s already been debunked,” the post read. “As shown in our video, anti-ICE agitator Aliya Rahman clearly had enough room to move herself and her vehicle out of the way. Officers even walked away from her vehicle, thinking she was going to leave the scene. Instead, she remained at the location, continued to impede our officers, and found out the hard way.”

The agency didn’t respond to HuffPost’s questions as to why it deleted the posts. Federal agencies are required to preserve all records by law, including social media posts. At least one other post mentioning Rahman is still available on ICE’s X profile. 

“Agencies cannot delete records from a social media platform or from a recordkeeping system without a disposition provided by a NARA-approved records schedule,” the National Archives and Records Administration told government agency leaders in a November 2022 memo.  

A Homeland Security spokesperson told HuffPost, “We are aware of the lawsuit and look forward to vigorously defending ourselves in court.”

items.title: Ukraine Loses Starlink Access as Jared Kushner Lands in Russia
items.content_text:
Is Elon Musk messing with Ukraine’s Starlink access again?

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskiy claimed Thursday that the country’s Starshield, the military-grade version of Starlink communication systems, had once again experienced “significant disruptions” over Russian-occupied areas of Ukraine for the past “several days.”

“The Ukrainian military have already investigated the circumstances, and these are not random errors but systematic speed restrictions,” Zelenskiy wrote in a statement on X.

News of these disruptions came as U.S. envoys Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff arrived in Moscow Thursday morning to continue peace deal negotiations with Russian President Vladimir Putin.

Last month, SpaceX also interrupted the country’s military-grade Starlink terminals, blinding the Ukrainian government. That disruption came just days after President Donald Trump publicly criticized Ukraine for continuing to attack Russian oil refineries in the wake of the U.S. lifting sanctions on the sale of Russian oil.

Initially, SpaceX CEO Elon Musk claimed that it was Trump’s idea, while the president played dumb. The order to slow the service reportedly came directly from the White House, and later reporting suggested that Musk approached Trump about disrupting his own military communications service in Ukraine.

In a separate post on X Thursday, Zelenskiy said that the Starshield disruptions directly affected Ukraine’s ability to intercept Russian jet-powered drones with drones of their own. “This means more Russian strikes get through, and more of our people are killed by Russia,” he wrote.

“We are trying to get the details from the American side, but so far, we know very little,” he wrote. “If someone in America is making decisions that basically treat Ukrainian territory as if it is not Ukrainian, then this tells us where things are going.”

items.title: Republicans Say They’re “Stupid” and “Urinating” All Over Themselves
items.content_text:
Some Republican lawmakers are clearly fed up with their “stupid” GOP colleagues who refuse to learn from the party’s sweeping losses in the midterm elections.

Following total disaster in the midterm elections, Republican lawmakers have responded by refusing to impeach Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, whose leadership of the unpopular Iran war contributed greatly to Republican losses, and choosing Representative Jim Jordan, a MAGA extremist, to serve as the new House minority leader.

Republican Senator John Kennedy slammed anyone who tried to downplay the disastrous midterm during an appearance on Fox News’s Hannity Thursday.

“This was not a normal midterm election loss. If you think that, congratulations, you’re stupid,” Kennedy said. (Of course, host Sean Hannity was among the figures who had attempted to minimize the Republicans’ midterm massacre.)

Rather than simply stay home, Kennedy claimed that voters had actively rejected the MAGA agenda. “They voted for Democrats, and we’ve gotta get Toby and Edith back,” he said.

Earlier on the Senate floor, Kennedy said Republicans were basically urinating on themselves.

“A smart man washes his hands after he urinates. A wise man doesn’t urinate on his hands. We need to stop urinating on our hands.... We Republicans in the Senate need to stop thinking we’re so smart,” Kennedy said.

🚨 NOW: Sen. John Kennedy drops this line on the Senate floor

"A smart man washes his hands after he urinates. A wise man doesn't urinate on his hands. WE NEED TO STOP URINATING ON OUR HANDS." 😭

"The only way we can actually do that in the remaining time we have left is… pic.twitter.com/4GY7hmyYex

— Eric Daugherty (@EricLDaugh) November 11, 2026

Kennedy wasn’t the only Republican who appeared frustrated with the response from his party.

Republican Representative David Joyce spoke to CNN’s Manu Raju Wednesday, about Republicans who’d signaled their intention to double down on the MAGA agenda.

“They can’t double down on stupid,” Joyce said.

“What happened to us was a message, clear and very loud, that people don’t like the way we’re been moving in the wrong direction, and you can’t lie to people about the things that they feel,” he said. “They feel it at the pump. They feel it at the grocery store. They feel it in their kids’ education, in the potential for losing their jobs to AI. And we haven’t done anything to address those.”

items.title: Republicans Turn Against Howard Lutnick as Nvidia Chips Scandal Grows
items.content_text:
Republicans are turning on Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick after he stalled a crackdown on companies suspected of diverting Nvidia chips to China. Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang has been at the center of the news cycle after it was revealed he had an affair with a Chinese spy.

Politico reports that Republican leaders are criticizing Lutnick for not taking action against Megaspeed, the Singapore-based firm with ties to the Chinese government whose executive was in a relationship with Huang. Several Republicans say they want Lutnick and his deputies to answer their questions, possibly in sworn testimony.

“The obvious question is why did [Lutnick] choose to sell advanced chips?” Republican Senator John Kennedy told Politico Wednesday. “Secretary Lutnick needs to answer that in front of God and country. If I were he, I’d call a press conference this afternoon and explain what happened and why he agreed to sell them chips, and I would stop doing it.”

Republican Representative Bill Huizenga called on Lutnick to testify before Congress, saying, “I don’t think he’s been very responsive.” He added that the Bureau of Industry and Security, an agency in the Commerce Department that is responsible for blacklisting overseas companies from using American technology, has “been less responsive than they should be.”

Lutnick is also receiving pressure from elsewhere in the Trump administration. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent reportedly criticized him in a White House meeting last week for not taking earlier action on Megaspeed.

“I’d say we want to get to the bottom of the matter and to really have transparency on this,” said Republican Representative John Moolenar, who chairs the House Select Committee on the Chinese Communist Party. Moolenar told Politico that he wants Lutnick and others in the administration to brief Congress on the Chinese government’s influence on Nvidia, and how that in turn influenced U.S. security policy.

items.title: Transcript: Trump Christian Allies Unnerved as His On-Air Rage Darkens
items.content_text:
The following is a lightly edited transcript of the November 12 episode of The Daily Blast podcast. Listen to it here.


Greg Sargent: This is The Daily Blast from The New Republic, produced and presented by the DSR Network. I’m your host, Greg Sargent.

It took many years, but Donald Trump’s Christian and evangelical allies have finally grown unnerved by his public displays of malevolence and hate. This came after Trump’s interview with CBS this week, in which he refused to say he’d forgive his enemies, even in order to get into heaven. This comes amid other related developments. A lot of Trump’s evangelical supporters stayed home in the midterms, and a number of Democratic candidates ran overtly on liberal Christian themes and won.

So we’re checking in on all of this with Holly Berkley Fletcher, who covers right-wing Christianity on her Substack, A Zebra Without Stripes. Holly, thanks for coming on.

Holly Berkley Fletcher: Thanks for having me.

Sargent: So before we get deep into Trump’s latest, can you just explain his relationship to evangelical Christianity—how he’s viewed as a very flawed vessel who’s nonetheless carrying out divine providence to realize Christian nationalist ends, all that?

Fletcher: Yeah. So I don’t think you’d have Trump without white evangelicals. They voted for him at over 80 percent every election, and they’ve voted for Republicans at above 80 percent as well for a while, including this current election.

And I think his appeal, and the Christian nationalists’ appeal, is rooted in their fear of cultural decline, accompanying their longtime sense, that goes back decades and decades, that they are sort of God’s chosen people and God’s chosen nation.

So as their numbers and sort of cultural influence have declined, they have responded with fear and authoritarianism, basically.

Sargent: And Trump is basically the guy who said, I will do whatever it takes to save the Christian America that you think is slipping away, basically.

Fletcher: Correct. He’s explicitly tapped into that feeling.

Sargent: And as you said, he’s been hijacking long-running trends on the religious right, the move toward Republicans that really kind of took off in the ’80s and now is culminating.

Fletcher: Yes, absolutely.

Sargent: So let’s go to Trump’s remarkable moment on CBS. Speaking to CBS’s Ross Douthat, Trump first confirms that he hopes he goes to heaven. Then Trump is asked if he would be able to forgive his enemies in order to pass God’s judgment. The back-and-forth is long, but worth it. Listen.

Ross Douthat (voiceover): You pass away. You’re entering the next life. And all you have to do to enter paradise is feel love and forgiveness for James Comey, Nancy Pelosi, anyone who you have expressed hate for over the years. Do you think you can do it?

Donald Trump (voiceover): Well, then I wouldn’t be real, would I? I mean, if I said to you, sure—the easy answer to that’s yes, I could forgive.

Douthat (voiceover): Is the answer no?

Trump (voiceover): The answer is no. I want to be honest.”

Douthat (voiceover): Before the judgment throne of God.

Trump (voiceover): Before the judgment. No, I think they were very bad people. And I dislike—I can use the word hate. I do hate some of my enemies. I think they’ve been terrible. Look what they put me through, the weaponization. I get indicted.

Douthat (voiceover): Mr. President, you have had the most charmed and remarkable life of any American in my entire lifetime. And you are telling me you couldn’t find it in your heart to forgive some of your enemies, after all that’s been given to you?

Trump (voiceover): I mean, it’s such an easy answer. All I have to do is say, yes, I can.

Douthat (voiceover): Again, I don’t think it’s an easy answer.

Trump (voiceover): That’s my—can I be honest? I probably cannot do that now. Because I do hate some of my enemies, and I always will.


Sargent: So Holly, I know that Donald Trump has said similar things before. He has said that he won’t forgive his enemies before. He’s very much confirmed that he hates his enemies.

But it’s a little remarkable for him to talk this way after such a dramatic national repudiation of him, isn’t it?

Fletcher: Yes. Well, I mean, if he was a rational actor, which he’s not, of course, he should be scrambling to shore up his support from his evangelical base. And this is certainly not the way to do it.

Again, whenever he puts them on the spot by just, like, countering explicitly a really foundational evangelical Christian belief, like loving your enemies, or repenting, or forgiving, these types of things, it really puts them in a very tough spot and sort of sends them scrambling.

And that’s not what they want and need at this time, when they’re sort of feeling deflated. And that’s not what he should really be doing at this time. But again, not a rational actor.

Sargent: I’m going to float a theory, OK, and see what you think of it. I think Trump was essentially giving his evangelical supporters the middle finger in some sense. He knows they didn’t show up in quite the numbers that he needed in this election. We’ll get to that in a sec.

But he was very much out there in red America saying, you’ve got to turn out for us, you’ve got to turn out and save us. And they didn’t. And I just wonder whether, on some level, he was basically saying, you know what? I don’t really give a shit about your heaven. What do you think of that?

Fletcher: I don’t know that he’s that calculating. I think he’s, you know—again, he usually tells us what he’s thinking. I think he’s long worried about the eternal destination of his soul on some level. He lets that slip a lot of times. So I don’t know if he’s that calculating. But he’s got to be upset with them right now, you know. And we know he sort of lashes out when he’s upset.

Sargent: I don’t really believe that he’s religious. I’m sorry. What do you think of that?

Fletcher: I’m shocked, Greg. I’m shocked that you would say that? So yeah, no, I think he’s completely without belief of any kind. I think he’s amoral. He only believes in his own narcissism. And I think he’s been using religious voters this entire time.

They’re a very easy mark for a con man, because they have very deeply held, easily hijacked beliefs. You say certain things, you champion the issues that they want—which, of course, he did on abortion, and gave them their Supreme Court, you know—and he’s been using them the whole time.

They’ve been a very cheap date, and he’s taken advantage.

Sargent: I don’t think he’s worried about the state of his soul. He’s worried about dying, which he confuses with worry about the state of his soul, maybe.

Fletcher: I think he thinks—I don’t know, sometimes I think he thinks that maybe he won’t ever die. I think he might be that narcissistic.

Sargent: Yeah, possibly. Well, you know, with his health issues, I have a feeling he’s really looking straight into the abyss right now. That’s the way I see it.

Well, anyway, a number of leading Christians took issue with this. Pastor Franklin Graham, who’s a leading Trump ally, posted a long response. He said this:

“To enter heaven, the Bible tells us that you must acknowledge your sins, turn from them in repentance, and receive Jesus Christ by faith. Religion can’t save you. Only a relationship with the Savior, Jesus Christ, can save you. Do you have that assurance?”

Holly, Franklin Graham didn’t exactly say he was addressing Trump here in that last line, but I think he was. And he’s basically telling Trump, you may not get into heaven, given not just your answer there, but also the state of your soul, Mr. President. What do you make of that?

Fletcher: Yeah, again, I think the reaction, whenever he does one of these, like, major boo-boos, theological boo-boos, it puts evangelicals in just a really terrible position, especially the ones like Graham, who has at various times vouched for his, you know, his itty-bitty baby faith.

He’s just an itty-bitty baby Christian and growing in his faith. But when he makes a sort of theological mistake, they often sort of gently correct the record, if not directly him. And so Franklin Graham has done that.

Others have been a little bit more pointed, saying it’s extraordinary, and to pray for him. A lot of them are praying for him today. Some of them are saying that they appreciate his honesty. He’s struggling in his faith right now. Anyway, he needs a lot of prayer, Greg, is what the bottom line is.

Sargent: Well, Denny Burk, a right-wing pastor and influencer, did say exactly that. He put this on Twitter: “Ross Douthat’s interview with the president is one of the most extraordinary things I’ve ever seen. Pray for the president.”

Fletcher: And then he lists Bible verses that say, forgive your enemies. So that one was actually quite pointed, from someone—we call them theobros in my world.

What we mean by that are sort of MAGA evangelical pastor-slash-influencer types who think they are the authority on all things Christianity. And Denny Burk is a well-known name in that world. So I thought that was more pointed than I’ve seen, for sure.

Sargent: Talk a little bit more about what a theobro is. It strikes me that this is a very unique phenomenon to our time. You’ve got the MAGA movement, which is really very large and multifaceted, and it’s got all sorts of different strains, different kind of rivulets and stuff like that running into it.

And there’s this right-wing Christianity element to it that’s sort of riding the MAGA train in some sense, but bringing all this religious talk to it. What is that world?

Fletcher: Yeah. Well, the theobros are—some of them are pastors, but they’re very much the online sort of crowd of men. They’re all men, generally younger-ish men. Like, I wouldn’t quite call Franklin Graham a theobro.

But they’re very much online, and they basically police their corners of the internet and their evangelicalism. They tend to really go after women in particular. One of their favorite targets is historian Kristin Du Mez, whose book Jesus and John Wayne, and now her latest book, Live, Laugh, Love, has been very critical of white evangelicalism. So they’ve gone after her quite a bit.

Some of them are extreme types, of the Pete Hegseth model, where they don’t think women should have the right to vote. That’s been a newer strain of the theobros lately. But generally they’re the online sort of white evangelical bulwark that trolls and argues and polices the boundaries of that religious movement.

Sargent: There are these others as well who are sort of a little more in the post-liberal vein. I guess Rod Dreher is one of them. He’s a thinker in that world. He reacted very strongly to Donald Trump’s quotes to Ross Douthat there.

Rod Dreher said this: “My God, the pettiness and hatred in that man’s heart. Despite being given so much in life, he hates his enemies more than he fears God.”

I mean, I think that’s exactly right. And what’s so striking about the Douthat interview is, when Ross Douthat confronts Trump directly on that point, he says to him, why are you so fucking crazy?

He doesn’t say it in those terms. But he basically says to him, you always win, you’re rich, you had everything handed to you, why the hell are you so filled with rage and hate? That’s basically what Ross Douthat said to him. And the answer was pretty interesting. He basically said, I don’t know, I just hate people.

Fletcher: Yeah. Well, the answer is, of course, he’s a malignant narcissist, and they can’t take any sort of criticism.

Sargent: Well, let’s talk about white evangelical support for Trump in the election that we just had. The exit polls show that white evangelicals voted Republican by huge margins, but notably they declined as a share of the national vote, down to 17 percent. Can you talk about those findings and what they mean?

Fletcher: Yeah. And I went and did the sort of basic math, looking at the raw vote numbers as well, to determine whether the actual numbers went down, or if they were just overwhelmed by turnout.

And they definitely were diluted by the overall turnout, but their actual raw numbers went down by about seven million. That’s, like, really significant.

Sargent: Wow.

Fletcher: Yeah. And granted, caveat everything: this is looking at early exit data, which is always adjusted later, and the real data, you know, will be done over the coming months and will adjust a lot of that.

But comparing to previous midterm exit data in particular, they’re usually about a quarter of the electorate, which is huge. That’s why they’re so influential. They’re only about 13 to 15 percent of the population, but they come out like no other group in our electorate.

They are overrepresented at the polls, and they still were this time. Seventeen percent is an overrepresentation of their numbers in the population. But it’s a massive decline from the 25 percent.

And they vote so much in lockstep. That’s why they’re the ultimate electoral prize for the Republicans: you have the combination of overwhelming turnout, overwhelming conformist support, and the immovability.

I have to confess, as heartbroken as I’ve been watching their behavior for the last 10 years, I thought maybe this time there would be more actual switching sides. And the data so far do not show that. A little bit in Kansas.

It looks like in the Senate race, about 5 percent of them actually did cross the aisle and vote for Adam Hamilton, which is not surprising really, because he codes really evangelical. His personal faith, the way he talks about his faith, is much more evangelical than, say, James Talarico’s. His church is the largest church in Kansas and has kind of a megachurch flavor to it, even though it’s technically part of a mainline denomination.

So if anybody was going to get them to cross over, Adam Hamilton was probably the type of candidate that would. But even then, not many of them did. They mostly just couldn’t bear it, and they just stayed home.

Sargent: Well, let’s talk about James Talarico for a second. In this midterm, we saw Democratic candidates seeking to offer an alternative to white evangelical Christianity. James Talarico, obviously, right, running very emphatically on a liberal Christian vision.

You saw him really do this with immigration. Talarico insisted that we have a duty to the stranger. And he actually pulled ahead of Ken Paxton on who was trusted to handle the immigration issue, which is really a rare thing for Democrats. And that was in Texas. I really wonder whether the religious talk helped there, maybe including with religious Latinos. What do you think of all that?

Fletcher: Yeah, I think so. I think the importance for Democrats of including these more liberal Christian voices is to create kind of permission structures and comfort with religion. White Christianity has been sort of the driver of a lot of authoritarianism in our history, going back to pro-slavery Christianity and the reaction to the Civil Rights Movement.

And even the ancestors of us mainliners were in a lot of that camp as well. And white Christianity has really driven this MAGA movement. So I think it’s really important for white Christians to be out there driving a wedge in between the Republican Party’s definition of faith and these voters, and just presenting another view of what Christianity can be.

And I want to say that the Black church has long been that. The Black church has long been a very strong voice for democracy and justice throughout American history.
