In the UAE’s case, Trump disregarded his own government’s evidence that the UAE was sharing missile technology with China. In both instances, Trump set a price that had nothing to do with protecting national security. People say that Trump is an inconsistent decision-maker, and that’s true. But when it comes to corruption, Trump is very consistent. He always wants to wet his beak.

items.title: Who Let Roy Cohn Off the Hook?
items.content_text:
The photograph of Roy Cohn that graces the cover of Kai Bird’s new biography, American Scoundrel: Roy Cohn’s Dark Journey From Joe McCarthy to Donald Trump, was actually the author’s second choice. As Bird describes in the book’s acknowledgments, he was denied the right to use his preferred option, Robert Mapplethorpe’s stark portrait of Cohn’s cold-eyed visage that calls to mind a Halloween mask. In Bird’s accounting, the Mapplethorpe Foundation feared losing its nonprofit status if it licensed the photograph to appear on the cover of a book critical of the current president, Cohn’s most famous acolyte. This anecdote underscores two truths of living under our current regime. First, acts of self-censorship are likely outnumbering—and may prove as distorting as—restrictions that are officially imposed. Second, purportedly independent and robust institutions are facing unprecedented pressure to yield under the weight of competitive authoritarianism.

Those lessons are repeated numerous times throughout Bird’s energetic, readable, and meticulously researched examination of Cohn, written with his wife and “Director of Research,” Susan Goldmark. Bird is best known for American Prometheus, a Pulitzer-winning biography of J. Robert Oppenheimer that inspired Christopher Nolan’s 2023 film. But his strongest work might be The Color of Truth, an analysis of the lives of McGeorge and William Bundy, bureaucrats essential to the Cold War liberal order who helped mislead the country into an unwinnable war in Vietnam. By his own accounting, Bird is a “biographer of the American establishment,” driven to understand the men (because it’s almost always been men) and systems that facilitated American global dominance following World War II. In taking on Cohn as a subject, Bird explores the other half of the story: In his telling, Cohn is the quintessential antiestablishment figure who has indelibly shaped the political culture of postwar America.

American Scoundrel assiduously charts Cohn’s path to fame and infamy, tracing his roles as federal prosecutor (supporting cases against Alger Hiss, William Remington, and the Rosenbergs); attack dog for Senator Joseph McCarthy; mob lawyer (with clients drawn from all of the New York underworld’s “Five Families”); celebrity divorce specialist (Si Newhouse, Gene Pope, Bianca Jagger); nefarious businessman; serial tax dodger; and conservative political operative (for, among others, Richard Nixon in 1972 and Ronald Reagan in 1980 and 1984).

Many of the anecdotes that drive the narrative have previously appeared on page and screen, including in Nicholas von Hoffman’s 1988 biography, Citizen Cohn, the 2019 documentaries Where’s My Roy Cohn? and Bully. Coward. Victim., as well as in Cohn’s own posthumously published 1988 autobiography (written with the journalist Sidney Zion). In their efforts to contribute to what could be seen as a picked-over subject, Bird and Goldmark have worked through a remarkable amount of new material, declassifying Cohn’s FBI file through a FOIA request, uncovering insightful archival materials (including a number of unpublished memoirs), and conducting dozens of interviews with key players. This research is all the more impressive because Cohn left behind no central archive; many of his personal papers were reportedly burned at the time of his death and his personal effects distributed to friends or sold at auction. (Two boxes of ephemera were purchased by R.E.M. lead singer Michael Stipe, who gave Bird and Goldmark access to them.)

These discoveries allow Bird to give the most complete accounting of Cohn to date. Though his conclusions are not markedly different from those of other biographers and scholars, they are founded on a richness of evidence that makes them more profound. The resulting portrait details a life of impunity. Seen from this angle, American Scoundrel is as much an indictment of the people and systems who failed to rein in Cohn’s criminality and corruption as it is a judgment of the man himself.


Roy Cohn was born in 1927, the only child of Albert Cohn, a Democratic district attorney (and later judge) aligned with FDR’s political machine, and Dora Marcus, a wealthy socialite whose family had made their money in banking. By all accounts, Cohn’s parents hated each other and often enlisted Roy in their various battles. But they both seemed to believe that their son was destined for great things. He sped his way through New York City’s most elite educational institutions (Horace Mann, Columbia College, Columbia Law School) and used his father’s connections to be named an assistant U.S. attorney for the Southern District of New York in 1948. Bird deftly traces the key cases that made Cohn’s name as an anti-Communist crusader, including the successful prosecutions of William Remington and the Rosenbergs. These successes attracted the attention of the greatest red-hunter of them all, Joseph McCarthy, and in January 1953, Cohn began an eventful 19-month stint as the lead investigator for the Wisconsin senator’s Permanent Subcommittee on Investigations.

Cohn soon became McCarthy’s right-hand man, running investigations, leading the questioning of witnesses, serving as the senator’s liaison to other government branches, and—perhaps most importantly—directing the public relations operation that kept McCarthy and his subcommittee at the forefront of the national consciousness. It was a role that threw him into the spotlight, with journalists blurring the line between news and gossip as they tracked his every move. Much has been written on the irony of Cohn fueling the Lavender Scare, the Cold War–era persecution of homosexuals, at the same time he was having sex with men. The infamous Army-McCarthy Hearings, broadcast to a national TV audience in the spring of 1954, exposed McCarthy and Cohn as bullies and severely damaged their political reputations. Cohn resigned from McCarthy’s staff and returned to Manhattan, where he crafted a second act as a pugnacious, well-connected, and unscrupulous attorney. Those successes would ultimately lead him back to the world of politics, and he held significant sway as a conservative fixer in the 1970s and ’80s.

Throughout Bird’s narrative, we see the constant failure of institutional leaders to punish Cohn for his illegal and immoral activities. President Dwight Eisenhower allowed McCarthy and Cohn’s investigations of supposed Communists to continue apace, fearful that the then-powerful McCarthy would fracture the Republican Party. When the Army-McCarthy Hearings revealed that Cohn had fabricated evidence against enemies in the Department of Defense, the Eisenhower administration declined to pursue charges of perjury against him, again for fear of alienating the right wing of its coalition. When, in 1973, a suspicious fire on Cohn’s yacht scuttled the vessel and killed one crew member, no charges were filed, in spite of the local sheriff’s “strong suspicion that foul play was involved.” The IRS moved glacially in investigating Cohn’s lifelong tax evasion. The City of New York took no legal action against Cohn and his business partner Paul Dano for their corrupt management of parking lots and subway newsstands from the mid-1970s to the early 1980s, quietly canceling the contracts instead of pursuing charges. The Office of Court Administration could have—and should have—sought to disbar Cohn far sooner than the early 1980s (Cohn ultimately lost his law license two months before his death from AIDS-related complications in August 1986).*

The powerful politicians, businessmen, entertainers, and journalists with whom Cohn surrounded himself were wise to his misconduct but looked the other way because he had connections, was good for a favor, and demonstrated personal loyalty to them. Cohn was, by many accounts, an entertaining friend: witty, mischievous, generous, and a fantastic source of gossip. In the words of syndicated columnist Liz Smith, “I got a big kick out of watching him operate.” During Cohn’s disbarment proceedings, Barbara Walters testified in his defense, highlighting her friend’s “integrity” even though she had extensive knowledge of his transgressions. Other New Yorkers who supported Cohn during that investigation included William Safire, Congressman Mario Biaggi, comedian Joe Adams, New York Post editor Steven Dunleavy, William F. Buckley Jr., and Donald Trump. Even the use of the word “scoundrel” in this biography’s title seems winking, as if Cohn was a Victorian rogue or a kid who got his hand caught in the cookie jar, rather than a lifelong criminal.

The biography’s most troubling chapter recounts the story of Richard Kerr, an orphan from Northern Ireland who was pressed into sexual slavery by the leaders of Belfast’s Kincora Boys’ Home. In an interview with Bird and Goldmark, Kerr states that he was raped by Cohn in a Venice hotel in 1977, a few weeks shy of his sixteenth birthday. Kerr did not report the assault to authorities at the time, and this story has not been previously published. Its inclusion serves as a horrifying reminder of the long trail of trauma that followed in the wake of Cohn’s many misdeeds. “Roy was a party to this sordid business,” Bird concludes, his language oddly mild for behavior so evil.

In Bird’s accounting, the key to unlocking Cohn is deceptively, damningly simple: He was a man driven purely by self-interest and greed.

At points, the biography frustrates by failing to trawl the depths of Cohn’s character to craft a more complete psychological and intellectual portrait. He was a man of numerous, fascinating contradictions—a homophobic homosexual, an antisemitic Jew, a wealthy man who paid no taxes, a right-wing operative whose father was a key player in New York City’s Democratic machine, a lawyer who thumbed his nose at the law—and one could imagine a more robust excavation of the roots of his complexities. Many of those who knew Cohn did undertake such a quest, with Liz Smith remarking, “To the end of his life [Cohn] remained this very strange Jewish son who was still trying to please his mother and father’s portrait over his piano.”

Bird’s conclusions are less Freudian. In his—accurate, I believe—accounting, the key to unlocking Cohn is deceptively, damningly simple: He was a man driven purely by self-interest and greed. “Fundamentally,” Bird writes, “he was an empty vessel. He had no coherent personal philosophy unless you count his shallow mirroring of Ayn Rand’s unadulterated selfishness.” His entire life was transactional, every action calculated with future payout in mind. In the words of journalist and friend Murray Kempton, “I early learned that Roy had no interior to speak of.”


However multifariously malevolent Cohn was, he may have become a historical footnote were it not for his association with his most famous client. Cohn met Donald Trump in 1973 at Le Club, a members-only restaurant on Manhattan’s Upper East Side. Trump and his father, Fred, were in search of an attorney to defend them from Justice Department charges that the Trumps had discriminated against Black renters. Cohn’s solution was to countersue for $100 million, charging the federal government with defaming his clients. The countersuit was promptly dismissed, and the Trumps eventually signed a settlement, promising to adhere to a consent decree designed to combat housing discrimination. Those inconvenient facts did not preclude Cohn and the younger Trump from calling a press conference and declaring victory against government overreach. (The Trumps breached the consent decree and were again charged with violating the Fair Housing Act in 1978.)

It was the beginning of a beautiful friendship. For the last 13 years of his life, Cohn took Trump under his wing, mentoring him in the ways of his world. Their alliance was the stuff of legend, and Cohn proudly displayed a photograph of Trump in his office. It was signed, “To Roy, My greatest friend. Donald.” In the words of investigative journalist David Cay Johnston, Cohn taught Trump a bevy of lessons that the forty-fifth and forty-seventh president of the United States has put into action:

Ignore the rules, do what you want to do, don’t leave a paper trail, don’t keep a calendar, never do things in writing, and if somebody gets onto you, rat out other people to save yourself. Delay, delay, delay, [be]cause grand juries have limited time, and you can run out the clock. And call in the news media. Make up a fantastic story. We’re just honest businessmen who are being attacked by these corrupt New York City police, or FBI agents, or especially the corrupt and heartless IRS agents. And that’ll be the news story. It’ll put the government on the defensive.

It may have even been Cohn who suggested that Trump apply these tactics to the realm of politics. In a telephone interview with Bird and Goldmark, Trump recalled of Cohn, “He had a lot of respect for me. He said, ‘You’re going to be President someday. If you want to.’ He said that many times.”


Four months before his death in 1986, Cohn posed for a series of portraits by the celebrated photographer Mary Ellen Mark. Though haggard and ravaged by disease, he was incapable of refusing the opportunity for publicity; the shots were later used to illustrate posthumous articles in Vanity Fair and Life, the latter titled “the Snarling Death of Roy Cohn.” In perhaps the best-known image from the sitting, Cohn broods in a Queen Anne–style wingback chair, his legs crossed casually, staring at the camera as he clutches a small American flag, the kind waved by spectators on Inauguration Day and at Fourth of July parades.

The photo hinges on the juxtaposition of Cohn and the flag: his wan, scarred visage next to a symbol that is often used to evoke freedom, liberty, and hope. Mark’s photograph seems to suggest an essential dissonance between her subject and Americanness. This disparity is emphasized by those who have portrayed Cohn as a cancer on the American body politic, as a man who became powerful by flouting and ignoring the principles that define what it is to be American.

Cohn was an unheeded warning about the fragility of American institutions when confronted with unfettered greed and limitless egotism.

And yet, for the first half of Donald Trump’s second term, Cohn and his actions appeared less antithetical to American identity and more like elemental expressions of it. His strategy of going on the offensive has proven remarkably destructive in the hands of a president who has attempted to bend and break cherished institutions, from the Supreme Court and the legislative branch to freedom of speech, an independent press, and the sanctity of the vote. In the midterms, voters rejected the particular brand of authoritarianism Trump represents. But the damage is hard to undo. Like Cohn, Trump has shown how vulnerable the American system of government can be, and how easily it can be undermined by somebody with the motivation to do so.

Cohn was an unheeded warning about the fragility of American institutions when confronted with unfettered greed and limitless egotism. His most momentous act was to demonstrate continuously the fundamental impotence of the establishment. Cohn’s ethical and moral failings are clear. But the most troubling thing about his life—and the life of his most famous protégé—is the ease with which he was able to subvert the systems that should have held him in check.

In this light, Cohn’s failings are not merely his own. They belong to all of us. And it’s up to all of us—regardless of political persuasion—to deal with their fallout.

*An earlier version of this article incorrectly identified the body that should have sought to disbar Cohn.

items.title: Van Hollen Calls Out Schumer for Siding With AIPAC and Crypto
items.content_text:
Maryland Senator Chris Van Hollen is plotting out his position against Democratic leader Chuck Schumer.

“I am listening to all the people from around the country that were calling for big change,” Van Hollen said at the Popular Mandate national conference Tuesday, according to Semafor reporter David Weigel. “I am in the process right now of calling my colleagues.”

“We just saw democracy in America in action. We should bring a little more democracy to the United States Senate,” Van Hollen continued. “We have two newly-elected senators who would not be there if Schumer and the [Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee] had their way.”

Van Hollen then drew a line in the sand, arguing that Schumer and the DSCC had “sided with the crypto industry” and the American Israel Public Affairs Committee, better known by the acronym AIPAC.

A wave of Democratic voices have been opposing Schumer’s leadership and establishment politics since the party won the majority in Congress in last week’s elections. Maryland Senator Chris Van Hollen has emerged as a potential alternative, indicating a rising interest in progressive leadership. His office has received an “outpouring of calls and is now in active listening mode,” one source told Politico’s Playbook.

Van Hollen’s national profile rose last year when he traveled out of the country to visit his constituent Kilmar Ábrego García after García was illegally deported by the Trump administration to El Salvador’s notoriously lethal maximum security prison, CECOT.

Whether or not Van Hollen will officially commit himself against Schumer remains to be seen, though the Marylander has already started to draft an opposition platform that could put pressure on Schumer’s politics. On Tuesday, Van Hollen declared that the U.S. cannot spend “a penny more” on the Iran war, daring Donald Trump to either stop funding the war or face the possibility of a government shutdown.

So far, at least 10 major senators or senators-elect have either peeled away from Schumer outright or indicated interest in a different Senate majority leader. Another 14 have not yet committed as to whether they will support Schumer, according to an analysis published Monday by Primary Democrats. Altogether, that’s 24 Democrats—or nearly half of the at least 54 Democratic seats that will dominate the upper chamber come January.

But Schumer remains undeterred by the mounting opposition.

“I’m confident I will be elected majority leader,” Schumer said at a press conference Tuesday afternoon. “Our caucus is really united in focusing on bringing down costs, on ending the corruption, on ending the chaos, on ending the war. We have great unity in our caucus and I’ll be proud to lead as majority leader.”

items.title: Disabled Woman Sues Trump Admin After ICE Dragged Her From Her Car
items.content_text:
A Minneapolis woman who was violently pulled out of her car and arrested by Immigration and Customs Enforcement agents while she was on her way to a doctor’s appointment in January is suing the federal government.

Aliya Rahman, a Minneapolis resident, filed the lawsuit in U.S. District Court in Minnesota Tuesday claiming that she was the victim of false arrest and imprisonment, negligent supervision, negligence, assault, and battery.

“I am one of many who have been impacted by this government’s vile abuse of power,” Rahman said in a statement. “And while this lawsuit stems from what happened in January, the terror did not start there and has not stopped.”

Rahman, who is autistic and has physical disabilities, was traveling to a medical appointment on January 13 during Operation Metro Surge, the federal government’s immigration crackdown in Minnesota’s twin cities. ICE agents surrounded her car and smashed her window after she said, “They needed to learn how to respect human beings,” her complaint states. They then dragged her out of the car and sent her to a federal detention facility for hours. She said that she was denied medical care while in ICE custody, and had to go to the hospital after losing consciousness.

Her violent arrest was captured on video and went viral online, and she later testified before Congress. She went on to attend President Trump’s State of the Union address in February as a guest of Representative Ilhan Omar, and was arrested by Capitol police for “disruption of Congress.”*

Rahman’s lawsuit comes after multiple attempts to hold ICE agents accountable. She filed a Federal Tort Claims Act claim alleging unlawful force and detention in April, and in June filed a federal complaint with the Department of Homeland Security’s Office of Civil Rights and Civil Liberties. The tort claim was a prerequisite for Tuesday’s lawsuit.

Rahman’s attorney, Jessica Gingold of the MacArthur Justice Center, said at a news conference Tuesday that part of the lawsuit’s goal was identifying the agents responsible for the violent attack.

“We will find the names,” Gingold said. “We have their pictures…. We have a right to depose them. We have a right to get their records to understand who these individuals were who heard Aliya, frustrated and confused, and reacted with such violence.”

* This story has been updated to reflect Rahman’s arrest at the State of the Union.

items.title: Trump Admin Is Secretly Destroying Documents, Whistleblowers Warn
items.content_text:
Trump officials are destroying documents related to his pet projects in Washington, D.C., according to whistleblowers.

CNN reports that whistleblowers have warned House Democrats that key documents have already been destroyed before Democrats take over Congress in January. Democratic Representative Jared Huffman, the ranking member of the House Natural Resources Committee, plans to issue letters to the Department of the Interior, as well other federal agencies and private companies involved in the president’s projects, demanding that they “preserve all records and data responsive to oversight.”

Huffman is also sending letters to the National Park Service, the Bureau of Land Management, and the Department of Agriculture, as well as companies such as Lockheed Martin and John Deere, which have donated to Trump’s projects in the past.

The recipients of Huffman’s letters must reply to certify their compliance. This means that they should make efforts to “preserve existing records collections and productions,” as well as “identify and recover any deleted information” and “suspend any destruction and deletion practices.”

“Everything is coming; it’s all coming,” Huffman told CNN. “It’s just going to be an entirely new day.”

Huffman told CNN that his committee could stop some of Trump’s projects, “especially because we have standing to go to court if we have to,” he said. “We’ll have tools to be able to stop a lot of it.”

The Interior Department said that the whistleblowers were “100 percent false,” saying that “the department follows all federal records management obligations as directed by the department’s ethics officials.”

Documents on Trump’s ballroom, his renovation of the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool, his takeover of the East Potomac Golf Links course, and his triumphal arch could all be at risk.

items.title: Bernie Sanders Warns Chuck Schumer His Days as Senate Leader Are Up
items.content_text:
Vermont Senator Bernie Sanders has added his name to the growing list of liberal-minded lawmakers asking Chuck Schumer to hand over the reins of the Senate.

“I like Chuck. Nobody works harder than Chuck Schumer,” Sanders said at a joint press conference with Senator Elissa Slotkin Tuesday. “But in my view, the time is now for change, and I will not be supporting Chuck to be reelected as the Democratic leader.”

The Democratic Socialist encouraged “vigorous debate” as the party searched for an alternative, and highlighted that such a process should take place “out in the open.”

“We need … to show the American people that a new day has come, and that their votes meant a new direction in Washington,” Sanders said.

Sanders told reporters earlier in the day that he would not support Schumer’s bid for Senate majority leader in the new year. When asked by The Washington Times’s Lindsey McPherson if he would support Schumer even if the current leader runs unopposed, Sanders responded: “He’s not going to run unopposed, I don’t think.”

A wave of Democratic voices opposing Schumer’s possible return atop the Senate emerged after the party won an overwhelming majority in Congress last week, rebuking the septuagenarian’s establishment politics. In the days since, Maryland Senator Chris Van Hollen has emerged as a potential alternative, indicating a rising interest in progressive leadership.

Van Hollen rose as a leading progressive last year, when he travelled out of the country to visit his constituent Kilmar Ábrego García after García was illegally deported by the Trump administration to El Salvador’s notoriously lethal maximum security prison, CECOT.

Whether or not Van Hollen will officially commit himself against Schumer remains to be seen, though the Marylander has already started to draft an opposition platform that could put pressure on Schumer’s politics. On Tuesday, Van Hollen declared that the U.S. cannot spend “a penny more” on the Iran War, daring Donald Trump to either stop funding the war or face the possibility of a government shutdown.

So far, at least 10 major politicos have either peeled away from Schumer outright or indicated an interest in a different Senate majority leader. They include:

  • Vermont Senator Bernie Sanders
  • Michigan Senator Elissa Slotkin
  • Michigan Senator-elect Abdul El-Sayed
  • Connecticut Senator Richard Blumenthal
  • Illinois Senator-elect Juliana Stratton
  • Minnesota Senator-elect Peggy Flanagan
  • Kansas Senator-elect Adam Hamilton
  • Maine Senator-elect Troy Jackson
  • New Hampshire Senator-elect Chris Pappas
  • Texas Senator-elect James Talarico

Another 14 senators or senators-elect have not yet committed as to whether or not they will support Schumer, according to an analysis published Monday by Primary Democrats. Altogether, that’s 24 Democrats—or nearly half of the at least 54 Democratic seats that will dominate the upper chamber come January.

New York Representative Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez has also refused to support her home state senator, though the decision is ultimately up to the Senate.

This story has been updated.

items.title: House Republicans Pick Election Denier Jim Jordan to Lead Them
items.content_text:
House Republicans elected Representative Jim Jordan of Ohio as their new minority leader on Tuesday.

Jordan, who has served as a representative for Ohio’s 4th district since 2007, won the secret ballot vote 106–73, two people present for the tally told Politico. He was up against Representative Steve Scalise of Louisiana, who currently serves as the number two Republican in the House.

Jordan was selected following sweeping Democratic victories in the midterm elections that flipped the House and Senate, prompting House Speaker Mike Johnson to announce he would step down from Republican leadership.

There are plenty of reasons that Jordan has previously been kept out of such a powerful position. That is, until now.

Years before Jordan was elected to the House, he served as an assistant coach to Ohio State University’s wrestling team between 1986 and 1994. The Ohio Republican has faced severe blowback for allegedly participating in a coverup of the rampant sex abuse by team doctor Richard Strauss, who committed 1,429 sexual assaults and 47 rapes against at least 177 male student-athletes during his tenure, according to a 2019 university report.

Jordan also has earned a reputation as a vocal election denier who assisted President Donald Trump in his proven efforts to overturn the results of the presidential election in 2020. Along with several of his Republican colleagues, Jordan refused to comply with a subpoena from the House Select Committee that investigated the January 6 attack on the U.S. Capitol. The committee unearthed evidence that Jordan had materially relevant communications with Trump and others related to January 6. In July this year, Jordan referred former special counsel Jack Smith to the Department of Justice for possible prosecution, alleging that he’d made false statements to Congress.

As House Judiciary Committee chairman, Jordan enjoyed playing Trump’s personal attorney. Now he’ll get to lead the much-diminished party as it fends off investigations from Democratic lawmakers.

This story has been updated.

items.title: Trump Media Filings Show How Much He Makes From Truth Social Scheme
items.content_text:
President Donald Trump is raking in cash from his pay-to-play scheme giving companies early access to his social media posts.

In a recent Securities and Exchange Comission filing, Trump Media & Technology Group reported that revenue for Truth Social’s parent company had surged 205 percent in the third quarter to a whopping $3 million.

At least $1.8 million, or 60 percent, of that spike was “primarily driven” by subscriptions to Truth API, which offers Truth Social users early access to posts from government officials for as much as $100,000 a month, the company said.

This would be the kind of thing that would raise a red flag for the SEC—if it were still functioning as an independent agency.

At the moment, the SEC has two commissioners, both Republican: Trump sycophant Paul Atkins, who serves as the SEC chairman, and the reliably pro-business Mark Uyeda, whom Trump appointed as acting chairman before Atkins took office. Republican administrations are historically less interested in enforcing the nation’s securities laws, but Trump 2.0 takes that laissez-faire approach to legality to stratospheric new levels.

Media and watchdog groups have alleged that Trump is exploiting his office to benefit a private company that he owns. In August, The Intercept and the nonprofit Freedom of the Press Foundation sued Trump, alleging that Truth API violates the First and Fifth Amendments.

In September, Trump and his aide Natalie Harp, who helped to develop the service, were named in a lawsuit from the groups American Oversight and Campaign for Accountability. A separate lawsuit out of San Francisco alleges that Truth API is a “corrupt business scheme” that violates federal laws against insider trading as well as California’s Unfair Competition Law.

Trump Media’s latest filing caused the value of the company’s stock to jump Tuesday, adding a whopping $34 million to the president’s net worth.

items.title: House Oversight Says DOJ Never Interviewed Key Epstein Witnesses
items.content_text:
The Republican-led House Oversight Committee released a report Tuesday detailing how the Department of Justice mishandled investigations into sex offenders Jeffrey Epstein and Ghislaine Maxwell, failing to interview witnesses.

“The crimes committed by Epstein after 2005 could have been prevented and justice served had it not been for the repeated failures of law enforcement and federal prosecutors,” the 136-page report states.

The report detailed how the DOJ failed to interview key witnesses while investigating Epstein and Maxwell’s abuse, pointing out that “too many survivors and other witnesses informed this committee that they were never approached or properly questioned by federal authorities.” The report called on the DOJ to reinterview witnesses, especially Epstein’s assistant Lesley Groff, who survivors say lied to Congress about her role in Epstein’s abuse.

The committee pointed out other failures as well, including how the U.S. Attorney’s Office for the Southern District of Florida entered into a nonprosecution agreement with Epstein in 2007 that allowed him to serve a lesser sentence. Notably, the report also criticizes Trump’s DOJ for failures after the Epstein Files Transparency Act was passed in 2025, saying that the department “failed to adequately communicate about document releases and failed to sufficiently protect survivors. Deficient redactions exposed survivors’ sensitive personal information.”

The report still took aim at Democrats, claiming that they put politics first by “trying to implicate President Trump and insinuate that he was involved in the crimes of Epstein and Maxwell,” and calling their efforts an “unfounded witch hunt … without regard for the interests of survivors, even though the facts gathered during this investigation do not suggest President Trump is implicated in any of Epstein’s crimes.”

While this report is a step forward, the fact that it’s coming out after last week’s midterms, where Republicans lost in a landslide, shows that House Republicans are scrambling to save face. Republicans on the committee are using the report to make partisan attacks against Democrats and absolve President Trump, even though Democrats on the committee released their own report before the election that included a new rape allegation against the president. That woman, Beatrice Keul, is nowhere in Republicans’ report and wasn’t called before the committee.

items.title: Haley Stevens Spent First Day Back at Work Hiding on Republican Side
items.content_text:
Representative Haley Stevens apparently can’t face her caucus anymore.

The Michigan Democrat was caught hiding in the Republican cloakroom during Congress’s first day back in session, seemingly unable to confront her liberal colleagues after her recent public meltdown, The Washington Sun reported Monday night.

Stevens imploded her reputation and doomed her political prospects just days before the election, when she demanded that Dr. Abdul El-Sayed—the man who bested her in Michigan’s Democratic Senate primary—condemn an ad aired by one of his allies, and further apologize for his prior criticism of Israel.

Representative Debbie Dingell then waded into the mix, disinviting Stevens from a church event with El-Sayed and Representative James E. Clyburn, one of Stevens’s lower chamber mentors.

That’s when Stevens went berserk. Rather than attempt to make peace or let bygones be bygones, she did a complete 180 and endorsed Republican Senate candidate Mike Rogers, aligning herself with the MAGA nominee in an apparent effort to undermine El-Sayed’s odds. Notably, she did so without telling anyone, as her staff were reportedly at the El-Sayed event waiting for her arrival.

But her public tantrum did little to turn Michigan voters away from El-Sayed’s campaign, and by the middle of Election Night, it was clear that he had won the state’s Senate seat.

Stevens, meanwhile, now has to face the consequences of her actions. More than half of Stevens’s staff have already resigned, while Democratic leaders have condemned her duplicity. Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer called it a “despicable betrayal,” while House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries slammed it as a “terrible decision” that could result in Stevens’s expulsion from the Democratic House caucus.

But not every Democrat is in agreement that Stevens’s time in the Democratic Party is over.

“We have three more weeks or two more weeks of being in Congress, so I don’t think we should start making judgments about anybody in the caucus at this point,” said outgoing California Representative Nancy Pelosi. “I was disappointed, I conveyed that to her. I want to be helpful to her in terms of how she deals with this, but I’m not supporting kicking her out.”

Yet despite her sudden affinity for the opposing party, Stevens is still keen to cling to her political identity.

“I am a Democrat who has voted with my caucus 96 percent of the time this term and I don’t expect that to change,” Stevens told the Detroit Free Press Tuesday. (Well, it will change in that after January 2, 2027, she won’t have a vote with the caucus anymore.)

items.title: Todd Blanche Threatens to Arrest Democrats Over “Rhetoric”
items.content_text:
Attorney General Todd Blanche doubled down on Tuesday on his threat to go after Democrats in Congress.

Speaking on Fox & Friends, Blanche claimed his role in government was “to defend the administration.” From what, exactly? The supposedly “vile rhetoric” of incoming Democratic lawmakers arriving on Capitol Hill.

“You can disagree with this administration, you can want to legislate your way with new policies, but you cannot threaten, and that’s what we’re seeing, and that’s what we’re very concerned about at the Department of Justice,” he said.

“We cannot let the rhetoric turn from just honest debate to actual criminal conduct,” he added.

The attorney general didn’t deign to provide a single example of a criminal act by the Democratic Party. The so-called threats he was referring to, the rest of us simply know as oversight—something which was rendered impossible by the Republican majorities in the House and Senate. Now Democrats have warned the Trump administration to “lawyer up,” and clearly, its lawyer has responded by threatening free speech. What a show of confidence.

The attorney general’s role has historically been to represent the United States and provide legal advice to the president and his Cabinet officials. The Justice Department is meant to be an independent organization, free from presidential interference. Clearly, Blanche has stretched the role of U.S. attorney general to be weaponized against the president’s perceived political enemies.

During yet another public meltdown on CNN on Sunday, Blanche admitted that he’d target Democrats at Trump’s behest and openly accused Democrats of threatening “anybody that’s conservative and anybody that happens to be a Republican.”

items.title: Trump’s 60 Minutes Interview Was So Much Crazier Than We Realized
items.content_text:
Bari Weiss’s 60 Minutes edited its latest interview with Donald Trump to make the octogenarian’s responses appear much more sane than they actually were.

During one exchange between Trump and host Ross Douthat on the topic of Ukraine, the staff at 60 Minutes decided to trim several sections of Trump’s response that included false claims or total fabrications.

“There’s still a war going on. What’s the biggest obstacle to peace?” asked Douthat.

“It was the hatred between [Ukrainian President Volodymyr] Zelenskiy and [Russian President Vladimir] Putin,” Trump said in the version of the program that aired Sunday.

But much more was left on the cutting room floor, according to an unedited version published by Decoding Fox News founder Juliet Jeske.

“I believe that we’re very close to making a deal,” Trump said. “And I think it—two things, if I were president, because as you know, well you’re not going to admit it, it was rigged. That’s why I did it a third time. If I was president that war would have never started.”

During another portion of the interview, 60 Minutes cut Trump’s answer when he attempted to puff himself up as tough on Russia and soft on Ukraine: “Look what I did to them as an example. I gave them the anti-tank busters, right?

“I’ve given them, in fact there’s an old statement, that [Barack] Obama gave them sheets, and I gave them anti-tank busters, OK? That’s what I gave them,” Trump said.

“But now it’s Europe supplying weapons, not us?” asked Douthat.

“No, it’s us. We’re supplying the weapons, Europe is paying for them,” Trump answered. “Here’s the difference: [Joe] Biden gave them $350 billion worth of cash and weapons. I gave them nothing.”

It’s not unusual for news programs to edit interviews before they go live on air. But there is a deep irony that Trump seems perfectly content to have his answers edited for time and clarity, little more than two years after he went on a rampage against CBS News for doing the same to Kamala Harris while she was on the 2024 campaign trail.

At the time, Trump insisted that the network had selectively edited Harris’s answers to a question regarding Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu. Trump sued the network for $10 billion after the interview, claiming that the different clips were tantamount to “election interference” and merited CBS losing its broadcast license. CBS’s parent company, Paramount Global, settled the lawsuit for $16 million the following year.

But Trump’s campaign against 60 Minutes initiated its reputational descent. In the months that followed the settlement, Paramount Global merged with Skydance, allowing CBS News to be taken over by David Ellison, the son of Trump’s good friend Larry Ellison.

The younger Ellison thereafter appointed Free Press founder Weiss to run the CBS newsroom, despite the fact that she had zero qualifications to do so. Weiss has since dismantled large portions of CBS, including 60 Minutes, forcing out dozens of highly esteemed anchors, correspondents, and producers in the process, and replacing them with the likes of Douthat, a former conservative columnist for The New York Times.

Weiss’s indisputably negative impact on CBS News was made apparent last week during election night, when the network’s ratings finished dead last among all major broadcasters and cable networks, according to Nielsen data obtained by media reporter Brain Stelter.

A CBS News insider told The New Republic that the network “could not have been more transparent about this interview,” noting that 60 Minutes released the full, extended interview on YouTube.

This story has been updated.

items.title: Pete Hegseth Has Lost Over $1 Billion in Fighter Jet Parts
items.content_text:
Did Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth think it was too woke to keep track of $1.3 billion worth of fighter jet parts?

A report published on Monday by the Government Accountability Office, or GAO, found that the Defense Department has not kept adequate records of parts for the F-35 Lightning II, which are worth an estimated $31 billion in total.

As of March, 17,000 parts that were in maintenance or repair were missing from the F-35 Joint Program Office’s enterprise logistics management system. The total value of the parts was estimated to be $1.3 billion, but officials stated that the value could be as high as $2.5 billion when accounting for other burden costs.

The GAO also uncovered evidence that suggested serious data quality issues. Only 29 percent of the records in a December 2025 contract data requirements list contained serial numbers, and six percent of records showed an acquisition cost of $0.01 or less.

This report comes as the House of Representatives is poised to vote on a procedural motion on Hegseth’s impeachment on Tuesday evening. Outgoing Republican Representative Thomas Massie’s 34-page impeachment resolution accuses Hegseth of committing a slew of impeachable offenses such as illegally waging war against Iran, suppressing free speech, ignoring laws intended to minimize civilian casualties, and overseeing extrajudicial killings and the kidnapping of a foreign leader. Hegseth claimed on Tuesday that not only were his contested actions lawful, but they also resulted in military victories.

items.title: Trump’s Crypto Stocks Crater After Election Defeat
items.content_text:
President Donald Trump’s cryptocurrency products have plummeted in value following Republicans’ massive defeat in the midterm elections last week.

The Washington Sun reports that $WLFI, the “governance token” from Trump’s crypto firm World Liberty Financial, has dropped to $1.11 after a high of $40 last year. The meme coin marked by first lady Melania Trump, MELANIA, lost half its value after the midterms and has fallen 99.6 percent since last year.

Democrats’ plan to investigate Trump’s crypto products appears to be the main reason for their drop in value. Zach Everson, the research director at nonprofit Public Citizen, told the Sun, “This is all now worthless.”

“It’s the lame-duck period of Trump’s crypto investments: His political influence is waning and so is interest in his crypto offerings,” Everson said. “Not that there should have been any doubt, but these price drops clearly show how much the market for Trump’s crypto products relies on his political power.”

Everson calculated that Trump’s crypto investors have lost $4.7 billion. Trump, meanwhile, has increased his net worth by $3 billion in his second term as president, although he lost more than $200 million thanks to his stocks tanking after the midterms.

Trump tried to defend his increased wealth on 60 Minutes on Sunday, claiming that he devotes “almost no time to my net worth” and dismissing concerns about the foreign entities that invest in World Liberty Financial, such as the United Arab Emirates. In less than two weeks, he’s hosting a dinner for the top 185 holders of his meme coin, GetTrumpMemes.com, and the top 29 buyers get an invite to a “VIP Reception with YOUR FAVORITE PRESIDENT.” The top four get an 18-karat gold “Trump Victory” watch. It seems that Trump’s cash grab will continue as long as he is allowed.

items.title: DOGE Goon Brings Back One of Its Worst Policies for Federal Workers
items.content_text:
Elon Musk and Vivek Ramaswamy may be gone from the MAGA agenda, but their underlings from the Department of Government Efficiency are still wreaking havoc across the government.

Sam Corcos, a former DOGE staffer who was reassigned to the Technology Transformation Services office in the General Services Administration, or GSA, has resurrected one of Musk’s most unpopular mandates. On Friday, Corcos ordered more than 200 of his coworkers to provide daily reports about their job and responsibilities to him via email, The Washington Sun reported on Tuesday.

“The purpose of these updates is to help us better understand what everyone is working on, give TTS Front Office a clearer picture of progress across the organization, and identify any blockers,” Corcos wrote.

In order to comply with Corcos’s directive, some GSA employees must send in a summary of the work they completed that day, a plan for their work the next day, and any problems they need assistance to solve.

“Failure to comply may result in adverse action,” Corcos noted in his email.

But affected federal employees do not seem open to Corcos’s new rules, likening the initiative to Musk’s notoriously unsuccessful “five things” email requirement. One GSA employee told the Sun that the message is indicative of Corcos’s “basic distrust in and underestimation of federal workers.”

Another GSA staffer explained to the Sun that it didn’t feel like Corcos was genuinely interested in helping the agency surface problems but that it instead “feels like they’re trying to mess with our heads again.”

Weeks into President Donald Trump’s second term, Musk threatened thousands of federal employees with immediate termination if they failed to obey a similar self-report mandate, which required government workers to identify five things that they achieved in the previous week. The initiative was intended to radically size down the government, but it instead posed a major security threat and was shut down within days by the Office of Personnel Management.

items.title: Who Will Dems Investigate First?
items.content_text:
You’re reading The TNR Blue Book. Get daily scoops, strategy, and developments inside the liberal ideas factory delivered right to your inbox. Sign up for free.


Inside Washington

“LAWYER UP.” That was the election night message from Representative Robert Garcia, ranking member of the House Oversight Committee. In January, one of Democrats’ top priorities will be oversight of the Trump administration, corporate America, and Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE). With so many potential targets for subpoenas and hearings, the only question left is: Where will Democrats start?

“The malfeasance list is so large that ranking is a little bit like choosing amongst your children,” said Lisa Gilbert, co-president of Public Citizen, when I asked how she’d like Democrats to prioritize their oversight efforts. She has some ideas, though: “Pick corporate villains but not just corporate villains in a vacuum,” she said. “Those that really help connect Trump corruption to tangible harms regular people are experiencing.” To start, she suggested tech billionaires Elon Musk, Jeff Bezos, and Mark Zuckerberg.

Some incoming House Democrats, in town for their new member orientation, shared their priorities on Monday, which often mirrored their districts or experiences. They also pointed to opportunities to tie accountability to other concerns, like immigration and affordability, that drove voters to the polls last Tuesday.

“I was the mayor of a community that was under federal occupation,” said Representative-elect Daniel Biss, who was previously the mayor of Evanston, a suburb just north of Chicago. “I watched my constituents [get] abducted off the streets because of the color of their skin, where their entire community was terrorized and traumatized, and I just feel deeply compelled to hold ICE and the entire DHS process accountable.”

Randy Villegas, who was elected to represent a majority-Latino district in California’s Central Valley, also has his sights set on ICE. “I very much want to visit the detention center within my district, both Mesa Verde in Bakersfield, California, as well as the extension in McFarland,” he said. “Ultimately, I don’t believe any private corporation should be benefiting off the separation of our families. So I’ll definitely make immigration one of my top priorities.” Both of the facilities he mentioned are operated by the GEO Group, a private prison company contracted with ICE.

Adam Hamawy, a physician who was elected to represent New Jersey’s 12th congressional district, pointed to corporate corruption as his main priority. “Health care insurance has always been an issue, but really, it’s all the big mega corporations,” he said.

Many outside experts and advocates also have their eyes on investigating corporate misdeeds and pay-to-play schemes. “We’ve been following the Trump crypto conflicts of interest since he took office,” said Virginia Canter, chief counsel for ethics and anti-corruption at Democracy Defenders Fund. She also pointed to Musk’s contracts with the federal government and the ties between the Starlink system and the war in Ukraine. Musk reportedly ordered the slowdown of a Starlink system that Ukraine relied upon, blindsiding the Ukrainian government. “Should a private individual have the power to use technology in a fashion that could undermine U.S. national security interests?” Canter asked.

Legal scholar Melissa Murray, a professor at NYU Law, wants Congress to closely scrutinize potential ethics breaches in the court system, including the Supreme Court, and to consider specific reforms. “Real attention to recusal rules. Maybe questions about the court’s docket, its use of the shadow docket,” she suggested. After all, anything Democrats do in Congress “with regard to policymaking is going to be challenged, and it’ll ultimately end up in a federal court, probably the Supreme Court,” she said.

Democrats will have no shortage of people and corporations to investigate beginning in January. But it has to be a two-pronged effort, Gilbert said. Democrats will need “to tell the story, both with oversight, substantive investigations, and hearings that hold up and show accountability for these bad actors,” while also coupling those hearings with “substantive policy that lays out an agenda for fixing the systemic corruption we’re seeing,” she said. “It’s really going to be that one-two punch.”

—Emma Janssen


Outside Washington

As Stephen Miller, Trump’s immigration strategy architect, starts his new job as White House chief of staff, The New York Times published a brutal account of how the Trump administration’s policy of deporting court-protected asylum-seekers to third countries has resulted in “many of them being pushed back to the very countries where the Trump administration itself cannot legally send them,” where they face “torture, sexual abuse or persecution.” The Times’ Megha Rajagopalan, Edward Wong, Ruth Maclean, and Hamed Aleaziz have identified 110 individuals sent back to their origin countries in this way. Human rights groups say that’s “almost certainly an undercount.”

The 31st United Nations climate summit (COP31) is underway in Turkey this week. Like last year, there will be no official U.S. representatives there, but a number of non-federal politicians are attending. Among those politicians are 19 members of Congress, all of them Democrats, with Representative Sean Casten of Illinois so far leading the charge in terms of talking to the press. As the summit opened, the U.N.’s World Meteorological Organization issued a dire global climate update. University College London professor emeritus Bill McGuire tells The Guardian that “the latest research suggests we will cross the 1.5C limit permanently in 2028, and with the planet now heating at an extraordinary rate of 0.4C a decade, we can expect to smash through 2C in the late 2030s.” The takeaway? Democrats who kept quiet about climate change on the campaign trail may want to add it back to the to-do list—particularly given climate change’s well-documented contributions to the affordability crisis.

—Heather Souvaine Horn


The Ideas Factory

The Open Markets Institute published a troubling new report on how top tech companies (you know the ones) “could leverage their control over cloud computing, foundation models, operating systems, browsers, online search, and digital platforms to dominate AI agents, exclude competitors, and extend their power even further across the economy and society.” One of the report’s top recommendations: U.S. and European policymakers should “require interoperability and data portability,” authors Max von Thun, Courtney C. Radsch, George Colville, and Dora Wierzbicka write, to reduce top companies’ ability to suppress competition.

In case you missed it: At the Center for American Progress, Damian Murphy recently penned a guide for how Democrats can end the war on Iran. His top step is to “cut off funding for the war effort in an appropriations package.” A war powers resolution would be good, too, he writes, but “the single most powerful tool Congress has at its disposal to bring about an end to the war is the power of the purse.”

The Natural Resources Defense Council is among numerous groups continuing to oppose the permitting reform bill titled the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act of 2026—even with its recent modifications. “We support the elements of the legislation that help accelerate needed transmission, clean energy deployment, and grid modernization; but the current package goes too far in weakening essential environmental safeguards and public participation requirements,” said Manish Bapna, NRDC president, in a statement published on the organization’s website on Sunday. In his newsletter called The Crucial Years, environmentalist Bill McKibben has a user-friendly rundown of the reasons why environmental and some accountability advocates are opposing this bill.

—Heather Souvaine Horn


In Closing

Political Trivia Question of the Day  

Who was the first defense secretary, nominated by Harry Truman in 1947 after the modern Defense Department was created? (Sign up for The TNR Blue Book to find the answer in tomorrow’s newsletter.)

—Michael Tomasky

items.title: Trump Freaks Out on Live TV in Bizarre Post-Election Wipeout Rant
items.content_text:
On Monday night, President Donald Trump had the bright idea to call C-SPAN and rant on the air.

The call began with an unidentified woman laughing in the background. Then viewers got to hear Trump rant about immigrant drug dealers and rapists, even after the interviewer pointed out that Trump had expressed sympathy for working immigrants who paid taxes in a 60 Minutes interview that aired the day before.

Trump incorrectly claimed that the U.S. government hadn’t put the same pressure on those kinds of immigrants, and then he abruptly pivoted to the U.S.’s takeover of Venezuela, talking about how great he believes it’s going. He mentioned how the U.S. has taken “hundreds of billions of dollars and millions and millions of barrels of oil” from the country.

The president continued to rant about having “won” Venezuela and then how he won Iran, going on about how the Middle Eastern country wants to make a deal with him but “won’t say that.” When asked how much longer the war would go, he didn’t answer the question, claiming that he’d taken out the country’s nuclear program and that the country was in shambles.

Why Trump picked C-SPAN is anyone’s guess, considering that his usual network of choice for phone calls is Fox News. But on Monday night, viewers of the public access cable channel got to hear Trump’s delusions continue even after a Democratic midterm landslide. We seem to be in for another two years of clear cognitive decline.

items.title: Pete Hegseth Plays Major Victim Card in Weird Speech on Impeachment
items.content_text:
Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth claimed Tuesday that he was being threatened with impeachment for being too good at his job.

Speaking at a press conference at the Pentagon, Hegseth began by denying any wrongdoing and claiming that the United States had actually won victories in both Iran and Venezuela.

“For the first time in American history, a Cabinet secretary overseeing America’s military is being attacked, not for losing conflicts with our enemies, but for winning them. Condemned not for defeat but for military victory,” he said.

Of course, that’s not why he’s being impeached at all: Outgoing Republican Representative Thomas Massie’s 34-page impeachment resolution accuses Hegseth of committing a slew of impeachable offenses by illegally waging war against Iran, suppressing free speech, ignoring laws intended to minimize civilian casualties, and overseeing extrajudicial killings and the kidnapping of a foreign leader. Hegseth insisted that these were not only lawful operations, but victories.

Hegseth claimed that efforts to remove him were being championed by “one disgruntled and defeated congressman,” and that people in the media would never admit to the military’s successes because they “hate the president more than [they] love our country or our troops.”

Hegseth also argued that the impeachment efforts were targeting something bigger than just one delusional Defense secretary. “Make no mistake about what is happening. This is not about me,” he said.

“Put the secretary on trial today, and the men and women who carried out those orders tomorrow,” he added. “If they want to come for the warriors, they’re going to have to come through me.”

Hegseth’s feeble DARVO manipulation strategy crumbles under the slightest pressure. As valorous of a gesture as that may appear, the only person to blame for the crimes committed by U.S. service members is the guy who ordered them—and his boss.

Speaking of President Donald Trump, Hegseth compared his situation to the president’s previous two impeachments.

“Now they’re trying a third time,” Hegseth said. “This time against a member of his Cabinet. They will fail again. And if standing with President Trump puts me in that company, I’ll take that company every day of the week.”

If impeachment is a badge of honor to Hegseth, it’s no wonder he has such backwards ideas about victories and defeats.

items.title: Transcript: MAGA Rages as Trump Lets Slip Damning Truth about GOP Loss
items.content_text:
The following is a lightly edited transcript of the November 10 episode of The Daily Blast podcast. Listen to it here.


Greg Sargent: This is The Daily Blast from The New Republic, produced and presented by the DSR Network. I’m your host, Greg Sargent.

Donald Trump just admitted to CBS News that his mass deportations helped cause the GOP’s electoral bloodbath last week. In one way, this is absurd, since he also just elevated Stephen Miller, the architect of that agenda, to chief of staff. But in another way, Trump admitted to something that really does undercut the MAGA movement, and even undermines JD Vance heading into 2028. And the MAGA rage has begun.

We’re sorting through what this means with political scientist Julia Azari, who’s been writing well on this election’s deeper currents for the Good Politics/Bad Politics Substack. Julia, thanks for coming on.

Julia Azari: Yeah, thank you for having me.

Sargent: So let’s start with Trump’s admission. Here he was asked by Ross Douthat of CBS whether immigration hurt the GOP in the midterms. Listen to this.

Donald Trump (voiceover): I think it both helped and hurt. I think I got an A-plus for closing up the border. I get very high marks for getting the bad ones out. But I get hurt because we also took people that had good jobs, that created one violation, or breaking of the law, and that was that they came into the country illegally. Now, there is a large part of the country that think that they should be put out, and there’s a large part of the country that think that they should be allowed to stay. If they’re good people working in a landscaping company or working in a hotel or doing something, right? And in some cases paying taxes. And a large group of people think that they should be allowed to stay.


Sargent: Julia, let’s break this up into pieces. The first key point, I think, is that Trump admitted there that Americans view a lot of undocumented immigrant workers as good people, as if they’re legitimately here in the U.S. despite having come here illegally. That’s anathema to MAGA, isn’t it?

Azari: Yeah, I mean, I think the thing that’s really interesting is that when you look at American political opinion about immigration, it’s actually really sensitive to how the question is phrased and what the framing is. And, you know, Americans consider a lot of different things and have a lot of different kinds of mixed feelings about immigrants and immigration.

But MAGA has been very clear that they’ve used this kind of law framing, but really that they’re also after legal immigration. They’re also out to decrease the number of foreign-born people living and working in this country. That’s been a very, very clear priority. And here Trump really kind of undercuts all of that.

Sargent: The 2024 election was heavily about that. When they went after the Haitians in Springfield, Ohio, for supposedly eating dogs and cats, those people were here legally. They had actually helped revive a Rust Belt city, Springfield. And they were very much targeted by JD Vance, who simply dismissed the idea that they had come legally.

He just declared them illegal, sort of by fiat. And so, yes, MAGA is not about law enforcement. It’s much more about, let’s make the country whiter, let’s reduce the number of immigrants here.

Azari: I mean, I think that it’s also worth noting that once Vance and Trump and Miller have been in power in the White House, their decision that some people are illegal just by fiat is no longer just rhetorical.

There are ways in which the executive branch can make those decisions, and they did do that to the Haitian population living in Ohio on temporary protected status.

Sargent: They absolutely did. The other thing Trump admitted to there is that removing undocumented workers has turned out to be terrible politics for the Republican Party. And this, critically, I think, goes beyond admitting that ICE’s violent enforcement tactics—the paramilitary raids of U.S. cities, the mass kidnappings, and so forth—were politically alienating to people.

It goes further and admits that the underlying ideological goal of removing immigrants itself was unpopular. That’s something that even a lot of pundits wouldn’t admit to for a long time. What did you make of that piece of it?

Azari: Again, this is sort of multifaceted, right? Some of it is about ICE. Some of it is about the kind of broader American experience of watching these kind of masked agents attacking people, removing people, hurting people, in a couple of cases killing people.

And in other cases, it’s really thinking about the role that undocumented immigrants play in our society, and how deeply integrated they are into the economy, particularly the service economy.

And I thought it was very notable to me that Trump brought up these service examples and talked about people working in hotels. It’s a very Trump example of the work that undocumented immigrants do. And it turns out that having people filling those roles is very popular with a lot of people.

Sargent: Yes, he chose landscaping and hotel work and so forth, but he was actually speaking to the experiences of many Americans, who maybe don’t spend as much time in hotels as Donald Trump does, but constantly and very regularly encounter undocumented immigrants in their daily lives. They encounter undocumented immigrants who are integrated into the economy all around us, right?

And I think Donald Trump was quite conscious, if you look at how he said that stuff, that he was delivering a twist of the knife to MAGA in some ways. He was essentially saying a lot of Americans view these undocumented immigrants as good workers, as doing important things, as complementing American workers. And that is a striking thing.

Again, he’s not going to do anything about it. We know that. But still, it’s interesting that he went there, I thought. What did you think?

Azari: Traditionally in Republican politics, I think they’ve really relied on this distinction between legal and illegal immigration. And I think one thing that has been sort of revealed over the last couple of years is that that distinction is not always super clear. Like I said, legal status is something that the executive branch can influence.

But also, what we’ve seen with ICE, and what I think is really worth pointing out, is that ICE has not been terribly discerning about the legal status of the people that they’ve gone after.

And there have been people who are perfectly documented, and people who are American citizens, who have either had encounters with ICE, or who have changed their lifestyle patterns to avoid having encounters with ICE.

Sargent: So in the interview, Trump also said he’s open to working with Democrats on immigration, which, again, is not going to happen, given Stephen Miller’s role. We’ll come back to that. But MAGA figures raged about this. I’m going to read a few.

One leading MAGA guy, Steve Cortes, said, “If President Trump softens on immigration enforcement, it will be a disaster.” MAGA influencer Nick Sortor went absolutely nuts, raging in all caps: “WITHOUT DEPORTATIONS, OUR COUNTRY IS GONE. PERIOD.” Still another MAGA guy, Joey Mannarino, posted: “If Trump does this, I’m done.”

Now, Trump won’t do it, but these MAGA figures are not wrong, in the sense that he admitted to something that’s anathema to them, i.e., that immigrants are good for America, right?

Azari: Yeah, I think that’s right. So I think there’s kind of two things, again, happening here. And one is, this is the danger of operating in polarized politics, is that you have this kind of unsavory choice between the politics—which is, a lot of your supporters are going to want you to demonize the other side—and the policy, which is, you’re probably going to have to work across party lines.

And I think that’s a problem that affects basically everybody in American politics. But I think it affects MAGA in particular, because kind of all they have is juicing up the base with grievance. That’s really an important foundation of the movement.

And so when you can’t do that, what are you left with? You’re left with a bunch of, you know, as you said, kind of angry online people who are very publicly breaking with you. And that’s, in a lot of ways, Trump’s political base.

Sargent: I think what you’re getting at is that MAGA, to an unusually dramatic degree, is all about enemy politics, right? And so whenever Trump is not demonizing the enemy, which he does very well and very frequently and very viciously—whenever he’s not doing that, it’s a big letdown to MAGA, right?

Azari: Yeah, exactly. There sort of is no MAGA without that. Like, Republicans, non-MAGA Republicans, and Democrats also are incentivized to demonize the other side, but there are other things going on in those politics.

Sargent: Yeah, absolutely. So this also breaks with JD Vance in an interesting way. In Vance’s now kind of infamous tweet blaming Trump’s war for the bloodbath, Vance also said he’s open to the idea of changing immigration enforcement.

Now, people have treated that as this big concession, but it just isn’t a concession, because Vance also said that the GOP absolutely cannot respond to this loss with, quote-unquote, amnesty. Vance won’t even entertain the idea that voters might have turned against the deeper ideological goal of ridding the country of immigrants. Yet Trump kind of said it.

Julia, I want to ask you this. I really wonder if this is going to become a real schism inside the GOP, because there’s still plenty of Republicans hanging around who would like to see immigration reform, even though they’ve been a lot quieter in the Trump years. And I wonder if a few of them start to step forward. In fact, we just saw one House member go quite forcefully in that direction. What do you think?

Azari: After I heard Vance’s comments initially, my prediction was that what we would see is a coalition that, instead of actually having it out over kind of core issues, tries to isolate the president. And I think this kind of happens when presidents are in their last two years and they’ve had a bad midterm.

And you kind of saw it with George W. Bush, right? It really becomes about the president and not about the broader political movement. And so, well, this is the person whose fault this is.

Sargent: Can you explain what you mean a little bit by isolate the president? So Vance is taking steps right now to sort of subtly push Trump into his own camp, kind of?

Azari: I think so, yeah. And really to blame bad things that have happened on things that you kind of pin on Trump specifically. So, you know, the decision to go to war in Iran, decisions that he’s made about immigration enforcement—and kind of say, well, these were specific Trump things. They weren’t about the broader kind of MAGA or populist ideology, or whatever it is that they’re going to want to maybe call it later on.

Sargent: It is really interesting. Let’s bring in Stephen Miller’s role here for a second. The New York Times reported something that I thought was of interest. I’m just going to read it, speaking about Miller here: “His top priority, aides said, is rebuilding the fractured MAGA coalition and pursuing policies that will energize the voters who elected Mr. Trump in 2024.” That’s by way of explaining Miller’s desire to continue with a hard-line agenda.

Julia, it seems like there’s, like, a core contradiction here that’s worth drawing out. Like, on the one hand, what Miller is saying is that what went wrong is that the MAGA coalition fell apart. On the other hand, he’s also saying hardcore MAGA voters need to be energized.

But those two things are, like, in contradiction with each other, because it’s the hard-line policies that fractured the MAGA coalition. Yet Miller wants to now double down on the violent white nationalism to energize those very core voters. I just don’t see the way forward for MAGA if that’s their fundamental understanding of the situation. Do you?

Azari: Yeah, I think there’s sort of a version of this, again, that’s kind of typical in American politics, which is that you have to make this trade-off between energizing your core voters and building a broader coalition. But I think this tension really has animated the Trump project from the beginning. And it’s always been a pretty narrow project.

And so if we’d been having this conversation eight years ago, I would say, well, what we’ve seen is, this is a president who lost the popular vote, and blah, blah, blah. But in 2024, there was, like, this glimmer of a broader Trump coalition. This more multiracial—it was more voters.

And so I think there was sort of, like, this glimmer of that. And I think nobody—not Stephen Miller, not people on podcasts, not Democrats—actually has, like, a clear picture of what that coalition was and kind of where it went.

Sargent: Right.

Azari: Yeah. I think it’s really complicated. But yeah, I mean, I think that’s sort of what Miller’s laying out. And he’s basically saying what you would expect anybody to say after a really bad midterm. But it’s interesting, because the merging of chief of staff and top political adviser, that’s a very complicated merging of roles. I have a lot of thoughts about that.

Sargent: Well, it just strikes me that if you’re going to respond to this election loss by doubling down on the violent white nationalism, you’re just never going to get back to anything close to the coalition that they got in 2024. And I don’t claim to understand that coalition. It is complicated.

I think maybe it’s an anti-inflation coalition, and kind of an anti-incumbent coalition to some degree, and a lot of young people who felt really, really, really disoriented by the upheavals of the post-Covid trauma and stuff. B

ut it just seems to me that Miller is such an ideologue that he is going to claim he wants to rebuild this coalition, but he doesn’t actually give a shit about that. He really just wants to make the country whiter. That’s what he wants, you know?

Azari: Yeah, I mean, everything about his background illustrates that. I mean, just to speak to just observable facts, right? He has no background in kind of building a national coalition. He’s not the architect of any kind of Trumpist 50-state strategy. He’s the immigration guy. He’s the homeland security guy.

And he’s been very clear on his take and his viewpoints. And when you combine that with an administration that can’t run again anyway, I mean, what is he even talking about?

Sargent: I guess the bottom line, though, is that, judging by this MAGA fury at this tiny little admission by Trump, you can really not see Vance get through a primary by moderating in any sense, I don’t think, can you?

Azari: No, I think that’s probably right. And I think that the safest prediction about what the 2028 primary will look like will be a situation in which candidates are really pressured to throw red meat to the base. I don’t know if we still use that terminology. This is, like, Bush-era terminology. But I think that that will be the set of pressures in that primary campaign.

And then when those pressures are really strong in a primary, then there are a lot of questions about whether that can be adaptable to a general election electorate. And that’s what Vance or Rubio or Ron DeSantis, or whoever is going to pursue that nomination in 2028, is probably going to face, some version of that dilemma.

Sargent: And Democrats have an opportunity to really torment Vance by just driving this wedge very deep, by pushing, I don’t know, for example, legislation creating new legal pathways for undocumented workers and stuff.

Sort of saying, well, the president said that these undocumented workers are good workers and good people. Well, does Vance not agree? And that could essentially force both Trump and Vance into some very uncomfortable positions, it seems, no?

Azari: Yeah, I think so. And those types of things that you’re talking about are quite popular and poll quite well. People generally support folks who’ve been living here having a path to legalization. But one thing Vance won’t have to do is cast the fifty-first vote in the Senate, so he’s off the hook for that.

Sargent: That is a very smart observation, and many of your observations today were. Folks, if you want to follow Julia Azari, go to Good Politics/Bad Politics on Substack. Julia, thanks so much for coming on.

Azari: Thank you so much for having me.

items.title: Leftists Weren’t the Only Ones Who Moderated In the Midterms
items.content_text:
In the week since Democrats won their most commanding victory in recent memory, the party’s so-called “moderates” have been eager to claim victory for their faction. Despite firebrand progressives winning Senate seats by healthy margins in states like Michigan and Minnesota, an adviser for the centrist think tank Third Way told the Financial Times that the “majority-makers were mainstream and centre-left Democrats.” The empirical argument here is that moderate candidates were both more numerous and overperformed their progressive counterparts who also won. Third Way likewise credits Democrats’ commanding battleground and red state margins to candidates’ willingness to recant more traditionally progressive positions on issues like immigration and energy. But what does it actually mean to be a moderate, and to moderate one’s views? And why does that responsibility only ever seem to fall on progressives?

Given that most campaign pledges and talking points tend to be pretty watery, pundits of all political stripes can fish around in Tuesday’s results for something to flatter their faction. Texas Senator-elect James Talarico said in September that he would support a national ban on gender-affirming care for minors, and supported an “all of the above” energy platform embracing oil and gas as well as wind, solar, and geothermal. Meanwhile, his victory speech would have been at home in a Bernie Sanders campaign stop; he called for universal health care and to “unrig this economic system that only benefits the top one percent.” The most online members of various camps within the Democratic coalition have spent the last week volleying these data points back and forth at one another, attempting to claim Tuesday’s massive victory as evidence of their own strategic brilliance.

This all feels a bit silly. For starters, Democrats won enough for everyone to have something to celebrate. Democratic Socialists won well beyond New York City’s so-called “Commie corridor.” DSA has sent six new representatives to the House, and elected its members as mayors in Washington D.C. and Los Angeles. But most candidates who won were not DSA members or endorsed by DSA chapters. Many took up positions that progressives generally oppose, while also bashing billionaires and Big Tech. The vast majority of voters, moreover, were not voting for one faction or another because most people don’t possess coherent political ideologies. These intraparty debates matter mostly insofar as they shape how Democrats will use their congressional majority, and—relatedly—whether they can convince voters to keep voting for Democrats in 2028. As moderate centrists make the case that moderate centrists won, they’re accordingly arguing that Democrats should govern as moderate centrists.

Vibes-based assessments of who counts as a moderate, however—and what it means to “moderate”—feel relatively divorced from the material factors that determine how politicians campaign and govern once they win. Although much of the discourse around Tuesday’s results has focused on how candidates “moderated” certain traditionally left-wing positions in order to win, there’s a case to be made that centrists walking back their own unpopular stances made just as big of a difference.

On one critical issue—U.S. support for Israel—Democrats have moderated enormously over the last two years. The party wouldn’t even agree to let a Palestinian state representative from Georgia address the Democratic National Convention in 2024.
